questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom — it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix — it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length — anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'
commonMistakes: Treats retry logic as the fix instead of eliminating the cause
Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains deadlock mechanics and victim selection
Identifies root-cause patterns (access order, long transactions, lock escalation)
Proposes durable architectural fixes, not just retry logic
Addresses tradeoffs of snapshot isolation or other mitigations

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options — read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK — and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness — I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs — the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive — a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom — reports and order entry fighting over row locks — I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free — it adds load to tempdb's version store — but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation — that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends NOLOCK as a general-purpose fix without flagging dirty-read risk
Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports
keyPoints: Explains why READ COMMITTED causes reader/writer blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and correctly rejects it for anything requiring correctness
Explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism and its tempdb cost
Recommends a readable secondary/replica as the durable architecture for resource isolation
Distinguishes lock contention from compute contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the locking behavior causing the blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and its risks accurately
Explains RCSI/snapshot isolation mechanism and cost
Recommends and justifies an appropriate architecture (replica vs RCSI)

questions.title: A Stored Procedure Is Recompiling Constantly Under Load
questions.prompt: A heavily-used stored procedure builds a large intermediate result set using a table variable, then joins it twice more inside the same procedure. Under load, you're seeing wildly inconsistent execution times and plan cache bloat. Diagnose why the table variable choice is likely the architectural root cause at this scale, and rewrite the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Table variables historically carry no real statistics — on many compatibility levels the optimizer assumes roughly one row regardless of actual size — so when the intermediate set is genuinely large, the optimizer builds a plan sized for one row: an undersized memory grant and a join strategy that's wrong for the real row count. The inconsistent timing comes from actual row counts varying run to run while the cached plan was compiled against that wrong, fixed assumption, so some executions get lucky and others spill to disk or pick a bad join type. A #temp table, by contrast, gets real statistics maintained by SQL Server, letting the optimizer size the plan for the two downstream joins accurately. The tradeoff: a significant change in a temp table's row count can trigger a recompile — but that's a feature here, not a bug, since it means the plan adapts to actual data instead of staying wrong. The fix is to replace the DECLARE @T TABLE with a CREATE TABLE #T, optionally indexed if the joins warrant it, keeping the rest of the procedure's logic unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening here is that the optimizer doesn't have real numbers to work with. A table variable, on most compatibility levels, gets treated as roughly one row no matter how big it actually gets, so the plan built for it is sized for the wrong workload — that's exactly why the timing is inconsistent: the actual row count varies, but the plan doesn't adapt. My fix is to swap it for a #temp table, because SQL Server maintains real statistics on those, so the two downstream joins get a plan that's actually shaped for the data. I'll be upfront that this trades one problem for a different, much smaller one — a temp table can trigger a recompile when its row count shifts significantly — but I'd rather have an occasional recompile that produces a correct plan than a stable plan that's confidently wrong every time.
questions.example:
-- Before: table variable, optimizer assumes ~1 row
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @ActiveOrders TABLE (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    INSERT INTO @ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM @ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

-- After: temp table, real statistics, optionally indexed
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    CREATE TABLE #ActiveOrders (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    CREATE INDEX IX_ActiveOrders_CustomerID ON #ActiveOrders (CustomerID);

    INSERT INTO #ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM #ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO
commonMistakes: Treats 'table variables are always faster' as a universal rule
Doesn't connect inconsistent timing to missing statistics on a large table variable
Recommends a CTE instead, missing that a CTE is re-evaluated/inlined and doesn't solve the cardinality problem either
Adds an index to the table variable via inline constraint without recognizing its limits
Ignores the recompile tradeoff when switching to a temp table
keyPoints: Explains the statistics difference between table variables and temp tables
Connects missing statistics to bad cardinality estimation and inconsistent plans at scale
Chooses #temp table over table variable or CTE for this specific large, multiply-joined scenario
Provides a correct before/after rewrite
Acknowledges the recompile tradeoff as acceptable here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing statistics as the root cause
Chooses the right replacement structure with justification
Provides correct, working SQL example
Acknowledges tradeoffs (recompilation) honestly

questions.title: Parameter Sniffing: One Cached Plan, Two Very Different Row Counts
questions.prompt: A stored procedure filters orders by @CustomerID. For a customer with a handful of orders it returns in milliseconds; for your biggest customer with several million rows, the exact same procedure call times out. Nothing about the query changed. Explain what's actually happening at the plan-cache level, and lay out the durable fixes you'd choose between, including the tradeoffs of each.
questions.modelAnswer: This is parameter sniffing: when a stored procedure compiles, SQL Server peeks at the actual parameter value supplied on that first call and builds one cached execution plan optimized for that value's estimated row count, then reuses that same plan for every subsequent call regardless of what parameter comes in next. If the plan was compiled against a small customer, the optimizer chose a plan shaped for a small result set — likely nested loops with a lookup — and that same plan is catastrophic against a customer with millions of rows, where a hash or merge join with a full scan would have been far cheaper. The symptom isn't random; it's entirely a function of which value happened to compile the plan, which is why it looks like it 'used to work.' Durable fixes, in order of how I'd actually choose: (1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) on the statement forces a fresh, value-specific plan on every execution — correct for every call, but pays the compilation cost every single time, which is wasteful for a high-frequency procedure; (2) OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR @CustomerID UNKNOWN) tells the optimizer to use the average-distribution estimate instead of sniffing any single value, which avoids the worst-case outlier plan but may make the common case slightly less optimal; (3) WITH RECOMPILE at the procedure level has the same cost profile as per-statement recompile but applies to the whole procedure; (4) query store plan forcing lets you pin a known-good plan once you've identified one that performs acceptably across the real distribution of parameter values, which is a strong operational fix but needs monitoring since data growth can eventually make the forced plan wrong too; (5) splitting the procedure into two paths (a small-customer branch and a large-customer branch, chosen by an IF before the query even runs) avoids a single plan ever having to serve both distributions, at the cost of more code to maintain. I'd pick based on call frequency and skew: for a rarely-called heavy procedure, RECOMPILE is cheap enough; for a hot-path procedure called thousands of times a minute, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN or query store plan forcing is usually the right call, because paying a full recompile on every call would itself become the bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the same way I'd explain it to the team that paged me: the procedure didn't change, the data behind one parameter value did, and the plan cache is still serving a plan that was shaped for a tiny customer. SQL Server only looks at the parameter value once, on the first compile, and then it's locked in until something invalidates that plan. So the fix isn't 'optimize the query' — the query's fine — it's deciding how we want the optimizer to handle that skew going forward. For something called rarely, I'd just slap OPTION (RECOMPILE) on it and move on, because paying for a fresh plan every call is cheap compared to how rarely it runs. For something hot, I don't want to recompile constantly, so I'd reach for OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN first, which tells the optimizer to plan for the average case instead of gambling on whichever value shows up first — and if I need something more surgical, I'll go find a known-good plan and force it through Query Store, which I'll then keep an eye on, because a forced plan isn't a fix I set once and forget; the data keeps growing underneath it.
commonMistakes: Describes the symptom (it's slow for one customer) without naming the plan-cache mechanism causing it
Jumps straight to adding an index without addressing that a single cached plan is the root cause
Recommends OPTION (RECOMPILE) everywhere without weighing its per-call compilation cost on hot paths
Doesn't mention Query Store plan forcing as an operational option
Treats the fix as permanent without noting that data growth can make a forced or optimized-for plan wrong again later
keyPoints: Correctly explains that one parameter value's estimate shapes the cached plan for all future calls
Distinguishes RECOMPILE (per-call cost, always-correct plan) from OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN (average-case plan, no per-call cost)
Mentions Query Store plan forcing as a monitored, surgical fix
Considers call frequency and data skew when choosing between the options
Notes that any chosen fix needs to be revisited as data distribution changes over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the parameter-sniffing / plan-cache mechanism
Presents multiple durable fixes (RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store forcing, branching)
Weighs the real tradeoffs (per-call cost vs. plan quality) rather than naming one fix blindly
Chooses between fixes based on call frequency / skew, not a one-size-fits-all answer

lessonLink.label: Review: Reading Execution Plans: Scans vs. Seeks

questions.title: Airflow Deferrable Operators: Not Blocking a Worker Slot While Waiting
questions.prompt: A pipeline has a dozen sensor tasks each polling for a file to land, and they're consuming enough worker slots that other, unrelated DAGs are getting delayed. Explain what Airflow's deferrable operators (and the triggerer component) change about how that waiting is handled, and why this is a scaling concern specifically, not a correctness one.
questions.modelAnswer: A traditional sensor in poke mode occupies a worker slot for its entire wait, periodically waking up to check a condition and going back to sleep but never releasing the slot, so twelve long-polling sensors can tie up twelve worker slots for hours even though almost none of that time is spent doing real work. A deferrable operator (built on Airflow's triggerer component) instead suspends itself entirely after an initial check: it hands its wait condition off to a lightweight async trigger running in a separate triggerer process, releases its worker slot completely, and only resumes on a worker when the trigger actually fires (the condition is met or it times out). The triggerer can run many thousands of these async waits concurrently in a single process because they're not blocking threads, just awaited coroutines, so the actual compute and worker-slot cost of 'waiting for a file' drops from 'one slot per sensor for the whole wait' to 'near zero, until the moment work is ready to resume.' This is a scaling and cost concern, not a correctness one — a poke-mode sensor and its deferrable equivalent both correctly detect the condition and both eventually succeed or time out; the difference is entirely in how much of your worker capacity (and therefore how many unrelated DAGs can run concurrently) gets consumed while nothing is actually happening.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with an analogy: a regular sensor is like twelve people standing in line holding a parking spot each, even though they're just waiting for a text message — a deferrable sensor is twelve people who leave and get a text when it's time to come back, freeing the spot in the meantime. The fix here isn't a correctness fix, nobody's pipeline is wrong — it's that we're burning worker capacity on waiting instead of working, which is exactly what's delaying the unrelated DAGs. I'd convert the file sensors to their deferrable equivalents (or a deferrable custom trigger if there isn't a built-in one for this exact file source), make sure the triggerer component is actually running and sized for the number of concurrent defers we'll have, and then show the before/after on worker slot utilization so it's clear this was a capacity problem, not a bug.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a bug in the sensors rather than a worker-slot capacity/scaling issue
Doesn't explain that the triggerer runs waits as async coroutines rather than blocking worker processes
Assumes deferrable operators change correctness or detection logic rather than just resource consumption during the wait
Forgets that the triggerer component itself needs to be running and appropriately sized
keyPoints: Explains poke-mode sensors occupying a full worker slot for the entire wait
Explains deferrable operators suspending to the triggerer and releasing the worker slot
Notes the triggerer runs many async waits concurrently in one process
Frames this correctly as a scaling/capacity issue, not a correctness issue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains poke-mode sensor worker-slot consumption
Correctly explains deferrable operators and the triggerer mechanism
Correctly frames this as scaling/cost, not correctness
Clear practical remediation (convert sensors, size the triggerer)

questions.title: Dynamic DAG Generation: Power and Its Scheduler Cost
questions.prompt: A platform team wants to generate one Airflow DAG per client (currently 40 clients, growing) from a single Python template rather than hand-writing 40 near-identical DAG files. Explain how dynamic DAG generation actually works in Airflow, and the real operational cost it introduces at the scheduler level that a hand-written-DAG approach doesn't have.
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic DAG generation means a single Python file (or a small set of files) programmatically constructs multiple DAG objects at parse time — typically by looping over a config source (a list in code, a database table, variables, or a config file) and calling a DAG-building function once per item, registering each resulting DAG object in the module's global namespace so Airflow's DAG file processor picks each one up as a distinct DAG. This is genuinely powerful for the 40-clients case: adding client 41 becomes a config change instead of a new file and a PR. The real cost is that Airflow's scheduler re-parses every DAG file on a recurring interval (min_file_process_interval) to detect new DAGs or changes, and if the config source for a dynamically generated set is slow to read (e.g., a live database query run at parse time rather than a cached/local file) or if the generation logic itself is computationally heavy, that parse cost is paid repeatedly, on every scheduler loop, for every one of those 40+ generated DAGs — which can measurably slow down the entire scheduler, not just the DAGs in question, because DAG parsing is a shared bottleneck resource. The standard mitigation is keeping the config source for generation fast and local (a cached file, not a live query) and keeping generation logic itself lightweight, since it runs on every parse, not once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team: yes, do it, but the thing that will bite us later isn't the DAG logic, it's where the 40 configs come from at parse time. If that's a live call to a database or an external API inside the DAG file, we've just made the scheduler's parsing loop dependent on that system's latency, multiplied by every parse interval, for every client — and that's the kind of thing that silently degrades the whole scheduler's health months after it ships, not something that fails loudly on day one. My recommendation is always: read the config from something fast and local, keep it out of the hot parse path, and I'd want to see DAG parse duration monitored from day one so if it creeps up as client count grows, we see it before it becomes 'the scheduler is slow and nobody knows why.'
commonMistakes: Describes dynamic DAG generation only at the code level without mentioning the scheduler's repeated re-parsing cost
Doesn't flag that a slow or live config source at parse time is the real risk, not the generation logic itself
Assumes this scales for free just because it reduces file count
Doesn't mention monitoring DAG parse duration as the way to catch this before it becomes a scheduler-wide problem
keyPoints: Explains looping over config to build multiple DAG objects registered in module globals
Explains that the scheduler re-parses DAG files on a recurring interval, not once
Identifies a slow/live config source at parse time as the main operational risk at scale
Recommends keeping generation logic and config source fast and local, with parse duration monitored

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanics of generating multiple DAGs from one file
Correctly explains the scheduler's repeated DAG-parsing cost
Identifies the config-source latency risk specifically
Gives a concrete mitigation (fast local config, parse duration monitoring)

questions.title: Governing Unity Catalog Across a Multi-Workspace, Multi-Business-Unit Metastore
questions.prompt: Your organization runs six Databricks workspaces -- one per business unit (Finance, Marketing, Supply Chain, HR, Engineering, and a shared Data Platform team) -- all attached to a single Unity Catalog metastore in the same region. Finance wants to lock down PII in their customer tables so only their own analysts can see raw SSNs, Supply Chain wants read access to Finance's cost-of-goods tables for a joint forecasting model, and the Data Platform team needs a consistent pattern for onboarding the next business unit without re-deriving governance rules from scratch. Design the catalog/schema structure, access-control model, and a scalable onboarding pattern for this environment.
questions.modelAnswer: A single metastore per region is correct here -- Unity Catalog is designed to be shared across many workspaces, and splitting it per business unit would duplicate governance work and break any cross-BU sharing. The structure should map one catalog per business unit (finance, supply_chain, hr, marketing, engineering) plus a shared catalog (e.g. shared_platform) for common reference/dimension data, with schemas inside each catalog separating raw/bronze from curated/gold layers. Access control is granted at the catalog or schema level using Unity Catalog's standard RBAC: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA grants scope who can even see an object exists, SELECT grants on specific tables or, for the SSN case, on a masked view rather than the raw table. For Finance's PII, the pattern is a dynamic view using CURRENT_USER()/IS_MEMBER() to mask the SSN column for everyone except a finance_pii_readers group, with the underlying raw table's SELECT grant restricted to a narrow service-principal/group -- row/column masking should live in SQL, not in downstream BI tool permissions, since that's the only enforcement point every consumer (notebooks, SQL warehouses, Power BI via Direct Lake) actually respects. For Supply Chain's cross-BU need, grant SELECT on finance.gold.cost_of_goods specifically to a supply_chain_analysts group rather than widening Finance's catalog-level grant, keeping the blast radius to one table. For onboarding, the Data Platform team should maintain this as Terraform/databricks provider code (catalog, schema, grant resources) rather than manual GRANT statements, so a new BU's catalog, standard schemas, and default group grants are created from a reviewed, repeatable module -- not tribal knowledge.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I get asked this, I start by pushing back gently on 'metastore per business unit' if anyone proposes it -- one metastore per region is the whole point of Unity Catalog, and splitting it defeats cross-BU sharing before you've even started. So I'd lay out catalog-per-BU plus one shared catalog for common dimensions, and get agreement on that shape first before touching a single GRANT statement. For the SSN problem specifically, I'd be direct that masking belongs in a SQL view, not in 'we'll just not give Marketing the Power BI workspace' -- because the moment someone connects a notebook directly to the raw table, that control is gone. For the Supply Chain ask, I'd resist the instinct to just grant them the whole Finance catalog because it's 'easier for now' -- one table, one grant, named group, done. And for onboarding, I'd tell the Data Platform team: if the sixth BU took a day of manual GRANTs, the tenth one will take two days and someone will typo a grant -- that's exactly the kind of thing that needs to be a Terraform module from day one, not a runbook.
commonMistakes: Proposes a separate metastore per business unit instead of one shared metastore with catalog-level separation
Masks PII in the BI tool or dashboard layer instead of a SQL-enforced dynamic view
Grants Supply Chain access to Finance's entire catalog instead of the single table they actually need
Treats onboarding as a manual GRANT runbook instead of codifying it as reusable IaC
Forgets USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA grants, so object-level SELECT grants silently fail to expose anything
keyPoints: Recommends one metastore per region, catalog-per-business-unit structure
Uses schema layering (raw/bronze vs curated/gold) within each catalog
Enforces PII masking via SQL dynamic views, not downstream tool permissions
Grants cross-BU access narrowly (table-level) rather than widening catalog grants
Codifies onboarding as IaC (Terraform databricks provider) rather than manual process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes correct catalog/metastore structure
Designs PII masking enforcement correctly
Scopes cross-BU access narrowly and justifies it
Proposes scalable, codified onboarding pattern

questions.title: Enforcing Data Quality Gates Across 40 Concurrent Lakeflow Pipelines
questions.prompt: Your platform team runs roughly 40 Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines feeding a shared gold layer that finance and executive dashboards depend on. Several incidents have occurred where a silently malformed upstream file let bad rows (negative revenue, null customer IDs) flow all the way to a dashboard before anyone noticed. Design a data-quality gating strategy using expectations that would have caught this, and explain the tradeoffs between expect, expect_or_drop, and expect_or_fail at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The three expectation modes differ only in what happens to a violating row, and choosing the right one per rule is the actual design problem here, not writing the SQL predicates. expect records and surfaces violations (visible in the pipeline event log/UI) but takes no corrective action -- appropriate for soft, informational signals a team wants to watch trend over time. expect_or_drop silently excludes violating rows from the output table while still counting and surfacing them in the event log -- appropriate for recoverable, row-level issues where losing a few bad rows doesn't change the meaning of the dataset. expect_or_fail stops the entire pipeline update on any violation -- appropriate for invariants that, if violated, actually corrupt downstream aggregates: a null customer_id breaking a join, or a negative revenue row skewing a sum, are exactly this category, and this incident happened because neither was enforced as a hard gate. The fix: map null customer_id and negative revenue to expect_or_fail at the bronze-to-silver boundary so a bad batch halts before reaching gold rather than silently reaching a dashboard; reserve expect_or_drop for genuinely recoverable issues (a missing but non-critical attribute). At 40-pipeline scale, the operational risk is duplicating these rule definitions independently in every pipeline file, so they should live in one shared Python module of expectation sets imported by every pipeline touching financial data, with violation rates reviewed via the pipeline event log on a recurring cadence rather than only when a dashboard incident forces someone to look.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming what actually went wrong: it wasn't that nobody validated the data, it's that the validation that existed lived in someone's downstream dashboard filter, which is the worst possible place for it, because by the time you're filtering in the dashboard, the bad row has already been written everywhere upstream of that filter too. So I'd walk through the severity ladder -- expect for 'watch it,' expect_or_drop for 'recoverable, quietly handle it,' expect_or_fail for 'this breaks the number, stop the pipeline' -- and map null customer IDs and negative revenue straight to expect_or_fail, because those are the two things from the actual incident. Then I'd make the case that with 40 pipelines, we can't have 40 copies of this logic drifting independently, so this becomes a shared module the moment it's written, not a follow-up task.
commonMistakes: Uses expect_or_drop for every rule regardless of severity, silently losing rows that should have hard-failed the pipeline
Uses expect_or_fail for soft/informational rules, causing unnecessary pipeline outages
Duplicates expectation definitions across 40 pipelines instead of sharing them from a common module
Never reviews the pipeline event log for violation rates, so a slowly rising drop rate goes unnoticed
Treats expectations as a one-time setup rather than something revisited as upstream sources change
keyPoints: Distinguishes expect (warn), expect_or_drop (quarantine), expect_or_fail (hard stop) and when each applies
Maps critical invariants (null customer_id, negative revenue) to expect_or_fail at the bronze/silver boundary
Uses expect_or_drop for recoverable row-level issues with dropped-row visibility
Shares expectation definitions across pipelines instead of duplicating per-pipeline
Monitors violation rates via the pipeline event log, not just pass/fail

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the three expectation modes and when to use each
Maps the actual incident to a concrete fix
Addresses sharing/consistency of rules across 40 pipelines
Proposes ongoing monitoring of violation rates

questions.title: Choosing Triggered vs. Continuous Mode Across a Pipeline Fleet, and Catching Failures Early
questions.prompt: Your team operates a mix of around 40 Lakeflow pipelines: some feed hourly executive dashboards, a few feed a near-real-time fraud-alerting table, and most are overnight batch loads. Right now everything runs in triggered mode on a cron schedule, and last week a fraud-alerting pipeline's upstream source went stale for three hours before anyone noticed because its scheduled run 'succeeded' on zero new rows. Decide which pipelines should move to continuous mode, and design a monitoring approach across the fleet that would catch a 'succeeded but suspiciously empty' failure like this one.
questions.modelAnswer: Triggered mode runs the pipeline once to process whatever's new, then shuts compute down -- cost scales with data volume and run frequency, which is exactly right for hourly dashboards and overnight batch loads where a few minutes of added latency is irrelevant. Continuous mode keeps the pipeline and its compute running permanently, processing data as it lands with minimal latency, but it bills for that compute 24/7 regardless of whether data is flowing -- it should be reserved for the handful of cases where staleness itself has a real cost, which here is specifically the fraud-alerting pipeline, not the dashboards or batch loads. Moving everything to continuous would be a cost mistake, not a resilience improvement. But the actual incident wasn't caused by the pipeline mode at all -- a scheduled run that processes zero new rows still reports 'succeeded,' because success and freshness are different signals, and that gap exists whether the pipeline is triggered or continuous. The real fix is monitoring: use the pipeline event log to track rows processed per run per table, and alert separately when a stream that should always have traffic goes beyond a defined staleness window (e.g., no new rows in 15 minutes for the fraud table) with no new data, distinct from ordinary pipeline failure alerting. That staleness threshold should be set per pipeline based on its actual expected cadence, not a single fleet-wide number, since 15 minutes is alarming for a real-time fraud feed and meaningless for an overnight batch load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team the real bug here isn't the pipeline mode, it's that we were treating 'succeeded' and 'healthy' as the same thing -- a run that processes zero rows when it should have processed thousands is not a success, even though Lakeflow will happily report it as one. So before I talk about continuous mode at all, I'd get freshness-based alerting in place using the pipeline event log, scoped per pipeline since a 15-minute staleness threshold means something very different for the fraud table than for an overnight batch job. Then, separately, I'd move only the fraud-alerting pipeline to continuous mode, and I'd be upfront with finance that this is a real cost tradeoff -- it runs 24/7 whether or not fraud events are actually happening -- which is exactly why I wouldn't extend it to the dashboards or batch jobs where triggered mode is already the right answer.
commonMistakes: Moves most/all pipelines to continuous mode instead of reserving it for genuinely latency-sensitive cases
Doesn't account for continuous mode's always-on compute cost vs triggered mode's pay-only-when-running cost
Equates pipeline success status with data freshness/health, missing the zero-rows-processed case
Builds per-pipeline ad hoc alerting instead of a consistent freshness-SLA check across the fleet
Sets a single staleness threshold for every pipeline regardless of its actual expected cadence

Explains the cost/latency tradeoff between triggered and continuous mode
Identifies that pipeline success status alone doesn't indicate data freshness/health
Designs row-count/freshness-based alerting using the pipeline event log
Proposes fleet-wide monitoring with per-pipeline SLA thresholds, not a single global threshold

questions.title: Cutting a $40K/Month Databricks Compute Bill Without Hurting SLAs
questions.prompt: Finance flags that Databricks compute spend has grown to roughly $40,000/month, and asks you, as the platform lead, to cut it meaningfully within a quarter without missing any existing SLA. A quick audit shows: most nightly ETL jobs run on long-lived all-purpose clusters that stay up all day 'just in case,' autoscaling is disabled almost everywhere, and a few ad hoc analyst notebooks are attached to the same large cluster as production jobs. Walk through where you'd cut first, what you would NOT touch, and how you'd verify savings didn't come at the cost of reliability.
questions.modelAnswer: The highest-impact, lowest-risk cut is moving scheduled ETL jobs off all-purpose clusters onto job clusters: an all-purpose cluster that stays up all day bills continuously regardless of utilization, while a job cluster spins up for the run and terminates on completion, so cost becomes proportional to actual compute time rather than wall-clock uptime -- this is almost always the single biggest lever in an audit like this one. Second, enable autoscaling with min/max bounds informed by historical load (not arbitrary defaults), so clusters stop paying for idle headroom sized for a worst-case that rarely occurs. Third, separate the ad hoc analyst notebooks onto their own interactive cluster with an auto-termination policy (e.g., terminate after 30-60 minutes idle), since sharing a cluster with production jobs means a runaway exploratory query can inflate the sizing production actually needs, or contend with it directly. Spot/preemptible instances are worth evaluating for fault-tolerant batch workloads where a preempted worker just gets replaced and retried, but I would explicitly exclude anything SLA-critical or stateful -- the fraud-alerting continuous pipeline's cluster, for example, should stay on-demand, because preemption risk there is a business risk, not a reliability inconvenience, and correctness/latency guarantees are not the place to shave compute cost. To verify savings are real and not masking a reliability regression, I'd tag every cluster by team/job for cost attribution, compare before/after DBU and cloud spend per workload, and specifically watch SLA-miss rate and job duration for two to three weeks post-change, since a change that looks fine under one week's load might not hold under a spike.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk finance through this as 'there's one obvious lever and three smaller ones, plus a line I won't cross.' The obvious lever: these ETL jobs don't need an all-purpose cluster sitting up all day, they need a job cluster that exists for the run and disappears -- that alone is usually most of the savings in a situation like this. The smaller levers are autoscaling with real bounds instead of none, and getting the analysts off the production cluster so their queries stop driving its sizing. The line I won't cross is the fraud-alerting pipeline's cluster -- I'd tell finance directly that's not a cost-cutting candidate, because a preempted spot instance there isn't an inconvenience, it's a missed fraud alert. And I wouldn't declare victory off one good week -- I'd watch SLA-miss rate for a few weeks before telling anyone the savings are safe.
commonMistakes: Suggests shrinking or spot-pricing a cluster backing an SLA-critical or stateful streaming workload
Treats autoscaling as a free win without setting sensible min/max bounds, causing scale-up thrashing
Doesn't separate ad hoc analyst workloads from production job clusters
Declares savings based on one day of lower cost without watching for SLA regressions over several weeks
Misses that all-purpose-vs-job-cluster billing is usually the single biggest lever available
keyPoints: Identifies all-purpose-vs-job-cluster mismatch as the primary cost driver
Enables autoscaling with bounds informed by historical load, not arbitrary defaults
Isolates ad hoc/analyst workloads from production clusters
Uses spot/preemptible instances selectively, excluding SLA-critical or stateful workloads
Verifies savings against SLA-miss rate over a meaningful window, not a single day

Correctly scopes where autoscaling/spot should and should not be used
Addresses workload isolation (ad hoc vs production)
Proposes a sound verification method against SLA risk

questions.title: Designing Active/Active vs. Active/Passive Kafka Replication Across Two Data Centers
questions.prompt: Your org runs Kafka clusters in two data centers (East and West) for disaster-recovery purposes. The East cluster currently serves all production traffic; West is idle, synced via a MirrorMaker-style replication tool. Leadership wants to know if moving to an active/active setup -- both regions serving writes -- would improve resilience, and what it would actually cost in complexity. Compare active/passive and active/active replication topologies for this scenario and make a recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer: Active/passive -- one cluster authoritative for writes, the other kept in sync via cross-cluster mirroring and promoted to primary only on failover -- is operationally simple: there's a single source of truth, no possibility of write conflicts, and a bounded (if nontrivial) failover story. Its real cost is idle standby capacity and the discipline required to keep offset translation actually tested, not just configured. Active/active, where both clusters accept writes for at least some topics, eliminates the idle-capacity waste and can lower write latency for geographically distributed producers, but introduces genuine complexity: Kafka itself provides no cross-cluster transaction or global ordering guarantee, so topics written in both data centers need either disjoint partitioning (producers in each DC write to DC-specific partitions or topics, avoiding true conflict) or an explicit conflict-resolution strategy at the application layer -- in practice, 'active/active' usually means two independently-written topic sets merged downstream, not one topic accepting genuinely concurrent conflicting writes from both sides. Given that the stated goal here is disaster recovery, not geo-distributed write latency or idle-capacity utilization, I'd recommend staying active/passive and hardening it rather than adding active/active's complexity for a problem it doesn't solve: specifically, verify that the mirroring tool's consumer-offset translation is tested in an actual failover drill, not just configured (replicated offsets don't automatically mean a consumer resumes at the right position), and establish a documented RPO and RTO measured during that drill rather than assumed from the fact that replication is 'running.' Moving to active/active would add significant engineering cost without addressing the DR goal, unless there's a separate latency or capacity driver that hasn't been stated.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I compare anything, I'd ask leadership what problem active/active is actually supposed to solve, because if the answer is still 'disaster recovery,' active/active doesn't get us anything active/passive doesn't already provide -- it just adds complexity we don't need. I'd walk through why: active/active sounds like more resilience, but Kafka doesn't give you cross-cluster write ordering or conflict resolution for free, so in practice you end up with two separately-written streams that need merging downstream, which is real engineering work, not a configuration flag. What I'd actually push for is hardening what we have -- specifically, running a real failover drill to see whether our consumer offset translation actually works, because 'replication is configured' and 'failover works' are two different claims, and right now we've only verified the first one.
commonMistakes: Recommends active/active without identifying any actual latency/capacity driver, just for 'resilience'
Assumes mirrored consumer offsets are automatically correct on failover without testing
Treats active/active as 'both clusters accept all writes freely' without addressing conflict/ordering
Doesn't define or measure RPO/RTO before declaring either topology adequate
Ignores the real engineering cost of active/active for a goal (DR) that active/passive already serves
keyPoints: Explains active/passive and active/active topologies accurately, including offset translation challenges
Correctly identifies that true active/active requires conflict resolution or partition-level write isolation
Matches the recommendation to the actual stated goal (DR) rather than defaulting to the trendier option
Proposes a concrete RPO/RTO measurement via failover drill as the real improvement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains both replication topologies and their tradeoffs
Correctly identifies the complexity cost of active/active (conflict/ordering)
Makes a recommendation matched to the actual stated goal
Proposes concrete RPO/RTO validation via failover testing

questions.title: Preventing a Breaking Schema Change From Taking Down Six Downstream Consumers
questions.prompt: Twelve teams produce and consume events through a shared Confluent Schema Registry. Last month, a producer team renamed a field in their Avro schema without realizing six other teams' consumers depended on it, breaking all of them simultaneously in production. As the platform team, design a schema governance model -- compatibility modes, review process, and tooling -- that prevents this from recurring without making every team file a ticket for every change.
questions.modelAnswer: Set the registry's compatibility mode to BACKWARD at the subject level (or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE for subjects with many historical consumer versions still in flight), so the registry itself rejects a schema registration that isn't compatible with the prior version -- a straight field rename is exactly the kind of change BACKWARD compatibility catches and blocks, because to a consumer, an old field disappearing and a new one appearing looks identical to a deletion plus an addition, which breaks any consumer still reading the old field name. This moves the check from 'someone remembers to look' to 'the registry enforces it automatically at registration time,' which is the actual fix -- no amount of process compensates for an enforcement gap like the one that caused this incident. For the producer team's underlying need (they wanted a clearer field name), the safe evolution pattern is additive: add the new field alongside the old one, mark the old one deprecated, migrate consumers over an announced window, and only remove the old field after confirmed migration -- never a rename as a single atomic operation. To avoid a ticket-per-change burden, enforcement should live in CI, not human review: a producer's CI pipeline calls the registry's compatibility-check endpoint against the candidate schema before merge, so compatible, additive changes sail through with zero human gatekeeping, and only an actually-incompatible change fails the build with a clear message -- which is also the right moment for a human conversation to happen. A lightweight ownership model, where each subject is owned by a team and consumers register their dependency on a subject, lets a producer query who's actually affected before proposing a change, rather than discovering it in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real lesson from this incident isn't 'be more careful' -- it's that we were relying on a human remembering something the registry could have enforced automatically. So the first thing I'd do is set BACKWARD compatibility on the subject and show the team that this exact rename would now be rejected at registration time, full stop, no process required. Then I'd address what the producer team actually wanted, which is a clearer field name -- I'd walk them through add-new-field, deprecate-old-field, migrate, remove, instead of a rename, because that gets them the outcome without the breaking change. And I'd be clear that none of this should mean more tickets -- it should mean the compatibility check runs in their CI pipeline automatically, so the only time a human needs to get involved is when something is genuinely incompatible, which is exactly when you'd want a conversation anyway.
commonMistakes: Proposes a manual change-review process instead of registry-enforced compatibility checking
Doesn't recognize a field rename as equivalent to delete+add from a consumer's perspective
Sets compatibility mode too loosely (NONE or FORWARD) when BACKWARD is what actually protects existing consumers
Requires a ticket/approval for every schema change instead of gating via automated CI compatibility checks
Has no mechanism for producers to know who consumes a given subject before making a change
keyPoints: Sets BACKWARD (or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE) compatibility mode to make the registry reject breaking changes automatically
Correctly identifies a field rename as a breaking change under backward compatibility
Proposes additive-then-deprecate-then-remove as the safe evolution pattern instead of atomic renames
Gates schema changes via CI compatibility checks rather than manual ticket-based review
Maintains consumer/subject ownership visibility so impact can be assessed before a change ships

Correctly identifies why a rename is a breaking change

questions.title: One Metastore or Many? Designing Unity Catalog for a Global Enterprise
questions.prompt: A company operating in the US and EU wants a single Unity Catalog governance model. Explain how the metastore-to-workspace relationship actually works in Unity Catalog, why a metastore is region-bound, and how you'd design the catalog/metastore topology so EU personal data never crosses into a US-managed metastore while still giving global teams one consistent governance model to administer.
questions.modelAnswer: A Unity Catalog metastore is the top-level container for metadata (catalogs, schemas, tables, grants, audit logs) and is created in a specific cloud region; it can be attached to multiple workspaces, but a workspace can only be attached to exactly one metastore at a time, and a metastore cannot span regions. That region-binding is the whole constraint: if EU data must never leave the EU, you cannot satisfy that with one metastore, because the metastore's underlying storage and catalog metadata live in one region. The correct design is one metastore per compliance boundary — a US metastore and an EU metastore — each attached to the workspaces that operate in that region, with the catalogs and managed storage locations underneath scoped to stay inside that boundary. 'One consistent governance model' then doesn't mean one metastore; it means standardizing everything one layer up: identical catalog/schema naming conventions, the same group-based (not user-based) grant patterns replicated into both metastores via infrastructure-as-code (Terraform), the same tagging and classification taxonomy, and centralized audit log aggregation (via system tables or exported audit logs) into one monitoring/governance dashboard so administrators get a single pane of glass even though the enforcement boundary is two separate metastores. Delta Sharing is the mechanism for the rare case where a specific, explicitly-approved dataset needs to cross from one region's metastore to the other without replicating raw storage access.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the premise gently: you can't have one metastore do this, because a metastore is pinned to a region and that's actually a feature here, not a limitation. So I'd propose two metastores — one US, one EU — each the enforcement boundary for its region's workspaces. Then I'd put the 'one consistent governance model' promise into the layer above the metastore: the same catalog naming standard, the same group-based grant templates checked into Terraform and applied to both, the same data classification tags, and a single audit dashboard that pulls system-table data from both metastores so compliance and security see one picture. If a specific EU dataset genuinely needs to be visible to a US team — say, a global rollup — I'd use Delta Sharing for that one dataset under an explicit approval, rather than trying to merge the metastores, because that keeps the regional boundary intact for everything else and makes the one exception auditable on its own.
commonMistakes: Assumes Unity Catalog metastores can span regions if configured correctly
Tries to solve a data-residency requirement with grants alone instead of metastore topology
Confuses 'one workspace per metastore' limit with 'one metastore per workspace' — a metastore can serve many workspaces
Overlooks that managed table storage location is also region-bound, not just the metadata
keyPoints: Explains the metastore-to-workspace relationship correctly (many workspaces, one metastore each)
Identifies that a metastore is region-bound and cannot span compliance boundaries
Proposes a metastore-per-region topology rather than forcing one global metastore
Describes how to standardize governance (naming, grants-as-code, tagging, audit aggregation) across the separate metastores
Uses Delta Sharing as the controlled exception for cross-boundary data needs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains metastore/workspace/region relationship
Proposes a compliant multi-metastore topology

questions.title: Delta Sharing Without Copying Data: How It Actually Works
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why Delta Sharing is better than just exporting a nightly CSV extract to a partner's S3 bucket. Explain the Delta Sharing protocol at a mechanical level — what a share, a recipient, and a sharing server actually are, how a recipient reads data without Databricks, and why no data is copied at share-creation time.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta Sharing is an open protocol, not a file copy: a 'share' is a named, versioned collection of tables (or partitions of tables) that a data provider grants a 'recipient' read access to; nothing is duplicated when the share is created — the share is just metadata pointing at the existing Delta tables and their transaction logs. When a recipient queries the share, their client (which can be Databricks, but also pandas, Spark, PowerBI, or any Delta Sharing connector) calls the Delta Sharing REST protocol against a sharing server, which authenticates the recipient (via a bearer token for open sharing, or Unity-Catalog-to-Unity-Catalog identity federation for Databricks-to-Databricks sharing), checks the grant, and returns short-lived, pre-signed cloud storage URLs scoped to exactly the Parquet files the recipient is entitled to for that query — not the whole table, and not a copy. The recipient's engine then reads those files directly from cloud storage. Because the protocol hands out live pointers into the provider's existing storage rather than a snapshot, the recipient always sees current data as of the share's latest committed version, and the provider never has to run, schedule, or monitor an export job, which is exactly the operational burden a nightly CSV-to-S3 pipeline carries. The tradeoff to be upfront about: the provider's storage must stay reachable and performant for the recipient's query patterns, and very fine-grained row/column security on the shared table needs to be enforced via a view-based share rather than assumed away.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it mechanically because the 'no copy' claim sounds too good until you see why it's true. A share is just a pointer — metadata saying 'recipient X can read these tables as of this version' — so creating it costs nothing in storage. When the partner actually queries, their tool talks to a sharing server over a simple REST protocol, the server checks the grant and hands back temporary, scoped URLs into our actual cloud storage, and their engine reads the Parquet files directly. No export job ran, nothing was duplicated, and they're seeing current data, not last night's snapshot. I'd contrast that directly with the CSV-to-S3 approach: that's a pipeline we own, schedule, monitor, and re-run when it fails, exporting a copy that's stale the moment it lands and that we now have to secure separately in their bucket. The one thing I wouldn't oversell is security — if we need row-level restrictions for this partner, we share a view, not the raw table, same as we would internally.

Doesn't know the recipient can use a non-Databricks client
Misses that credentials/URLs returned are short-lived and scoped per query, not a standing access key
Fails to mention that fine-grained security still requires sharing a view, not just the raw table

Explains the sharing-server protocol: authenticate recipient, check grant, return scoped pre-signed URLs

questions.title: Row Filters and Column Masks: How Unity Catalog Enforces Fine-Grained Access
questions.prompt: Two analysts query the same Unity Catalog table with the same SELECT * statement and get different results — one sees every row and every column in plaintext, the other sees a subset of rows and a masked SSN column. Explain the two Unity Catalog mechanisms that make this possible, what they're implemented as under the hood, and the performance implication of using them versus separate physical tables per audience.
questions.modelAnswer: Unity Catalog implements this through row filters and column masks, both of which are SQL user-defined functions registered against the table rather than separate copies of the data. A row filter is a function that takes column values as input and returns a boolean; Unity Catalog applies it as an implicit WHERE clause on every query against the table, and it commonly branches on is_account_group_member() so members of a restricted group see all rows while everyone else only sees rows matching a predicate (e.g., their own region). A column mask is a function applied to a specific column's value at read time — for example, returning the real SSN to members of a 'pii-readers' group and a redacted or hashed value to everyone else — and it's attached with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK. Because both are enforced centrally at the table definition rather than in each query or each BI tool, the same SELECT * returns different, correctly-scoped results to different callers without any application-level filtering logic, and the policy can't be bypassed by querying a different tool. The performance implication: masks and filters execute as part of the query plan on every read, so a complex filter function adds CPU cost per query compared to a separate pre-filtered physical table, but that cost is almost always worth it against the alternative, which is maintaining N physical copies of the same table (one per audience) that drift out of sync and multiply storage and refresh cost. Row filters and column masks keep one physical copy as the single source of truth.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as 'the same table, different lenses' — Unity Catalog doesn't store two versions of the data, it attaches functions to the table that run on every query. A row filter is a boolean function that gets quietly ANDed into the WHERE clause based on who's asking, usually checking group membership. A column mask is similar but swaps out a column's value — real SSN for one group, masked for everyone else — and it's set with an ALTER TABLE statement, not a view. The reason this matters operationally is that it's enforced once, centrally, so it doesn't matter if someone queries from a notebook, a BI tool, or a JDBC connection — they can't route around it. On performance, yes, there's a small per-query cost to evaluating the function, but I'd push back hard on 'just make two tables instead' — that trades a small CPU cost for an ongoing synchronization problem and a second thing that can silently drift from the source of truth.

Doesn't know they're implemented as SQL functions attached via ALTER TABLE
Misses that the policy is enforced centrally regardless of query tool, which is the actual security benefit
Dismisses the physical-table-per-audience alternative without naming its real cost (storage, drift, refresh overhead)

Explains both are SQL functions attached to the table definition
Explains row filters act as an implicit WHERE clause based on caller identity/group

questions.title: Directory Listing vs. File Notification Mode: Auto Loader at Massive Scale
questions.prompt: Explain the two Auto Loader source-discovery modes — directory listing and file notification — at a mechanical level, and justify which one you'd choose for a source landing hundreds of thousands of small files per hour across a deep, unevenly-populated partition tree.
questions.modelAnswer: In directory listing mode, Auto Loader incrementally lists the target cloud storage path on each trigger, tracks which files it has already processed in its own RocksDB-backed checkpoint state, and picks up only the new ones; it requires no cloud-side configuration, but its cost and latency scale with how expensive 'list this path' is, which gets worse as the file count and partition depth grow, because a full incremental listing still has to traverse the directory structure. In file notification mode, Auto Loader instead sets up cloud-native event notifications — an S3 event -> SQS queue, or an equivalent Event Grid/Pub-Sub setup on Azure/GCP — so the moment a file lands, a message is pushed into a queue, and Auto Loader simply drains that queue instead of listing anything. For hundreds of thousands of small files per hour over a deep, unevenly-populated tree, directory listing becomes the bottleneck: listing cost and latency are driven by directory structure, not by how many files actually changed, so a deep tree with sparse partitions means a lot of wasted listing work for very few new files. File notification mode decouples discovery cost from directory shape entirely — the queue only contains messages for files that actually arrived — so it's the right choice here despite requiring extra cloud infrastructure (an event source and a queue) and the operational responsibility of monitoring that queue's health and dead-letter behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the choice around what each mode's cost actually scales with. Directory listing is simple — no setup, it just lists the path and diffs against checkpoint state — but that listing cost tracks the shape of the directory tree, not the actual arrival rate, so a deep, sparse, high-file-count tree makes every trigger expensive even when almost nothing changed. File notification mode flips that: cloud storage pushes an event straight to a queue the moment a file lands, so Auto Loader's job becomes 'drain the queue,' which is cheap and fast regardless of how deep or sparse the tree is. For this workload specifically — huge file counts, uneven partitions — I'd go file notification every time, and I'd be upfront that it's not free: you're now standing up and owning an event pipeline (SQS or the Azure/GCP equivalent), and you need to watch queue depth and dead-letter messages, not just the streaming job itself.

Forgets that both modes still rely on Auto Loader's own checkpoint state to avoid reprocessing

questions.title: What an 'Expectation' Actually Does in a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline
questions.prompt: Explain the three expectation enforcement actions available in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines — warn, drop, and fail — what Lakeflow actually does with a violating row under each, and how you'd decide which action belongs on which expectation in a production bronze-to-silver pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer: An expectation in a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline is a boolean constraint declared on a table (e.g., @dlt.expect, expect_or_drop, expect_or_fail in the Python API, or CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT in SQL) that Lakeflow evaluates against every row as it flows through that table's definition. Under 'warn' (the default for a plain expectation), rows that violate the constraint are still written to the target table, but the violation is counted and surfaced in the pipeline's data-quality metrics/event log — nothing stops. Under 'drop,' violating rows are filtered out before they reach the target table, so the table only ever contains conforming rows, and the drop count is still recorded in metrics. Under 'fail,' a single violation halts the entire pipeline update and raises an error, which stops the flow of data downstream entirely rather than letting any bad rows through. The right action depends on what a violation means for the business: fail belongs on constraints where a violation indicates the pipeline itself is broken or trustworthiness is destroyed by any bad row at all — for example, a primary key suddenly being null, which suggests an upstream schema break. Drop belongs on expectations where some fraction of bad rows is normal and tolerable, like a malformed optional field that shouldn't block the batch but also shouldn't pollute silver. Warn belongs on soft data-quality signals you want visibility into without blocking anything, such as a value falling slightly outside an expected range that an analyst should investigate but that doesn't invalidate the row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about the three actions as three different severities of 'this row is wrong.' Warn says 'let it through, but tell me' — good for soft signals you want visibility into. Drop says 'quarantine it silently from the clean table, but keep the pipeline running' — good for the expected trickle of malformed optional fields. Fail says 'stop everything right now' — and I reserve that for constraints where a violation means the pipeline's basic assumptions broke, like a null primary key, because letting even one of those through would corrupt everything downstream. When I'm designing a bronze-to-silver pipeline I go constraint by constraint and ask 'if this fails, is the data still usable, is it usable but needs quarantining, or is continuing actively dangerous' — that answer picks the action, not a blanket policy applied to every expectation.

questions.title: Job Clusters, All-Purpose Clusters, and Serverless: The Cost Model Behind Databricks Workflows
questions.prompt: A FinOps lead wants to understand why the same Databricks Workflow can cost wildly different amounts depending on how its compute is configured. Explain the cost and lifecycle differences between a job cluster, an all-purpose cluster used by a job, and serverless compute for jobs, and recommend a default policy for a platform running hundreds of scheduled jobs.
questions.modelAnswer: A job cluster is created fresh when a Workflow run starts, exists only for that run's tasks, and is torn down automatically when the run completes, so you pay only for the exact duration of that run plus startup time, and compute is strictly isolated per run — no other job's tasks can ever compete for or be delayed by this cluster. An all-purpose (interactive) cluster is a long-lived, shared cluster that a job can be pointed at instead of spinning up its own; it's typically already running for interactive notebook use, so a job using it avoids cluster-startup latency and can be cheaper per run in isolation, but it bills continuously whether a job is running or not, and multiple jobs/users sharing it compete for the same compute, which risks one noisy job starving another's SLA. Serverless compute for jobs removes cluster management entirely — Databricks manages a pool of pre-warmed, auto-scaling compute behind the scenes, billing per second of actual task execution with near-zero startup latency, and you never choose instance types or tune autoscaling. For a platform running hundreds of scheduled jobs, the default policy should be serverless or job clusters for anything running unattended on a schedule — serverless where startup latency matters and workload is spiky/unpredictable, job clusters where you need specific instance types, init scripts, or tighter cost predictability per run — and all-purpose clusters should be reserved for interactive development only, with policy guardrails (cluster policies, auto-termination) preventing production jobs from quietly being pointed at a shared interactive cluster, which is the single most common source of unpredictable job cost and noisy-neighbor SLA breaches on a platform this size.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it through 'who pays for idle time.' A job cluster spins up for exactly one run and dies right after — you pay for the run, full stop, and nothing else touches it. An all-purpose cluster is already running for someone's interactive work, so pointing a job at it is tempting because it starts instantly and looks cheap per run, but you're billing for that cluster the whole time regardless of whether a job is on it, and now your production job's reliability depends on whatever else is happening on that shared cluster. Serverless takes the cluster decision away entirely — you pay per second of actual task time with effectively no startup wait, which is great for spiky, unpredictable schedules. For hundreds of scheduled jobs, my default policy is: production scheduled work gets job clusters or serverless, never all-purpose, and I'd enforce that with cluster policies rather than trust, because the all-purpose-cluster shortcut is exactly how a FinOps review finds one shared cluster quietly eating six teams' job budgets with no isolation.
commonMistakes: Assumes job clusters are always cheaper than all-purpose clusters without accounting for startup latency and isolation benefits
Doesn't mention that all-purpose clusters bill continuously regardless of job activity
Treats serverless as 'always best' without noting it removes low-level tuning control
Fails to propose an enforceable policy (cluster policies/guardrails) and just states a preference
keyPoints: Correctly explains job cluster lifecycle and billing (ephemeral, isolated)
Correctly explains all-purpose cluster billing and the noisy-neighbor/continuous-billing risk
Correctly explains serverless compute's per-second billing and managed nature
Recommends a sound default policy for production scheduled work at scale
Proposes an enforcement mechanism (policy/guardrail), not just a preference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains all three compute options' cost/lifecycle
Identifies the all-purpose-cluster cost/isolation risk
Recommends a sound default policy at scale
Proposes a concrete enforcement mechanism

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index — this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice — and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage — wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first — Status — because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation
keyPoints: Identifies both non-SARGable predicates
Rewrites the date predicate as a range
Removes the function wrapper on Status, citing collation
Designs index key order correctly: equality before range
Makes the index covering with INCLUDE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites both non-SARGable predicates
Index design uses correct key order (equality before range)
Index is fully covering via INCLUDE
Explains reasoning, not just the syntax
