questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume — I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate — I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: Generate One DAG Per Client From a Shared Config File
questions.prompt: Instead of hand-writing a near-identical DAG for each of 12 clients' nightly loads, write an Airflow DAG-generation script that reads a local JSON config file and produces one DAG per client, each with its own schedule and a single PythonOperator task.
questions.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator

CONFIG_PATH = Path(__file__).parent / "client_configs.json"
CLIENT_CONFIGS = json.loads(CONFIG_PATH.read_text())


def load_client_data(client_id: str, **context):
    print(f"Loading nightly data for client {client_id}")
    # real extraction/load logic goes here


def build_client_dag(client_id: str, schedule: str) -> DAG:
    with DAG(
        dag_id=f"client_load_{client_id}",
        schedule_interval=schedule,
        start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
        catchup=False,
        tags=["client-load", client_id],
    ) as dag:
        PythonOperator(
            task_id="load_client_data",
            python_callable=load_client_data,
            op_kwargs={"client_id": client_id},
        )
    return dag


for config in CLIENT_CONFIGS:
    dag_id = f"client_load_{config['client_id']}"
    globals()[dag_id] = build_client_dag(config["client_id"], config["schedule"])
questions.modelAnswer: The config (client_configs.json) is read from a local file at module import/parse time, kept deliberately cheap rather than a live database or API call, which matters because the scheduler re-parses this file on every parse interval and a slow config read would be paid repeatedly. build_client_dag constructs a distinct DAG object per client with its own dag_id and schedule; the critical step most people get wrong is the final loop assigning each built DAG to globals()[dag_id] -- Airflow's DAG file processor only picks up DAG objects that exist in the module's global namespace, so building DAGs inside a function and returning them without this assignment means Airflow never actually discovers them as separate DAGs. Each DAG gets a unique dag_id derived from the client identifier so they're independently visible, schedulable, and pausable in the UI, and tags make them filterable as a group without being a single combined DAG.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the two things people usually get wrong here: first, the config has to be fast and local -- if this read a live table instead of a JSON file, we'd be adding that query's latency to every scheduler parse cycle for every one of these DAGs, which is the kind of thing that looks fine with 12 clients and becomes a scheduler-health problem at 200. Second, that globals()[dag_id] = build_client_dag(...) line isn't cosmetic -- without it, these DAG objects exist in memory when the file is parsed but Airflow's DAG file processor never registers them, so you'd see zero DAGs in the UI despite the code running without errors. I'd add onboarding a new client to this as just appending one entry to the JSON file and letting the next scheduler parse pick it up automatically.
commonMistakes: Builds DAG objects in a function but never assigns them to the module's global namespace, so Airflow never discovers them
Reads configuration from a live database/API call at parse time instead of a fast local file
Gives every generated DAG the same dag_id or doesn't derive it from the client identifier, causing collisions
Forgets catchup=False, risking a backfill storm across 12 DAGs on first deploy
keyPoints: Reads config from a fast, local source rather than a live query at parse time
Builds a distinct DAG object per client with a unique dag_id and its own schedule
Assigns each generated DAG to the module's global namespace so Airflow discovers it
Sets catchup=False and reasonable defaults to avoid an unintended backfill on rollout

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DAG-generation loop producing one DAG per config entry
Correctly assigns generated DAGs to globals() so Airflow discovers them
Unique dag_id per client, config read from a fast local source
Explains the scheduler re-parsing implication clearly

questions.title: Dynamically Map a Task Over a Variable-Length List of Files
questions.prompt: A DAG needs to process however many files land in a staging folder each night -- sometimes 3, sometimes 30 -- without hand-writing a task per file or hardcoding a maximum count. Write the Airflow code using dynamic task mapping (.expand()) to fan out a processing task over that list.
questions.modelAnswer: list_staged_files runs once and returns however many filenames actually exist that night; process_file.expand(filename=files) is where the dynamic mapping happens -- Airflow creates one mapped task instance of process_file per element in that list at runtime, not at DAG-parse time, so the count genuinely varies night to night without any DAG code change or hardcoded maximum. Each mapped instance runs independently (and can retry independently, which matters if file 7 of 30 fails and the others succeeded), and summarize(results) automatically receives the full list of all mapped task outputs by depending on the expand() call's result, giving a single aggregation point after however many instances ran. This is distinct from writing a static for loop over files at DAG-definition time, which can't react to a count that isn't known until the DAG actually runs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the key distinction as 'known at parse time vs. known at run time' -- a plain for loop in the DAG file has to know the file count when Airflow parses the DAG, which it can't, since that count depends on what lands overnight. Dynamic task mapping defers that decision to execution time: list_staged_files runs, returns whatever it finds, and .expand() creates exactly that many task instances, each independently retryable, so one bad file doesn't take down the other 29. I'd also point out that summarize() depending on the expand() output is what gives us a clean single place to roll up a pass/fail report, instead of needing a separate join step.
commonMistakes: Writes a static Python for loop over files at DAG-definition time instead of using .expand()
Doesn't realize each mapped task instance can retry independently, treating the whole expand() as one atomic unit
Forgets to have a downstream task depend on the expand() result to aggregate/summarize outcomes
Hardcodes an assumed maximum file count instead of letting the list determine fan-out size at runtime
keyPoints: Uses .expand() to fan out a task over a runtime-determined list
Understands expansion happens at execution time, not DAG-parse time
Notes each mapped instance retries independently
Aggregates mapped results in a downstream task depending on the expand() output

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of .expand() for dynamic task mapping
Correctly explains parse-time vs. run-time determination of fan-out count
Includes a sensible downstream aggregation step
Notes independent retry behavior of mapped instances

questions.title: Convert a Polling File Sensor to a Deferrable Sensor
questions.prompt: A DAG uses a standard poke-mode S3KeySensor with a 5-minute poke interval and a 6-hour timeout, tying up a worker slot the entire time it waits. Rewrite it to use the deferrable equivalent so it releases the worker slot while waiting.
questions.code:
# Before: ties up a worker slot for up to 6 hours
# from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor
# wait_for_file = S3KeySensor(
#     task_id="wait_for_file",
#     bucket_name="client-staging",
#     bucket_key="nightly/{{ ds }}/extract.csv",
#     poke_interval=300,
#     timeout=60 * 60 * 6,
# )

# After: defers to the triggerer, releases the worker slot while waiting
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor

wait_for_file = S3KeySensor(
    task_id="wait_for_file",
    bucket_name="client-staging",
    bucket_key="nightly/{{ ds }}/extract.csv",
    poke_interval=300,
    timeout=60 * 60 * 6,
    deferrable=True,
)
questions.modelAnswer: Setting deferrable=True on a sensor that supports it (most AWS/GCP provider sensors do) changes its execution model without changing any of its matching logic: instead of occupying a worker slot and sleeping between pokes, the task runs an initial check, and if the condition isn't met yet, it defers -- handing the wait off to the triggerer process as an async trigger and fully releasing its worker slot -- then only resumes on a worker when the triggerer notifies it the file has arrived or the timeout is reached. The poke_interval and timeout semantics are preserved (the triggerer uses them to pace its async checks and enforce the same deadline); the only operational change is that during the wait, this task consumes no worker slot at all, just a lightweight entry in the triggerer, which matters a lot once you have many of these running concurrently. The prerequisite that's easy to forget is that an Airflow triggerer process has to actually be running in the deployment for deferrable=True to work -- without it, the task will be stuck unable to resume.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a one-line change on the task, but I'd flag to the team that it only works if we're actually running a triggerer component in this deployment -- if we're on a setup that's never needed one before, this is also an infrastructure change, not just a code change. Once that's confirmed, deferrable=True is close to a free win here: same timeout, same poke cadence from the user's perspective, but the worker slot that used to be pinned for up to 6 hours is now free for other DAGs almost the entire time we're waiting. I'd roll this out to our other long-polling sensors too once we've confirmed it works cleanly on this one.
commonMistakes: Assumes deferrable=True works without a triggerer process actually running in the deployment
Changes poke_interval or timeout semantics unnecessarily instead of just adding the deferrable flag
Confuses deferrable sensors with reducing the actual wait time, rather than just the worker-slot cost of waiting
Applies deferrable=True to a sensor/operator that doesn't actually support it
keyPoints: Adds deferrable=True to the existing sensor with matching logic unchanged
Explains that this releases the worker slot during the wait instead of blocking it
Notes the triggerer process must be running for this to function
Understands poke_interval/timeout semantics are preserved under deferred execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct minimal code change (deferrable=True) preserving existing sensor logic
Correctly explains the worker-slot release mechanism via the triggerer
Notes the triggerer-must-be-running prerequisite
Clear framing of the operational benefit at scale

questions.title: Configure Git Mode and a CI/CD Publish Pipeline for a Data Factory Instance
questions.prompt: A Data Factory instance has been built entirely by clicking in the browser UX with no source control, and the team wants Dev/Test/Prod promotion with pull-request review before anything reaches Test or Prod. Describe the Git configuration needed in Data Factory itself, and write the key snippet of the Azure DevOps YAML pipeline step that deploys the generated ARM template into the Test Data Factory using parameter overrides (so the Test linked service points at Test resources, not Dev's).
questions.code:
Repo layout after Git integration:
  adf_publish branch (auto-generated, holds ARMTemplateForFactory.json + parameters file)
  main / feature branches (collaboration branches, hold the factory's actual resource JSON)
questions.modelAnswer: Data Factory's Git configuration is set under Manage > Git configuration, pointing the Dev factory at a collaboration branch (commonly main or a release branch) in Azure Repos or GitHub. Every change an author makes in the UX is saved to a feature branch and merged into the collaboration branch via pull request, which is what provides the required review gate — nothing reaches the collaboration branch without a PR. Clicking 'Publish' from the collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template and pushes it to the auto-created adf_publish branch; adf_publish is a build artifact, not something anyone edits by hand. The CI/CD pipeline then takes ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and deploys it with an ARM/Bicep deployment task, overriding the environment-specific parameters (linked service connection strings, Key Vault references) defined in ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json so the same template deploys correctly to Test and then Prod without any hard-coded Dev values leaking through.
questions.professionalAnswer: First step, before any pipeline work, is wiring up Git configuration inside the Dev factory itself — under Manage > Git configuration, pointed at a collaboration branch like main. Once that's set, every change someone makes in the ADF UX lands on a feature branch, and getting it into main requires a pull request, which is exactly the review gate the team's asking for — nobody can push straight to the branch that matters. Publishing from that collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template into the auto-managed adf_publish branch; I'd explain that nobody should ever hand-edit adf_publish, it's purely generated output. For the actual promotion pipeline, I'd have the Azure DevOps YAML pull ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and run an ARM deployment task against the Test factory's resource group, passing overrideParameters so things like the Test SQL linked service connection string get substituted in instead of whatever was baked in for Dev — the template itself stays identical across environments, only the parameter values change per stage.
questions.example:
# Azure DevOps YAML — deploy ADF ARM template into the Test Data Factory
- task: AzureResourceManagerTemplateDeployment@3
  displayName: 'Deploy ARM Template to Test Data Factory'
  inputs:
    deploymentScope: 'Resource Group'
    azureResourceManagerConnection: 'AzureServiceConnection-Test'
    subscriptionId: '$(testSubscriptionId)'
    action: 'Create Or Update Resource Group'
    resourceGroupName: '$(testResourceGroupName)'
    location: 'East US'
    templateLocation: 'Linked artifact'
    csmFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateForFactory.json'
    csmParametersFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json'
    overrideParameters: >
      -factoryName "adf-test-bi"
      -AzureSqlDatabase_connectionString "$(TestSqlConnectionString)"
    deploymentMode: 'Incremental'
commonMistakes: Never configuring Git integration on the Dev factory, leaving all changes unversioned and unreviewable
Manually editing the adf_publish branch instead of treating it strictly as generated publish output
Deploying the same ARM template to Test without overriding environment-specific parameters, pointing Test at Dev's linked services
Using Incremental deployment mode assumptions incorrectly or switching to Complete mode, which can delete resources not present in the template
Allowing direct pushes to the collaboration branch instead of enforcing pull-request review via branch policy
keyPoints: Git configuration is set on the Dev factory, pointing at a collaboration branch with branch-policy-enforced PR review
adf_publish is auto-generated by Publish and should never be hand-edited
ARMTemplateForFactory.json plus its parameters file are the artifacts carried through the release pipeline
overrideParameters substitutes environment-specific values (connection strings, factory name) per stage
Incremental deployment mode is used so the deployment doesn't delete resources outside the template unexpectedly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes Git configuration and PR-gated collaboration branch workflow
Correctly explains adf_publish as generated, not hand-edited
Correct ARM deployment YAML task structure
Correct use of overrideParameters for environment-specific values

questions.title: Row-Level Security for a Shared Sales Table Across Regional Teams
questions.prompt: A shared catalog.sales.orders table in Unity Catalog needs to be visible to all five regional sales teams, but each region's analysts should only see their own region's rows -- and a separate exec_global group should see every row unmasked. Write the SQL to enforce this with a Unity Catalog row-level security view, without creating five separate physical tables.
questions.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW catalog.sales.orders_secure AS
SELECT *
FROM catalog.sales.orders
WHERE
  is_account_group_member('exec_global')
  OR region = (
    CASE
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_east')    THEN 'EAST'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_west')    THEN 'WEST'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_north')   THEN 'NORTH'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_south')   THEN 'SOUTH'
      WHEN is_account_group_member('sales_central') THEN 'CENTRAL'
    END
  );

-- Lock down the base table so it can only be reached through the view
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE catalog.sales.orders FROM `account users`;
GRANT SELECT ON VIEW catalog.sales.orders_secure TO `account users`;
questions.modelAnswer: is_account_group_member() is Unity Catalog's built-in function for checking the calling user's group membership at query time, which lets row-level security be expressed directly in SQL rather than in application code. The view's WHERE clause evaluates per-querying-user, not per-row-owner: exec_global always passes via the OR short-circuit regardless of region, while every other caller's rows are filtered by whichever single CASE branch matches their own group membership. Critically, this security guarantee only holds if the underlying base table itself isn't separately grantable -- if analysts retain direct SELECT on catalog.sales.orders, they can simply bypass the view and query the base table directly, seeing every row regardless of region. The REVOKE/GRANT pair isn't cleanup, it's the actual enforcement boundary; the view only provides security to the extent the base table is locked behind it. A user belonging to none of the listed groups and not in exec_global falls through the CASE to NULL, which matches no region and correctly returns zero rows rather than erroring. This same pattern generalizes to column masking by adding a similar CASE WHEN is_account_group_member(...) THEN real_column ELSE NULL END on sensitive columns within the same view.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always flag when reviewing this kind of view is the REVOKE statement, because without it the whole thing is security theater -- anyone who still has SELECT on the base table just skips the view and sees everything, and that's an easy thing to miss in a review because the view itself looks completely correct. I'd also point out that the filtering logic runs based on who's asking the question, not any flag stored on the row itself, so the same physical table serves five different results depending on who's logged in -- that's the part that avoids needing five physical tables. And I'd double check the fallback case: if someone isn't in any of these groups, does the CASE return NULL cleanly, or does it error? We want a quiet zero rows, not a broken query, for a user who simply doesn't belong anywhere yet.

Writes the region-matching logic per-row-owner instead of per-querying-user's group membership
Doesn't handle the case of a user in none of the groups, risking an error instead of a safe zero-row result
Creates five physical per-region tables instead of one filtered view, duplicating storage and maintenance
Forgets exec_global needs an OR short-circuit, not just another CASE branch, to see all regions at once

Revokes direct SELECT on the base table so the view is the only access path
Handles the exec_global case as an OR condition granting unrestricted access
Avoids per-region physical table duplication by using one parameterized view

questions.title: Write a Lakeflow Pipeline Enforcing a Hard Quality Gate on Revenue Rows
questions.prompt: Using the incident from the earlier data-quality discussion -- negative revenue and null customer IDs reaching the gold layer -- write the actual Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline code for the silver table that enforces these as hard invariants, while quarantining a separate, recoverable issue (missing region code) instead of failing the pipeline over it.
questions.modelAnswer: expect_or_fail on valid_customer_id and non_negative_revenue encodes exactly the two conditions from the incident as hard invariants -- any batch containing a violating row causes this pipeline update to fail outright rather than letting even one bad row reach silver or gold, which is the correct severity for data that corrupts downstream financial aggregates: a single null customer_id breaking a join, or one negative revenue row skewing a sum, is not something to drop and move past silently. expect_or_drop on has_region_code treats missing region code as recoverable: rows failing that check are silently excluded from the output table, but still counted in the pipeline's event-log metrics, rather than failing the whole run -- appropriate because a missing region code is useful-but-not-critical dimension metadata, not something that corrupts a revenue total. All three expectations are evaluated per row during the same pipeline run, and their pass/fail/drop counts are visible in the Lakeflow pipeline's event log and UI graph, so the quarantine isn't invisible -- someone can still see how many rows were dropped for missing region code and decide whether that number warrants investigation. The severity choices here are proportionate to business impact: fail hard on invariants that corrupt the gold layer's numbers, quarantine-and-count everything else.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this incident-first: the whole point of this code is that the two things that actually went wrong last time -- null customer IDs and negative revenue -- get expect_or_fail, full stop, because those are exactly the rows that corrupt a financial number if they sneak through. Missing region code is a different kind of problem; it's annoying, not dangerous, so it gets expect_or_drop instead, which quietly excludes those rows but still counts them so we're not flying blind. I'd push back on anyone who wants to make everything expect_or_fail 'to be safe' -- that just means a non-critical field like region code starts taking down the whole pipeline, which trades one kind of incident for another.

Uses expect_or_fail for the region_code check, causing unnecessary pipeline failures over a non-critical field
Doesn't cast/validate the revenue column's type before checking it, letting a type issue masquerade as a data issue
Writes the expectation as a plain Python assert instead of the @dlt.expect_or_* decorator, losing event-log visibility into violations
Forgets that dropped rows from expect_or_drop still need to be monitored, not just silently discarded

Correctly maps the recoverable issue (missing region code) to expect_or_drop
Explains why severity level should match business impact, not be applied uniformly
Notes that expectation outcomes remain visible via the pipeline event log/UI

questions.title: Bringing a Manually Created Event Hub Under Bicep Management
questions.prompt: Six months ago, someone manually provisioned a production Event Hub namespace through the Azure Portal under time pressure. It's never been touched since, but now it needs to go through the same CI/CD-managed Bicep pipeline as everything else. Explain how you'd bring it under IaC management given Bicep/ARM doesn't have a true 'import' command like Terraform, and write the Bicep you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer: Bicep/ARM deployments are declarative and idempotent by name -- there's no separate 'import state' step like terraform import, because ARM doesn't track resource ownership the way Terraform's state file does. 'Importing' in practice means writing a Bicep resource block whose type, name, and properties exactly match the resource's CURRENT live configuration, then deploying it. Because ARM resolves a deployment by matching resource type and name, deploying a Bicep definition that matches an existing resource's current state is effectively a no-op update, and from that point forward the resource is 'under management' in the sense that the next deployment touching this Bicep file will apply diffs to it going forward. The critical risk is capturing the TRUE current configuration before writing that block -- if the manually-created Event Hub has settings (a specific capacity, a non-default retention, a particular throughput configuration) that get guessed wrong in the Bicep definition, the first deployment silently changes production instead of leaving it alone. The existing keyword resource reference is the safe way to read and confirm current properties before writing the managed resource block, rather than guessing. I'd also run a what-if deployment (az deployment group what-if) before the real apply specifically to confirm it reports zero or no-op changes, which is the actual verification that the Bicep definition genuinely matches reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct is the premise that we're looking for a terraform-import equivalent -- Bicep just doesn't work that way, since ARM doesn't keep a separate state file tracking what it owns. What actually happens is: we write a Bicep resource block that matches this Event Hub's current settings exactly, and the moment we deploy it and it comes back as a no-op, that resource is under management. The part I'd be most careful about is getting 'exactly' right -- I'd use the existing keyword first to read its real current config rather than guess at what someone set six months ago, and then I would not run this against production without a what-if deployment first. If what-if shows anything other than no changes, that's a sign my Bicep doesn't actually match reality yet, and I'd rather find that out from a dry run than from an unintended change to a live Event Hub.
commonMistakes: Assumes Bicep has a terraform import equivalent command and looks for one instead of writing a matching resource definition
Writes the Bicep resource block from assumed/default settings instead of verifying the resource's actual current configuration first
Skips a what-if deployment before the real apply, risking an unintended production change
Uses the existing keyword as if it brings the resource under management, when it's read-only and changes nothing
Doesn't account for properties that are immutable or hard to change needing to match exactly from day one
keyPoints: Explains ARM/Bicep has no stateful import; management starts by matching a resource's current live config in code
Uses the existing keyword to safely read current configuration before writing the managed definition
Verifies the match with a what-if deployment before the real apply
Flags the risk of a mismatched property causing an unintended change to production on first deploy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Bicep has no true import and what bringing under management actually means
Correct use of the existing keyword to verify current state safely
Correctly matches the managed resource definition structure
Proposes what-if verification before the real deployment

questions.title: Enforcing Backward Compatibility on a Subject via the Schema Registry REST API
questions.prompt: Following the schema-governance redesign from the earlier incident, write the actual Schema Registry REST API calls your CI pipeline would run to (1) set a subject's compatibility mode to BACKWARD and (2) test a candidate schema against the current one before allowing a producer's CI build to merge.
questions.code:
# 1. Set BACKWARD compatibility on the subject (run once, or enforced via IaC)
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  --data '{"compatibility": "BACKWARD"}' \
  http://schema-registry:8081/config/orders-value

# 2. In CI, before merging a producer change: test the candidate schema for compatibility
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json" \
  --data '{"schema": "{\"type\":\"record\",\"name\":\"Order\",\"fields\":[{\"name\":\"order_id\",\"type\":\"string\"},{\"name\":\"amount\",\"type\":\"double\"}]}"}' \
  http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/orders-value/versions/latest

# Response: {"is_compatible": true} or {"is_compatible": false}
# CI should fail the build if is_compatible is false, before any registration happens
questions.modelAnswer: The /config/{subject} PUT endpoint sets the enforcement policy itself -- once set to BACKWARD, the registry will reject, at the /subjects/{subject}/versions registration endpoint, any new schema version that isn't backward-compatible with the latest registered version, which is the actual safety net. The /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest POST endpoint used in CI is a separate dry-run test: calling it doesn't register anything, it just returns is_compatible true or false for the candidate schema against the current one, which is exactly what a CI pipeline needs -- check compatibility as a build gate before the producer's code, which would register the new schema at deploy time, ever merges. The key operational point is that this has to run in CI on every pull request that touches a schema file, not just be available as a manual command someone might remember to run, and the build should fail loudly on is_compatible: false with the response body surfaced in the CI log, so the engineer sees exactly what broke compatibility rather than a generic failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as two different endpoints doing two different jobs, because mixing them up is the most common mistake I see. The /config endpoint is the policy switch -- flip it to BACKWARD once, and the registry itself now refuses any genuinely breaking schema at registration time, which is the real backstop. The /compatibility endpoint is what CI calls on every PR, and it's a dry run -- it tells you yes or no without registering anything, so you find out a change is breaking before it ever gets near deploy time. I'd insist this runs on every PR that touches a schema, not as an optional step, and I'd make sure the build output actually shows the registry's response, because 'compatibility check failed' with no detail sends an engineer hunting for a problem the API already described precisely.
commonMistakes: Confuses the /compatibility test endpoint with the /subjects registration endpoint, thinking compatibility testing registers a schema
Sets compatibility mode but never wires the /compatibility check into actual CI, leaving it manual/optional
Doesn't fail the CI build loudly on is_compatible: false, letting it merge anyway
Sets compatibility globally instead of per-subject, when different subjects may need different modes
Forgets this only protects the subject it's set on -- a renamed topic/subject starts with no compatibility mode by default
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes the /config (set policy) and /compatibility (dry-run test) endpoints
Wires the compatibility test into CI as a build gate, not a manual step
Fails the build and surfaces the response on incompatibility
Understands this is a per-subject setting, not global

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct REST API calls for setting compatibility mode and testing a candidate schema
Correctly distinguishes the dry-run test endpoint from registration
Describes correct CI gating behavior
Notes per-subject scoping of compatibility mode

questions.title: Configuring MirrorMaker 2 for Active/Passive Replication Between Two Data Centers
questions.prompt: Following the active/passive recommendation for the East/West DR design, write the MirrorMaker 2 connector configuration that replicates topics from the East (primary) cluster to the West (standby) cluster, including the settings that actually matter for a real failover drill -- not just basic topic mirroring.
questions.code:
# mm2.properties
clusters = east, west
east.bootstrap.servers = east-broker1:9092,east-broker2:9092
west.bootstrap.servers = west-broker1:9092,west-broker2:9092

east->west.enabled = true
west->east.enabled = false

# Replicate everything except internal topics
east->west.topics = orders.*, payments.*
east->west.topics.exclude = .*\.internal

# Sync consumer group offsets so failover can resume near the right position
east->west.emit.checkpoints.enabled = true
east->west.sync.group.offsets.enabled = true
checkpoints.topic.replication.factor = 3

# Preserve source partitioning / avoid renaming collisions
replication.policy.separator = .
east->west.replication.factor = 3

# Keep replication lag visible
east->west.emit.heartbeats.enabled = true
heartbeats.topic.replication.factor = 3
questions.modelAnswer: The directional flags, east->west.enabled = true and west->east.enabled = false, are what actually encode active/passive -- MM2 is bidirectionally capable, so leaving the reverse direction enabled by accident would create a replication loop or an unintended write path back into the primary, a common real-world misconfiguration. sync.group.offsets.enabled is the setting most teams skip and the one that determines whether failover is actually usable: without it, West has the replicated data but no translated consumer offsets, so a consumer failing over to West either reprocesses everything from the beginning or needs manual offset management. emit.checkpoints.enabled together with sync.group.offsets.enabled let MM2 periodically translate East's consumer offsets into West's offset space, so a failed-over consumer group can resume close to where it left off rather than from zero. emit.heartbeats.enabled gives an observable signal of replication health, specifically lag and whether replication is actually flowing, independent of whether any data happened to be produced recently, which matters for monitoring that the standby isn't silently stale. topics.exclude keeps MM2 from needlessly replicating its own internal/checkpoint topics. None of this is testable by configuration review alone -- the actual validation is running a failover drill: stop consuming from East, point consumers at West using the translated offsets, and measure how much, if any, reprocessing or data gap actually occurs, which is the RPO/RTO measurement the earlier design recommendation called for.
questions.professionalAnswer: The line I'd point to first in a review is west->east.enabled = false, because the single most common MirrorMaker mistake I see is leaving both directions on by accident and ending up with an unintended active/active loop when the intent was active/passive. The setting I'd insist on, though, is sync.group.offsets.enabled -- without it, this whole config replicates data beautifully and still leaves us with no usable failover, because our consumers would have no idea where to resume on West. And I'd tell the team configuring this alone doesn't prove anything -- the only way to know failover actually works is to run a real drill: stop consuming from East, flip to West, and measure exactly how much we reprocess or lose. That number is our real RPO, not whatever we assumed when we wrote this file.
commonMistakes: Enables both east->west and west->east, accidentally building an active/active loop instead of active/passive
Skips sync.group.offsets.enabled, leaving no path for consumers to resume cleanly on failover
Never actually runs a failover drill, treating 'replication is configured' as equivalent to 'failover works'
Doesn't exclude MM2's own internal/checkpoint/heartbeat topics from the replication topic list
Assumes topic names stay identical across clusters without accounting for replication.policy.separator renaming behavior
keyPoints: Correctly configures directional replication for active/passive (one direction only)
Enables checkpoint/offset sync so failover can resume without full reprocessing
Uses heartbeats to monitor replication health/lag independently of data flow
Recognizes configuration alone doesn't validate failover -- a drill is required

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct directional (active/passive) MM2 configuration
Correctly configures offset/checkpoint sync for usable failover
Includes replication health monitoring (heartbeats)
Notes the need for an actual failover drill to validate RPO/RTO

questions.title: Write a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline with Enforced Expectations
questions.prompt: Write a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (Python API) that reads raw order events from a bronze table, enforces three data-quality expectations on the way to a silver table — order_id must never be null (any violation should halt the pipeline), order_total must be non-negative (violating rows should be quarantined, not loaded), and ship_date should be on or after order_date (a soft rule you only want visibility into) — and briefly explain why you picked each enforcement action.
questions.modelAnswer: order_id is the primary key downstream joins and dedup logic depend on, so a null there means the upstream contract is already broken — continuing to process would silently corrupt every downstream table, which is why it's expect_or_fail: one violation halts the pipeline update entirely and forces investigation before any more data moves. order_total being negative is a data-quality problem that happens occasionally (a refund row mis-tagged, a parsing error) but shouldn't be allowed into silver, and it also shouldn't stop the whole batch over what's usually a small number of rows, so expect_or_drop quarantines those rows out of the target table while the rest of the batch proceeds, and the drop count still shows up in the pipeline's data quality metrics for someone to review. ship_date before order_date is suspicious but not necessarily wrong — timestamps across systems can be off, or it could be a legitimate pre-order — so it's a plain expect, meaning violating rows are still written to silver_orders but the violation is tracked and visible in the event log, giving analysts a signal to investigate without blocking anyone's pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd map each rule to how bad a violation actually is. Null order_id means something upstream is fundamentally broken, so I don't want the pipeline to quietly keep running on broken assumptions — expect_or_fail stops everything until a human looks at it. A negative total is a real but recoverable data problem; I don't want it in silver, but I also don't want one bad row from a vendor feed to take down the whole pipeline run, so expect_or_drop quarantines just those rows and the batch keeps moving. The ship-before-order case is the softest one — it might be legitimate, might be a clock skew issue — so I just want it logged and visible, not blocking or dropping anything, which is a plain expect. I'd walk through the metrics view with the team afterward so the warn and drop counts don't just get silently ignored.
questions.example: After a run, the pipeline's event log shows: 0 violations of valid_order_id (none dropped — pipeline never halted), 14 rows dropped by non_negative_total out of 50,000 processed, and 3 rows flagged by ship_after_order but still present in silver_orders for an analyst to review.
commonMistakes: Uses expect_or_fail for the negative-total rule, needlessly halting the pipeline over a routine, recoverable data issue
Uses a plain expect for the null order_id rule, letting primary-key violations silently flow into silver
Forgets that expect (warn) still writes the violating row to the target table
Doesn't explain the reasoning behind each enforcement action, just lists the syntax
keyPoints: Correctly applies expect_or_fail to the primary-key null check
Correctly applies expect_or_drop to the recoverable negative-total check
Correctly applies a plain expect to the soft ship-date rule
Justifies each choice by the real-world severity of a violation
Mentions that drop/warn counts remain visible in pipeline metrics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Pipeline code correctly reads bronze and writes silver with streaming tables
Correct expectation syntax and enforcement action per rule

Notes visibility of violations in metrics/event log

questions.title: Configure Auto Loader for Schema Evolution at Scale
questions.prompt: Write the Auto Loader streaming read configuration for a bronze ingestion job reading JSON files from cloud storage where the upstream schema adds new fields periodically and you cannot afford to have the stream fail every time that happens, but you do want a controlled, reviewable record of what changed and when. Explain your schema evolution and checkpoint choices.
questions.modelAnswer: schemaEvolutionMode is set to addNewColumns, which means that when Auto Loader detects a field it hasn't seen before, it does not fail the stream — instead it stops the current micro-batch, records the new schema in the schema location, and the stream automatically restarts and picks up the new column going forward; this is exactly the 'don't fail every time the schema changes' requirement. The schema location (cloudFiles.schemaLocation) is what makes this reviewable: it persists the inferred schema as versioned JSON files, so every evolution event is a discrete, diffable artifact a platform engineer can inspect to see precisely what changed and when, rather than the change being invisible or only discoverable by reading query errors. inferColumnTypes is enabled so new fields get a reasonable inferred type instead of defaulting everything to string, which would otherwise force a downstream cast for every new field. mergeSchema on the write side lets the target Delta table itself absorb the new column without a separate ALTER TABLE step. The one thing addNewColumns does not protect against is a column's type changing incompatibly (e.g., a field that used to be an integer starting to arrive as a nested object) — that still requires addNewColumns to add it as a new, differently-named inferred column or, if truly incompatible, still halts for manual review, which is the intended safety valve for a change severe enough that silently guessing would be worse than stopping.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set schemaEvolutionMode to addNewColumns specifically because the requirement is 'don't fail on routine schema growth, but still make it visible.' That setting means a new field triggers a one-time, automatic micro-batch restart that picks up the column going forward, rather than an ongoing production failure someone has to get paged for. What makes it reviewable is the schema location — Auto Loader writes out the schema it inferred as versioned files there, so if someone asks 'when did this field show up,' I can point to an actual artifact instead of guessing from a log. I'd also turn on inferColumnTypes so we're not defaulting every new field to a string and creating cast problems downstream, and mergeSchema on the Delta write so the table itself doesn't need a manual ALTER TABLE. I'd be clear that this doesn't cover a field changing type incompatibly — that's a different, rarer failure mode, and I think it's correct that it still gets escalated rather than silently patched over.
commonMistakes: Uses the default (or 'failOnNewColumns') schema evolution mode, which halts the stream on every new field
Omits cloudFiles.schemaLocation, losing the auditable record of schema changes
Forgets mergeSchema on the write side, so the Delta table rejects the new column even though Auto Loader detected it
Doesn't distinguish addNewColumns (new field) from an incompatible type change on an existing field
keyPoints: Chooses addNewColumns as the schema evolution mode and explains why
Explains the role of cloudFiles.schemaLocation in making changes reviewable/auditable
Explains inferColumnTypes avoiding an all-string fallback
Explains mergeSchema on the write path to let the Delta table absorb new columns
Correctly scopes what addNewColumns does and does not protect against

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Auto Loader configuration for schema evolution
Explains the stream-restart behavior on new column detection
Explains how the configuration makes changes auditable
Correctly scopes the limits of addNewColumns

questions.title: Set Up a Delta Sharing Share for an External Partner
questions.prompt: Write the SQL statements to create a Delta Sharing share containing one table from a sales catalog, create a recipient for an external partner organization, and grant that recipient access to the share — then explain how the partner actually retrieves the credential they need to connect.
questions.modelAnswer: CREATE SHARE defines an empty, named container; ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE then explicitly adds exactly one table to it, which is the point — a share is an opt-in allowlist, so no other table in the catalog becomes visible just because it lives in the same schema. CREATE RECIPIENT registers the external identity that will be granted access; since this is an external organization without its own Unity Catalog metastore, this is open sharing, which auto-generates an activation link rather than federating identity directly. GRANT SELECT ON SHARE ... TO RECIPIENT is the actual authorization step connecting the two. After the grant, the provider retrieves the recipient's activation link (DESCRIBE RECIPIENT acme_partner_corp or the Catalog Explorer UI shows it) and sends it to the partner out-of-band; the partner opens that one-time link, which generates a bearer-token credential file (a .share file containing the token and sharing server endpoint) they download once and then use with any Delta Sharing client — Databricks, a Python/pandas Delta Sharing connector, Power BI, or Spark — to query the share going forward. That token can be rotated or the recipient's access revoked at any time with REVOKE, without touching the underlying table at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as three separate, deliberate steps because each one is an explicit allowlist action. First I create an empty share and add just the one table I actually want to expose — nothing else in that schema becomes visible by accident. Then I create a recipient record for the partner; since they're external and don't have their own Unity Catalog, this is open sharing, so Databricks will generate an activation link rather than trusting their identity directly. Then I grant that recipient SELECT on the share — that's the step that actually turns access on. After that, I'd pull up the recipient's activation link and send it to them outside of this system entirely, like email; they click it once, get a credential file with a token in it, and from then on any Delta Sharing-compatible tool on their end can use that file to query the share. And if the partnership ends, I revoke the grant — I'm not managing a key rotation process on their infrastructure, I'm just turning off a grant on mine.
questions.example: DESCRIBE RECIPIENT acme_partner_corp; returns the activation_link column, which is a one-time URL the provider copies and sends to the partner's engineering contact out-of-band (not committed anywhere, not emailed as plaintext credentials).
commonMistakes: Grants access on the whole catalog/schema instead of a deliberately scoped share containing one table
Confuses open sharing (external recipient, activation link) with Databricks-to-Databricks sharing (identity federation, no activation link)
Doesn't know how the partner actually gets usable credentials after the grant
Forgets REVOKE is available to cut off access without touching the underlying table
keyPoints: Correctly creates a share and explicitly adds only the intended table
Correctly creates a recipient and grants it SELECT on the share
Explains open sharing's activation-link credential flow for an external, non-Databricks recipient
Notes the recipient can use any Delta Sharing-compatible client, not just Databricks
Mentions REVOKE as the access-termination mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SQL for share creation, table addition, recipient, and grant
Correctly explains the activation-link credential retrieval flow
Distinguishes open sharing from Databricks-to-Databricks sharing
Mentions revocation as an available control

questions.title: Implement Row-Level Security and Column Masking in Unity Catalog
questions.prompt: Write the SQL to enforce that a customer_orders table is only fully visible to members of the 'regional-managers' group, with everyone else restricted to their own region's rows, and to mask the customer_email column so only members of the 'pii-readers' group ever see the real value.
questions.code:
-- Row filter function: full access for regional-managers, else restrict to caller's own region
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sales.region_row_filter(region STRING)
RETURN is_account_group_member('regional-managers')
  OR region = current_user_region();

ALTER TABLE sales.customer_orders
SET ROW FILTER sales.region_row_filter ON (region);

-- Column mask function: real email for pii-readers, redacted otherwise
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sales.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('pii-readers') THEN email
  ELSE regexp_replace(email, '(^.).*(@.*$)', '\\1***\\2')
END;

ALTER TABLE sales.customer_orders
ALTER COLUMN customer_email
SET MASK sales.mask_email;
questions.modelAnswer: The row filter function takes the row's region value as its argument and returns true (row is visible) for any caller in the regional-managers group regardless of region, or for anyone else only when the row's region matches a current_user_region() lookup (a helper mapping the caller's identity to their assigned region, typically backed by a small reference table or a custom SQL function); ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER ... ON (region) attaches it so Unity Catalog applies it as an implicit predicate on every query against the table, regardless of query tool. The column mask function receives the real customer_email value and, for pii-readers, returns it unchanged; for everyone else, it returns a redacted form via regexp_replace that keeps the first character and the domain but masks the rest, which is enough for a non-privileged analyst to recognize a record without exposing the full address. ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK attaches this at the column level, independent of the row filter. Both functions are evaluated per-row at query time using the caller's actual identity (is_account_group_member checks group membership against the Unity Catalog identity the query is running as), so the enforcement travels with the table no matter what tool or user queries it, and a single SELECT * from two different analysts can legitimately return different row counts and different email values with no application code involved.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as two independent, composable policies on the same table. The row filter is a function that says 'if you're a regional manager, see everything; otherwise, only see rows matching your own region' — and once I attach it with SET ROW FILTER, that logic runs on every query against the table automatically, so nobody has to remember to add a WHERE clause. The column mask does the same thing for the email field: pii-readers get the real value, everyone else gets a redacted version that still looks like an email so it doesn't break downstream tooling, but doesn't leak the actual address. What I like about doing it this way instead of separate views is that it's attached directly to the table definition, so it's enforced the same way whether someone's querying from a notebook, a BI tool, or a JDBC client — there's no secondary view someone can forget to use instead of the raw table.
commonMistakes: Builds a separate filtered view instead of using native row filters/column masks, which can be bypassed by querying the base table directly
Hardcodes a list of regions instead of looking up the caller's assigned region dynamically
Masks the email with a static placeholder instead of preserving a recognizable, non-identifying pattern
Forgets that is_account_group_member checks the caller's actual Unity Catalog identity at query time, not a static role column in the data
keyPoints: Correctly implements a row filter function using is_account_group_member and a region predicate
Correctly attaches the row filter with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER
Correctly implements a column mask function with a group-conditional CASE expression
Correctly attaches the mask with ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK
Explains that both are enforced centrally regardless of query tool/user

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct row filter function and attachment
Correct column mask function and attachment
Explains per-row, per-caller evaluation at query time
Explains why this is preferable to a separate filtered view

questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events — either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session — and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally — widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary — so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone — I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary — but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;

Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification

questions.title: A Report Query That Used to Run in 2 Seconds Now Takes Over a Minute
questions.prompt: A nightly report query filtering orders by date has gone from roughly 2 seconds to over a minute as the Orders table grew past 40 million rows. The WHERE clause uses a function on the indexed OrderDate column to normalize it before comparing. Nobody changed the query text or the index. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and provide the corrected query.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the actual execution plan (not estimated) for the query and check whether it's doing an Index Seek or a Scan on OrderDate — on a 40M-row table, a scan where a seek should be possible is the key signal. The WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in CONVERT(date, OrderDate), and applying a function to the column itself makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server can't use the index's sorted order to seek, because it would have to evaluate CONVERT() against every row's OrderDate before it even knows which rows match, forcing a full scan. This likely always technically had this issue, but it only became painfully visible once the table grew enough that scanning became expensive — small tables hide non-SARGable predicates because a full scan is cheap when there's little data. Fix: rewrite the predicate to leave the column bare and move the transformation to the literal side, using a range comparison instead of transforming OrderDate: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-10-08' AND OrderDate < '2026-10-09'. This lets the optimizer seek directly against the OrderDate index. I'd confirm the fix by re-checking the execution plan for an Index Seek and comparing logical reads/duration before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't start by looking at the index or assuming it got dropped or fragmented — I go get the actual execution plan first, because 'nothing changed' usually means the query had a latent problem the whole time that only became expensive once the table crossed some size. And sure enough, the plan shows a full scan on a 40-million-row table even though there's an index sitting right there on OrderDate. The WHERE clause is the giveaway: CONVERT(date, OrderDate) = '...' wraps the indexed column in a function, and the moment you do that, the optimizer can't use the index's sort order to seek — it has to convert every single row before it can compare anything, so a scan is the only option it has left. This bug was there on day one, it just didn't matter when the table was small enough that a full scan was basically free; growth is what exposed it, not a change to the query or index. The fix is just to stop touching the column and instead express the same filter as a range against the raw OrderDate value — greater than or equal to midnight on the target day, less than midnight the next day — so the predicate stays SARGable and the optimizer can seek straight to the right rows. I make the change, pull the plan again, confirm it's an Index Seek now, and compare logical reads before and after so I have real numbers to point to, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming something must have changed (index dropped, stats stale) instead of checking whether the predicate was always non-SARGable
Not pulling the actual execution plan and instead guessing based on query text alone
Rebuilding or adding indexes without first fixing the function-wrapped predicate that prevents any index from being seek-able
Fixing it by wrapping the literal in the same function (CONVERT on both sides) instead of removing the function from the column side entirely
Not validating the fix by comparing before/after execution plans or logical reads
Blaming table growth alone as 'just needs more hardware' instead of identifying the specific non-SARGable predicate
keyPoints: Pulls the actual execution plan to confirm a scan where a seek should be possible
Correctly identifies the function-wrapped column as the SARGability problem
Explains why this was a latent issue exposed by growth rather than a new regression
Rewrites the predicate as a range comparison against the bare column instead of transforming the column
Confirms the fix via execution plan (Index Seek) and reads/duration comparison
Understands that the index itself was never the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses actual execution plan to diagnose scan vs seek
Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicate as root cause
Corrected SQL properly rewrites as a bare-column range predicate
Validates fix with plan/read comparison
