questions.title: The Airflow Scheduler Is Falling Behind Across All DAGs
questions.prompt: Multiple unrelated DAGs across different teams are all starting later than scheduled, by a growing margin each day, even though no individual DAG's logic has changed. Walk through how you'd diagnose a platform-wide Airflow scheduler problem like this.
questions.modelAnswer: A delay that affects unrelated DAGs growing worse over time points at the scheduler itself rather than any individual DAG's logic, so I'd start with scheduler health metrics: DAG file parsing duration (via the dag_processor logs or the `dag_processor_manager` stats), scheduler heartbeat/loop duration, and the total count of DAGs and tasks the scheduler is managing. The most common root cause at scale is DAG parsing cost growing faster than anyone noticed — if teams have been adding DAGs (including dynamically generated ones with slow or live config sources) without anyone watching total parse time, the scheduler spends an increasing fraction of every loop just re-parsing files rather than scheduling task instances, and that cost is shared across every DAG in the deployment, which is exactly why unrelated teams' DAGs are all affected together. I'd also check for a spike in total concurrently running tasks against the deployment's parallelism and max_active_tasks_per_dag limits, since hitting a global parallelism ceiling queues otherwise-ready task instances regardless of which DAG they belong to, and I'd check whether the metadata database itself is under load (slow queries, connection pool exhaustion) since every scheduler decision round-trips through it. I would not look at any single DAG's own code first, because a problem that's growing and cross-cutting this way is almost never caused by one team's DAG logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: The tell here is 'unrelated DAGs, growing delay' — that's a shared-resource problem, not a DAG-logic problem, so I wouldn't spend time in any individual DAG's code first. I'd go straight to DAG parse duration and scheduler loop metrics, because the single most common cause I've seen at this scale is parse cost creeping up as more DAGs (especially dynamically generated ones with a slow config source) get added without anyone tracking the aggregate number. I'd also sanity-check global parallelism limits and metadata DB health, since both can produce exactly this symptom — tasks sitting ready but not actually launching. Whatever I find, the fix is almost always structural (reduce parse cost, raise parallelism limits appropriately, or split scheduler capacity), not a fix to any one DAG.
commonMistakes: Investigates individual DAG logic first instead of recognizing a cross-cutting, growing delay as a shared-resource symptom
Doesn't check DAG parsing duration/scheduler loop metrics as the primary hypothesis
Doesn't check global parallelism/max_active_tasks limits as a queuing cause
Overlooks metadata database health/connection pool exhaustion as a scheduler bottleneck
keyPoints: Recognizes a cross-cutting, growing delay as a shared scheduler-resource symptom, not a DAG-logic issue
Checks DAG parsing duration as the most common root cause at scale
Checks global parallelism/max_active_tasks limits for queuing
Checks metadata database health as a scheduler dependency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a scheduler/shared-resource issue, not individual DAG logic
Identifies DAG parse duration growth as the primary hypothesis
Considers parallelism limits and metadata DB health
Clear, methodical diagnostic ordering

questions.title: Deferred Airflow Tasks Are Stuck Forever
questions.prompt: After converting several sensors to deferrable operators, you notice a growing number of tasks sitting in a 'deferred' state well past when their condition should have been satisfied, never resuming. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: Tasks stuck in deferred state that never resume point directly at the triggerer component — a deferred task hands its wait off to an async trigger running inside the triggerer process, and if the triggerer isn't running at all, is undersized relative to the number of concurrent deferred triggers it needs to run, or has crashed/restarted and lost in-memory trigger state, tasks will sit deferred indefinitely with no worker-side error, because from the worker's perspective it correctly handed off the wait and is just waiting to be told to resume. I'd first check whether the triggerer process is actually running and healthy in this deployment (it's a separate component from the scheduler and workers, and it's easy for a team new to deferrable operators to not have deployed it at all, or to have deployed only one under-resourced instance). If it is running, I'd check its own logs for errors on the specific trigger classes involved, and check how many concurrent triggers it's managing against its configured capacity, since a single triggerer process handling far more concurrent async waits than expected can start silently falling behind or dropping triggers under memory pressure. I'd also confirm this started exactly when the sensors were converted, which would point squarely at either a missing/undersized triggerer or a bug in how the specific operator's trigger class was implemented, rather than anything else changing concurrently.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always the triggerer, because that's the one new moving part we introduced by switching to deferrable operators. First question: is a triggerer process even running in this deployment, and if so, is it just one instance now expected to handle a lot more concurrent deferred tasks than it was sized for? I'd check its logs directly for errors on the specific trigger classes, and I'd check whether it's been restarted recently, since a triggerer restart can lose in-flight trigger state and leave tasks stuck. Given that this started right after the sensor conversion, I'm treating the triggerer as guilty until proven innocent before I look anywhere else.
commonMistakes: Investigates worker or scheduler logs first instead of recognizing this as a triggerer-specific symptom
Doesn't check whether a triggerer process is running and healthy at all
Doesn't consider triggerer capacity/sizing relative to the number of concurrent deferred tasks
Misses that the timing correlation with the sensor conversion is itself diagnostic
keyPoints: Identifies the triggerer component as the primary suspect for stuck deferred tasks
Checks whether the triggerer is running at all, and whether it's appropriately sized/resourced
Checks triggerer-specific logs for errors on the relevant trigger classes
Uses the timing correlation with the sensor conversion as a diagnostic clue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the triggerer component as the root-cause area
Checks triggerer running state and sizing/capacity
Checks triggerer-specific logs for errors
Uses timing correlation with the recent change as a diagnostic signal

questions.title: Unity Catalog Cross-Workspace Access Fails After a Metastore Split
questions.prompt: Your company runs three Databricks workspaces attached to a single Unity Catalog metastore in East US. After a platform team migrates one workspace to a new region for latency reasons, analysts in that workspace suddenly get 'PERMISSION_DENIED: metastore does not exist for this workspace' errors on tables that worked fine the day before, while the other two workspaces are unaffected. Diagnose the root cause and describe the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A Unity Catalog metastore is a region-scoped object — exactly one metastore can be assigned per region per account, and a workspace can only attach to a metastore that lives in the same region as the workspace itself. When the platform team moved the workspace to a new region, the workspace's metastore assignment did not silently follow it; Databricks either detached the workspace from its original metastore or left it pointing at an assignment that is now cross-region and therefore invalid, which is exactly what produces the 'metastore does not exist for this workspace' error — it is not a permissions bug on any table, grant, or catalog, it is that the workspace has no valid, region-matched metastore assignment at all, so every object underneath that metastore becomes unreachable from that workspace regardless of the ACLs on it. The fix is to either provision or identify a Unity Catalog metastore that already exists in the new region and explicitly re-assign the migrated workspace to it, or, if the organization wants a single logical catalog of data rather than duplicated metastores, to use Delta Sharing to publish the relevant catalog's tables from the original region's metastore to the new workspace instead of trying to force a same-metastore attachment across regions, which Unity Catalog does not support. Before doing either, the team should audit whether any table/view definitions, external locations, or storage credentials referenced a region-specific path, since those will also need re-pointing. The deeper governance lesson is that metastore assignment should be treated as an immutable constraint during any workspace relocation planning, not an afterthought discovered via a production incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to the platform team is: you didn't break any grants, you broke the geography. A Unity Catalog metastore is pinned to a region, one per region per account, and a workspace can only ever attach to the metastore sitting in its own region — so the moment you moved that workspace to a new region, its old metastore attachment became invalid, and that error message is Databricks telling you exactly that, even though it reads like a permissions problem. My first move is to confirm there's no metastore provisioned yet in the new region, then decide: do we stand one up and re-assign the workspace to it, or do we keep this workspace reading from the original metastore's catalogs via Delta Sharing instead of forcing a direct attachment that the platform doesn't support. I'd also flag that this should never have shipped as a surprise — workspace relocation needs a pre-flight checklist that calls out metastore region-matching explicitly, because this exact failure mode is completely predictable once you know the constraint.
commonMistakes: Treats the error as a grants/ACL problem and starts re-running GRANT statements on the affected tables
Assumes the metastore 'moved with' the workspace automatically during region migration
Tries to attach the relocated workspace directly to the original region's metastore, not realizing cross-region attachment is unsupported
Doesn't check whether external locations/storage credentials also need re-pointing after the fix
Jumps to provisioning a new metastore without first considering Delta Sharing as a lighter-weight alternative
keyPoints: Identifies metastore-to-region binding as the root cause, not a permissions issue
Recognizes a workspace can only attach to a metastore in its own region
Proposes either provisioning/assigning a region-matched metastore or using Delta Sharing
Checks for region-specific external locations/storage credentials needing updates
Recommends region-matching become a pre-flight step for future workspace relocations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses metastore region-binding as root cause
Rules out grants/ACLs as the actual problem with sound reasoning
Proposes a valid fix (region-matched metastore or Delta Sharing)
Addresses downstream concerns (external locations, process improvement)

questions.title: A Lakeflow Pipeline Is Silently Dropping Records
questions.prompt: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that ingests order events has been running green for three weeks with no failed runs, but a downstream finance reconciliation job discovers that roughly 2% of source records never made it into the target Delta table. There are no pipeline errors, no failed flows, and the run metrics show 'success.' Diagnose how this could happen and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: A pipeline reporting success while silently losing rows is almost always an expectations configuration issue: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines let you attach data-quality expectations to a flow with three distinct enforcement modes — warn (log the violation but keep the row), drop (discard the violating row but keep the pipeline green), and fail (stop the pipeline on violation). If an expectation such as a null check or a referential constraint was set to drop instead of fail, every row that violates it is quietly removed from the output and counted in the pipeline's own metrics as 'dropped by expectation,' which does not surface as a run failure because, by design, it isn't one — the pipeline did exactly what it was told to do. The reason nobody caught it for three weeks is that 'success' status and 'dropped record count' are two different signals, and the team was almost certainly only watching the former. The fix starts with checking the pipeline's event log / data quality metrics tab for the specific expectation and its violation count — that will show precisely which rows and why. Then the team needs to decide, with the business, whether those specific rows genuinely are bad data that should be dropped (in which case drop is correct but needs active monitoring and alerting on the drop count, not silent tolerance), or whether the expectation is too strict or miscoded and should be loosened or changed to fail so bad upstream data gets caught immediately instead of silently vanishing. Longer term, any expectation using drop in a financially sensitive pipeline should have an explicit alert threshold wired to its violation metric, because 'green pipeline' cannot be the only signal anyone is watching when correctness, not just availability, is the actual requirement.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'the pipeline isn't lying, it's just not telling you the whole story' problem. In Lakeflow, expectations have three modes, and drop is the quiet one — it strips out violating rows but still reports the run as a success, because from the pipeline's point of view it succeeded at doing exactly what you configured. So my first stop isn't the run logs, it's the data-quality metrics panel for that pipeline, where the actual drop counts per expectation live. Once I find which expectation is eating 2% of rows, the real conversation is with finance and whoever owns the source system: is dropping those rows actually correct, or did someone configure drop when they meant fail? If drop is genuinely the right call, fine, but it can't go unmonitored in a pipeline feeding financial reconciliation — I'd wire an alert on that specific violation count so a silent 2% doesn't become a silent 10% next quarter. The bigger fix is cultural: 'pipeline succeeded' and 'pipeline produced correct, complete output' are two different claims, and this incident is what happens when a team only ever checks the first one.
commonMistakes: Assumes a 'success' pipeline run guarantees complete data and looks elsewhere (source system, network) for missing rows
Doesn't know Lakeflow expectations have distinct warn/drop/fail modes with different observability implications
Finds the dropped rows but doesn't check whether drop vs. fail is actually the business-correct choice
Fixes this one expectation but doesn't audit other expectations in the same or other pipelines for the same silent-drop risk
Proposes alerting on pipeline failure status instead of on the violation/drop-count metric itself
keyPoints: Identifies expectations' drop mode as the likely silent-loss mechanism
Distinguishes 'pipeline succeeded' from 'pipeline output is complete/correct'
Locates the actual violation counts via pipeline data-quality metrics, not just run status
Evaluates whether drop vs. fail is the business-correct enforcement mode here
Proposes alerting on violation/drop counts, not just on run failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies drop-mode expectations as root cause
Explains why this is invisible to standard success/failure monitoring
Proposes locating and reviewing the specific violation metrics
Proposes a durable monitoring/alerting fix

questions.title: Databricks Job Cluster Costs Spike 10x Overnight
questions.prompt: Your Databricks cost dashboard shows DBU consumption jumped roughly 10x overnight with no new workload launched by anyone on the team, and finance is asking for an explanation before the month closes. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd expect to find.
questions.modelAnswer: A sudden 10x overnight spike with no new workload points to one of a small number of mechanisms, and the investigation should rule them in or out in order of likelihood rather than guessing. First, pull the account's cluster event logs and billable usage system tables (system.billing.usage) filtered to the spike window, grouped by cluster and job, to see which specific compute resource actually drove the jump — this turns 'costs spiked' into 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of its normal 20 minutes.' The most common root causes at this signature are: a runaway autoscaling job where a bad join or skewed partition caused the cluster to scale to its max node count and stay pinned there without actually making progress; a job whose cluster was configured without an automatic termination timeout, so it kept running (and billing) long after the job's actual work finished or failed; or a zombie all-purpose cluster that someone left running interactively and forgot, accumulating idle DBU-hours at full size overnight. Each has a distinct signature in the event log: autoscaling-to-max with flat progress looks very different from a cluster sitting idle at a fixed size for hours. Once the specific cluster and cause are identified, the immediate fix is to terminate it and look at whether a cluster policy would have prevented this — enforcing a max node count, requiring auto-termination after N minutes of idle time, and restricting interactive all-purpose clusters from running unattended overnight are all policy-level guardrails, not one-off fixes. For the finance conversation, the answer needs to be the specific mechanism and dollar amount, plus the policy change that makes this structurally harder to repeat — not just 'we turned off a cluster.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I say anything to finance, I want the actual billing data, not a guess — so I'm pulling system.billing.usage filtered to the spike window and grouping by cluster to find exactly which compute resource drove the number up tenfold. In my experience this is almost always one of three things: a job that autoscaled to its ceiling and got stuck there churning on a bad join, a cluster with no auto-termination timeout that just kept running after the actual work was done, or an all-purpose cluster someone left running interactively overnight. Whichever it is, I want to be able to tell finance the specific story — 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of 20 minutes because of a skewed join' — rather than a vague apology. And the fix I bring back isn't just killing that one cluster; it's a cluster policy that caps max nodes and forces auto-termination, because the actual failure here is that nothing was stopping a misbehaving job from running up an unbounded bill, and that's a policy gap, not a one-off mistake by whoever launched the job.
commonMistakes: Speculates about the cause without pulling actual billing/usage system table data first
Doesn't distinguish between autoscaling-to-max-with-no-progress vs. simple idle/forgotten cluster — different root causes, different fixes
Fixes the one cluster but doesn't propose a cluster policy to prevent recurrence
Doesn't consider that a missing auto-termination timeout is often the simplest and most common cause
Reports the dollar impact to finance without identifying the specific mechanism
keyPoints: Uses system.billing.usage / cluster event logs to find the specific resource responsible
Distinguishes runaway autoscaling, missing auto-termination, and zombie interactive clusters as distinct causes
Connects root cause to a specific, verifiable story (which cluster, how long, why)
Proposes cluster policies (max nodes, auto-termination) as the durable fix
Separates the immediate incident fix from the structural prevention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes concrete investigation using billing/usage data
Correctly enumerates plausible root-cause mechanisms
Proposes cluster policy guardrails as the durable fix
Frames findings in terms finance/stakeholders can act on

questions.title: A Kafka Consumer Group Spirals Into a Rebalance Storm After Failover
questions.prompt: After a datacenter failover, a critical Kafka consumer group with 24 consumers across 8 pods gets stuck cycling through rebalances every 30-60 seconds for over an hour, and lag climbs continuously even though the pods all report healthy. Diagnose what's likely happening and how you'd stabilize it.
questions.modelAnswer: A rebalance storm after a failover almost always traces to the session/heartbeat and max-poll-interval settings interacting badly with a sudden load or latency change, rather than any single consumer actually being unhealthy. The most likely mechanism: after failover, brokers or network paths changed, so poll latency or processing time per batch increased for some consumers; if a consumer's processing time between polls exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the broker's group coordinator considers it dead and evicts it, triggering a rebalance — but the consumer itself never crashed, so it rejoins, triggers another rebalance to get repartitioned, and if its processing is still too slow under the new conditions, it gets evicted again, producing exactly the 30-60 second cycling observed. Each rebalance also pauses the entire group's consumption (classic eager rebalancing stops all partition assignment during the protocol), which is why lag climbs continuously — the group spends more time rebalancing than actually consuming. The fix has an immediate and a structural layer. Immediately: check consumer logs for 'Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing' and 'member sent heartbeat but is marked as leaving' patterns to confirm this specific cause, then either reduce batch processing time per poll (smaller max.poll.records) or raise max.poll.interval.ms to give slower post-failover processing enough headroom to complete without eviction. Structurally, migrating to incremental cooperative rebalancing (the CooperativeStickyAssignor) prevents full-group stop-the-world rebalances, since it reassigns only the partitions that actually need to move rather than revoking every partition from every consumer on each rebalance — this alone would have kept the other partitions consuming throughout the incident instead of stalling the whole group.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd tell the incident channel first is: nobody's actually crashed, this is a rebalance loop, and the usual cause after a failover is that something got slower — network hop, broker response time, whatever — and now some consumers are taking longer between polls than max.poll.interval.ms allows, so the coordinator keeps kicking them out and triggering a rebalance, they rejoin, and if they're still slow, they get kicked again. That's your 30-60 second cycle. I'd grep consumer logs for heartbeat-failed-during-rebalance messages to confirm it, then buy headroom immediately by either raising max.poll.interval.ms or shrinking max.poll.records so each poll cycle finishes faster. But the fix I actually want to land afterward is switching this group to the cooperative sticky assignor instead of the default eager one, because eager rebalancing stops every partition in the group on every rebalance — which is exactly why lag climbed even on the consumers that were fine. Cooperative rebalancing only reassigns what actually needs to move, so a bad apple doesn't stall the whole barrel next time.
commonMistakes: Assumes consumer pods are actually crashing/restarting rather than being evicted and rejoining
Doesn't connect increased post-failover latency to max.poll.interval.ms eviction
Doesn't recognize eager rebalancing pauses the entire group, explaining why healthy consumers also show rising lag
Jumps to restarting pods or scaling consumers without diagnosing the actual eviction loop
Doesn't propose the cooperative sticky assignor as the structural fix
keyPoints: Diagnoses eviction due to exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, not consumer crashes
Explains why lag climbs even on healthy consumers (eager rebalancing stops the whole group)
Confirms via consumer log patterns (heartbeat/rebalance messages)
Proposes immediate relief (poll interval/batch size tuning)
Proposes cooperative sticky assignor as the structural fix to avoid stop-the-world rebalances

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the eviction-rejoin rebalance loop mechanism
Explains why healthy consumers' lag also rises (eager rebalance)
Proposes correct immediate mitigation
Proposes cooperative rebalancing as structural fix

questions.title: A Breaking Schema Change Takes Down Six Downstream Consumers at Once
questions.prompt: A producer team pushes a change to an Avro schema for the orders topic that renames a required field, and within minutes six downstream consumer applications start throwing deserialization exceptions. The schema registry is running in backward-compatibility mode. Explain how this got through, and design both the immediate fix and a process change to prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer: Backward compatibility mode checks whether consumers using the NEW schema can read data written with the OLD schema — it does not check the reverse, so it offers no protection against a change that breaks consumers who are still running the OLD schema against newly-produced data, which is exactly what happened here. Renaming a required field is, under Avro's semantics, a genuinely breaking change unless the old field name is preserved as an alias: without a matching alias, a consumer deserializing with the prior schema has no mapping for the incoming field and fails outright. Critically, backward compatibility checking would have flagged this as incompatible and rejected the registration at the registry if it had been enforced correctly — so the real question is whether compatibility checking was actually set to a mode and enforcement level that should have caught this (e.g., someone used FORWARD or NONE instead of BACKWARD, or compatibility checks were bypassed via a force-register flag), because a correctly-configured BACKWARD-compatible registry should never have accepted a field rename without an alias in the first place. The immediate fix is to roll back the schema registration to the previous version (registries support this) so existing consumers resume working, then have the producer team add the rename as an alias-preserving change or, better, add the new field name without removing the old one and run both in parallel during a deprecation window. The process fix is to require schema changes to go through a CI check that calls the registry's compatibility-check API before merge, not at production-push time, and to adopt a stricter default compatibility mode like FULL (requiring both backward and forward compatibility) for shared, multi-consumer topics like orders, since backward-only is not sufficient protection when a dozen independent teams consume the same topic.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify for the team, because it's the actual root cause here, is that 'backward compatible' doesn't mean 'safe for everyone' — it means new-schema consumers can read old data, not that old-schema consumers can survive new data, and a field rename without an alias breaks exactly the direction backward compatibility doesn't check. So either the registry wasn't actually enforcing BACKWARD mode correctly, or someone force-pushed past the check, because a properly enforced backward-compatible registry should have rejected this rename outright. Immediate move: roll the schema registration back to the previous version so the six consumers recover right away, then tell the producer team the rename needs to come back as an additive change — new field alongside the old one, deprecate on a timeline, never a same-release rename. Longer term, I don't want compatibility checking happening implicitly at push time at all; I want it gated in CI before merge, and for a shared topic like orders with a dozen consumers, I'd push for FULL compatibility as the default, not backward-only, because backward-only clearly wasn't enough protection for a topic this widely consumed.
commonMistakes: Assumes 'backward compatible' mode would have caught any breaking change, without understanding its directionality
Doesn't recognize a field rename needs an alias to be non-breaking under Avro semantics
Fixes the immediate outage (rollback) without investigating why the registry allowed the change through
Proposes no CI-level gating, leaving the same bypass possible next time
Doesn't consider upgrading to FULL compatibility for a widely-shared topic
keyPoints: Explains backward-compatibility directionality correctly (new schema reads old data, not vice versa)
Identifies the rename-without-alias as the specific breaking change
Investigates why the registry check didn't block the change (misconfigured mode or bypass)
Proposes rollback as immediate fix and additive/alias-based change as the correct producer fix
Proposes CI-gated compatibility checks and stricter (FULL) mode for shared topics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains backward-compatibility semantics and why this slipped through
Proposes correct immediate recovery action
Proposes correct producer-side fix (additive/alias, not rename)
Proposes process fix: CI gating and/or stricter compatibility mode

questions.title: Exactly-Once Semantics Quietly Break After a Kafka Transactional Producer Restart
questions.prompt: A Kafka Streams application configured with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 is restarted after a crash, and a downstream audit discovers a small number of duplicate records in the output topic — something the team believed exactly-once guarantees should have prevented entirely. Diagnose how duplicates could still appear and what you'd check.
questions.modelAnswer: Exactly-once semantics in Kafka guarantee that a transactional producer's writes across its input offset commits and output records are atomic — either the whole set of writes for a transaction commits or none of it does — but that guarantee is scoped to the Kafka cluster boundary and to records produced through the same transactional producer with a consistent transactional.id. The most common ways duplicates still appear despite exactly_once_v2 being configured are: first, if any part of the pipeline writes to a non-Kafka sink (a database, an external API call, a side effect inside a transform) as part of processing a record, that write is entirely outside Kafka's transactional boundary and will be re-executed on reprocessing after a crash, since Kafka can only guarantee exactly-once for the Kafka-to-Kafka portion of the pipeline, not external side effects; second, if the transactional.id was not held stable across the restart — for instance if it's generated dynamically per-instance rather than being a stable per-partition identity — the producer may be treated as a new transactional session rather than resuming the prior one, which breaks the fencing mechanism that prevents zombie-producer duplicate writes; third, if the consumer reading the output topic downstream is itself not read_committed (isolation.level=read_committed), it will read uncommitted/aborted transactional records that later got rolled back, appearing as duplicates or phantom data. The investigation should check all three in order: confirm whether any non-Kafka side effects exist in the topology, confirm transactional.id generation is stable and partition-scoped across restarts, and confirm every downstream consumer explicitly sets read_committed rather than relying on the (non-transactional) default read_uncommitted behavior for non-Streams consumers.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd push back on gently is the assumption baked into 'exactly-once should have prevented this entirely' — Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka writes inside the transactional boundary, it is not a blanket guarantee over the whole pipeline. So my first question is whether this topology has any side effect outside Kafka — a database write, an API call — because those happen outside the transaction and will absolutely replay on restart no matter how correctly exactly_once_v2 is configured. If there's nothing external, my next check is the transactional.id: it has to be stable and partition-scoped across restarts for Kafka's producer fencing to actually resume the same transactional identity instead of starting a new one, which is a surprisingly easy thing to get wrong if it's generated per-process-start instead of per-partition. And last, I'd check every downstream consumer's isolation.level — if anything reading that output topic is sitting on the default read_uncommitted instead of explicit read_committed, it's going to see aborted transactional writes as if they were real, which looks exactly like a duplicate. Exactly-once is a precise, scoped guarantee, and duplicates usually mean something fell just outside that scope, not that the guarantee itself failed.
commonMistakes: Assumes exactly_once_v2 is a blanket guarantee across the entire pipeline including non-Kafka side effects
Doesn't check for external (non-Kafka) writes inside the processing topology as the likely real cause
Doesn't know transactional.id must remain stable/partition-scoped across restarts for fencing to work correctly
Doesn't check downstream consumers' isolation.level, assuming read_committed is the default everywhere
Treats this as a Kafka bug rather than a scoping/configuration issue
keyPoints: Explains exactly-once is scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka transactional writes, not external side effects
Identifies non-Kafka side effects in the topology as a primary duplicate source
Checks transactional.id stability across restarts for correct producer fencing
Checks downstream consumers' isolation.level (read_committed vs. default read_uncommitted)
Correctly frames this as a scoping issue, not a Kafka guarantee failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the scope of Kafka exactly-once guarantees
Identifies external side effects as a likely duplicate source
Checks transactional.id stability/fencing across restarts
Checks downstream consumer isolation.level

questions.title: Auto Loader Is Falling Behind and Cloud Notification Costs Are Spiking
questions.prompt: A production Auto Loader stream in file notification mode is both falling further behind the arrival rate every day and generating an unexpectedly large cloud bill from the queue service it depends on. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether the bottleneck is discovery, processing, or the queue configuration itself, and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by separating discovery from processing using the Spark UI / streaming query listener metrics: if numFilesOutstanding and backlog in the Auto Loader source metrics are climbing while batch processing duration stays flat, the stream can't keep up with intake, not that each batch is slow — that points at under-provisioned compute or a maxFilesPerTrigger/maxBytesPerTrigger cap set too low relative to arrival rate. If instead batch duration itself is growing, the bottleneck is downstream (a wide transformation, a shuffle-heavy join, or small-file compaction pressure from too many tiny output files), not discovery. Separately, I'd check the queue (SQS/Event Grid/Pub-Sub) directly: rising ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible with a flat consumption rate confirms Auto Loader isn't draining it fast enough, which again is a compute/throughput issue, not a notification-volume issue. The cost spike is a distinct question: file notification mode bills per notification and per queue poll, so if the source is producing a flood of very small files, the fix isn't more compute, it's reducing file-notification volume at the source — batching upstream writes into fewer, larger files, or if the upstream can't change, enabling cloudFiles.useNotifications with a longer backfill interval and tuning maxFilesPerTrigger upward so each trigger drains more of the backlog per queue poll instead of polling constantly for tiny gains. I'd also check for an accidentally duplicated or orphaned notification setup (a second Auto Loader stream or an old backfill job still registered against the same queue), which silently doubles notification cost without doubling useful throughput.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split the investigation into two separate questions, because 'falling behind' and 'costing too much' aren't necessarily the same root cause. For falling behind, I pull the streaming metrics and ask: is the backlog of undiscovered files growing, or is each micro-batch just taking longer? Growing backlog with flat batch time means discovery or trigger sizing is the problem — I'd bump maxFilesPerTrigger and check the cluster isn't under-provisioned. Growing batch time points downstream, at the transformation logic, not Auto Loader itself. For the cost spike, I'd go straight to the queue metrics — if message volume is through the roof, that's almost always a small-files problem upstream, so I'd push to get the source writing fewer, larger files before I touch anything on the Databricks side, because no amount of Spark tuning fixes a notification bill driven by file count. And I'd specifically check for an orphaned second consumer or leftover backfill job quietly polling the same queue — that's a classic silent-cost bug.
commonMistakes: Throws more compute at the cluster without first confirming whether the bottleneck is discovery, processing, or queue drain rate
Treats the cost spike and the backlog growth as the same root cause without checking separately
Doesn't check for a duplicated/orphaned consumer silently polling the same notification queue
Tunes maxFilesPerTrigger down (thinking it reduces cost) when the real fix is addressing small-file volume at the source
keyPoints: Distinguishes discovery backlog from processing-duration bottleneck using streaming metrics
Checks queue-level metrics directly to confirm drain rate vs. arrival rate
Identifies small-file volume at the source as the primary driver of notification cost
Proposes addressing file size/volume upstream rather than only tuning Databricks-side settings
Checks for an orphaned/duplicated consumer against the same queue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates discovery vs. processing bottleneck diagnosis
Correctly diagnoses the cost spike via queue-level metrics
Identifies small-file volume as the likely cost driver and proposes a source-side fix
Checks for an orphaned/duplicated consumer

questions.title: Cross-Workspace Access Denied Despite Correct Unity Catalog Grants
questions.prompt: A data engineer has been granted SELECT on a table and can query it fine from Workspace A, but gets a permission-denied error querying the exact same table from Workspace B. The grant clearly exists when checked with SHOW GRANTS. Walk through the likely causes and how you'd diagnose which one it is.
questions.modelAnswer: Since SHOW GRANTS confirms the table-level grant exists, the problem is almost never the grant itself — it's something environmental to Workspace B. First I'd check whether Workspace B is attached to the same metastore as Workspace A at all (Account Console > workspace > metastore assignment); if B is attached to a different metastore, the table simply doesn't exist in B's catalog namespace regardless of any grant in A's metastore, which is the most common version of this problem. Second, assuming it is the same metastore, I'd check whether the user's identity is resolved consistently across both workspaces — if the account uses SCIM provisioning and the user or their group membership hasn't synced into Workspace B yet, is_account_group_member()-based checks (or even direct user grants tied to account identity) can resolve differently. Third, I'd check for a workspace-level catalog binding: Unity Catalog supports restricting which catalogs are even assignable to a given workspace, so a catalog can exist in the shared metastore but be explicitly unbound from Workspace B, which blocks access there independent of table grants. Fourth, I'd check cluster/SQL warehouse configuration in Workspace B — an old, non-Unity-Catalog-enabled cluster (no-isolation-shared mode predating UC, or a cluster pinned to a legacy Hive metastore) would simply never evaluate Unity Catalog grants in the first place and would fail or silently resolve against a different catalog.
questions.professionalAnswer: Because the grant itself checks out, I immediately stop thinking about permissions and start thinking about plumbing. First question: are both workspaces even attached to the same metastore? That's the single most common cause of 'the grant exists but doesn't work here' — if B is on a different metastore, the table isn't visible there at all, grant or no grant. If they are on the same metastore, I'd check whether the catalog is actually bound to Workspace B — Unity Catalog lets admins restrict which workspaces can see which catalogs, and that's an easy thing to forget during a workspace onboarding. Then I'd check identity sync — if this account's group membership hasn't propagated to Workspace B yet, a group-based grant can look fine in A and fail in B. And finally I'd just check what compute they're running on in B — if it's an old cluster that predates Unity Catalog enablement, none of this matters because it's never even asking Unity Catalog for permission.
commonMistakes: Re-checks or re-applies the same grant repeatedly instead of investigating workspace/metastore attachment
Assumes identity is automatically consistent across workspaces without checking SCIM/group sync status
Doesn't know catalogs can be explicitly bound/unbound per workspace independent of grants
Overlooks that the compute resource in Workspace B might not be Unity-Catalog-enabled at all
keyPoints: Checks whether both workspaces share the same metastore first
Checks catalog-to-workspace binding as a separate layer from table grants
Checks identity/group sync consistency across workspaces
Checks whether the compute resource in the failing workspace is Unity-Catalog-enabled
Correctly reasons that the grant itself is unlikely to be the fault given SHOW GRANTS confirms it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies metastore attachment as the primary suspect
Identifies catalog-to-workspace binding as a distinct possible cause
Identifies identity/group sync as a possible cause
Identifies compute/cluster Unity-Catalog-enablement as a possible cause

questions.title: A Lakeflow Pipeline Keeps Failing Its Expectations in Production
questions.prompt: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that has run cleanly for months suddenly starts failing a fail-severity expectation on every run, blocking the whole pipeline. The on-call engineer's instinct is to just change the expectation from expect_or_fail to expect so the pipeline stops blocking. Walk through how you'd actually triage this and why you'd push back on that fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A fail-severity expectation that held for months and suddenly breaks on every run is almost always a signal that something upstream changed, not that the expectation was wrong — so the first move is the pipeline's event log and data quality metrics to see exactly which rows are failing and what they look like, not to touch the expectation definition. I'd check the bronze source for a recent schema change (a new nullable field, a type change, a renamed column that's now landing as null under the old name), check whether an upstream job or vendor feed changed its export format or timezone handling around the same time the failures started, and check whether this coincides with a backfill or late-arriving batch that's structurally different from steady-state data. Downgrading expect_or_fail to expect would make the symptom disappear from the on-call's perspective, but it would also mean whatever is now violating the primary-key-or-equivalent guarantee silently flows into silver and every downstream consumer from that point forward, which converts a loud, contained, at-the-door failure into a quiet, systemic data-quality incident that's far more expensive to unwind later. I'd push back on the severity change specifically and instead either fix the upstream cause, or, if the business rule genuinely changed (e.g., nulls are now legitimately allowed here), update the expectation's logic to reflect the new, intentional rule — not just lower its enforcement level.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop the on-call engineer before they touch the expectation itself, because downgrading expect_or_fail to expect doesn't fix anything — it just hides the symptom and lets whatever broke flow straight into silver. Instead I'd go look at what actually changed: pull the failing rows from the event log, and check whether the upstream source changed its schema, format, or an export job around the same time this started. Nine times out of ten this is a vendor or upstream team quietly renaming or retyping a field. Once I know the real cause, there are two legitimate outcomes: either we fix the upstream issue and the expectation goes back to passing as-is, or we learn the business rule genuinely changed, in which case we update the expectation's logic to reflect the new reality — but we don't just lower its severity to make the alert go away, because that's choosing not to know about a real problem instead of solving it.
commonMistakes: Immediately downgrades the expectation severity to unblock the pipeline without investigating the cause
Doesn't check the upstream source for a recent schema/format change coinciding with the failure onset
Treats 'the pipeline runs again' as success rather than 'the underlying data problem is resolved'
Fails to distinguish 'the expectation is now wrong because the business rule changed' from 'the data is now wrong and the expectation correctly caught it'
keyPoints: Investigates the event log/failing rows before touching the expectation
Checks for an upstream schema, format, or export change coinciding with the failure onset
Explains why downgrading severity converts a contained failure into a silent downstream data-quality issue
Distinguishes a genuine business-rule change (update the expectation logic) from a data problem (fix upstream)
Pushes back on the severity-downgrade fix with a clear rationale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes investigating root cause via event log/failing rows before any fix
Correctly identifies likely upstream causes to check
Explains the real risk of downgrading expectation severity
Distinguishes a legitimate business-rule update from masking a data problem

questions.title: Databricks Workflows Cost Is Spiraling Across a Multi-Team Platform
questions.prompt: Monthly Databricks compute spend has tripled in a quarter, and the finance team is asking the platform team to explain it before approving next quarter's budget. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether the cause is orchestration design (serial vs. parallel tasks, job cluster reuse), workload growth, or something else, and what you'd fix first.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start with the system tables (system.billing.usage joined to job run metadata) to break total spend down by job/workflow rather than guessing, because 'cost tripled' could mean a few jobs got dramatically more expensive or the whole platform's workload volume genuinely tripled — those require completely different fixes. If spend-per-run for existing jobs is flat but run count/data volume grew proportionally with the business, that's legitimate growth, and the conversation with finance is about unit economics, not a bug. If a small number of jobs show dramatically higher per-run cost, I'd look at their task graphs next: a common anti-pattern is a workflow where tasks that could run in parallel are chained serially, which doesn't increase total compute-seconds dramatically but does increase wall-clock job-cluster lifetime (and therefore cost, since the cluster sits paying for idle wait between dependent serial steps that didn't need to be sequential). Another common anti-pattern is each task in a multi-task job spinning up its own fresh job cluster instead of sharing one cluster across tasks in the same job — that multiplies cluster startup overhead and can leave several clusters running concurrently when one right-sized cluster would do. I'd also check for jobs accidentally pointed at idle all-purpose clusters that are now running 24/7 because a job keeps the cluster's auto-termination timer from firing. Finally, I'd check for duplicate or redundant jobs — multiple teams independently built similar pipelines against the same source because there was no shared, governed version, which is a platform/catalog-discovery problem, not a tuning problem, and is unusually common past a certain team count.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch anything, I'd pull cost by job from the billing system tables, because I want to know if this is a few expensive jobs or the whole platform growing. If it's proportional to real usage growth, that's a finance conversation about unit economics, not an engineering fix. If it's concentrated in specific jobs, I go straight to their task graphs and look for two classic patterns: tasks chained serially that didn't need to be, which burns cluster time on idle waiting, and each task spinning up its own cluster instead of sharing one within the job, which multiplies startup overhead and sometimes leaves multiple clusters running at once for no reason. I'd also check whether any production jobs are quietly pointed at an always-on all-purpose cluster instead of an ephemeral job cluster — that's a very common, very expensive mistake. And past a certain org size I always check for duplicate pipelines — different teams independently solving the same ingestion problem because there was no visibility into what already existed is a governance gap, not a compute-tuning gap, and no amount of cluster-sizing fixes that.
commonMistakes: Jumps to cluster-sizing recommendations before breaking down which jobs actually drove the cost increase
Doesn't distinguish legitimate workload growth from an orchestration/configuration regression
Misses serial-task-chaining and per-task cluster duplication as specific, diagnosable anti-patterns
Overlooks duplicate/redundant pipelines across teams as a governance-level cause, not a tuning-level one
keyPoints: Uses billing/usage system tables to break cost down by job rather than guessing
Distinguishes legitimate workload growth from a design/configuration regression
Diagnoses serial-vs-parallel task chaining as a cost driver via wall-clock cluster lifetime
Diagnoses per-task cluster duplication vs. shared job-cluster usage
Considers duplicate/redundant cross-team pipelines as a platform-governance cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes data-driven cost breakdown by job before diagnosing
Correctly distinguishes growth from a design regression
Diagnoses serial task chaining and cluster-sharing anti-patterns
Considers cross-team duplication as a governance-level cause

questions.title: A Delta Sharing Recipient Reports Stale or Missing Data
questions.prompt: An external partner receiving data through Delta Sharing reports that the numbers they're seeing are out of date or that rows they expect are missing, while your own internal queries against the same source table look correct. Walk through how you'd diagnose where in the sharing path the discrepancy is coming from.
questions.modelAnswer: Because internal queries against the source table look correct, the data itself is fine, so the investigation is entirely about what the share is actually exposing. First I'd check whether the share is pointing at the table itself or at a snapshot/view with a stale definition — DESCRIBE SHARE / SHOW ALL IN SHARE shows exactly which object and, if applicable, which historical version or time-travel pin is attached; a share can be explicitly bound to a specific table version for stability, which is correct behavior for some use cases but will look exactly like 'stale data' to a partner if nobody told them it's intentionally pinned. Second, I'd check if the shared object is a dynamic view with its own filtering logic (for row-level security on the shared data) — if that view's predicate is wrong or references a stale reference table, the partner would see fewer rows than the base table has, which looks like 'missing data' but is actually a filter working as designed, just incorrectly configured. Third, I'd check the recipient's own client-side caching or refresh schedule — many BI tools and even some Delta Sharing connectors cache query results or only poll periodically, so the partner's tool might simply not have re-queried since the last update, which is a client-side problem, not a provider-side one. Fourth, I'd check for a partition or column-level share scoped to only part of the table (ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE supports a partition filter), which, if someone added it for a legitimate reason and then the partitioning upstream changed, would silently start excluding rows that used to be included.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since our own queries against the source look fine, I know the problem lives somewhere in the sharing path, not the data itself, so I'd check that path end to end. First: what exactly is in the share — is it the live table, or did someone pin it to a specific version for stability reasons without telling the partner? That alone explains 'stale.' Second: is the shared object a view with its own row-filtering logic for the partner's restricted access — if that filter's underlying reference data changed, the partner could legitimately see fewer rows now, which looks like 'missing' but is the filter doing its job on bad inputs. Third, and I always check this before assuming it's our problem: is the partner's own tool caching results or on a slow refresh schedule — that's an extremely common false alarm. And fourth, if the share was scoped to a specific partition range, I'd check whether upstream partitioning changed since, because that would silently start leaving new data outside the shared scope.
commonMistakes: Assumes the problem must be on the provider's underlying table without checking what the share object itself actually points to
Doesn't check for a version pin or partition filter on the ADD TABLE statement
Overlooks that the shared object might be a row-filtered view, not the raw table
Doesn't rule out client-side caching/refresh behavior on the recipient's end before escalating internally
keyPoints: Confirms the data itself is correct and scopes the investigation to the sharing path specifically
Checks whether the share is pinned to a specific version or time-travel snapshot
Checks whether the shared object is a filtered view with potentially faulty filter logic
Considers recipient-side caching/refresh behavior as a possible non-provider cause
Checks for a partition/column scope on the share that may have become stale as upstream structure changed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes the investigation to the share definition, not the base table
Checks for version pinning/time-travel on the share
Checks for filtered-view or partition-scope causes
Considers recipient-side caching as a possible cause

questions.title: Design a Multi-Datacenter Kafka Replication Architecture With Schema Governance
questions.prompt: A company operates Kafka clusters in three datacenters (US-East, US-West, EU) for regulatory data-residency and latency reasons, but needs a consistent view of certain global topics (like a product catalog) across all three, plus a single governed schema evolution process that doesn't let any one region break the others. Design the replication topology and schema governance model, and justify active/active versus active/passive for the topics involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The topology decision should be made per-topic-class, not globally, because 'active/active vs active/passive' is really a question about who legitimately produces to a topic. For genuinely global, single-source-of-truth data like a product catalog, I'd use active/passive replication (via a tool like MirrorMaker 2 or a managed cross-region replication service): one region is authoritative and produces to the canonical topic, and the other two regions consume a replicated, read-only copy — this avoids the conflict-resolution problem entirely, since there is never a case where the same key is written independently in two regions and needs reconciling. For topics where each region genuinely needs to produce its own regional data that must also be visible globally (e.g., regional order events that roll up into a global reporting topic), active/active replication is appropriate, but only with a deliberate partitioning/keying strategy that guarantees no two regions ever own the same partition or key space, so active/active never actually means 'conflicting concurrent writes to the same record' — it means 'independent writes to disjoint key spaces that get aggregated,' which sidesteps the hard conflict-resolution problem that true multi-master systems face. Regulatory data residency constrains this further: PII or regulated data that must stay in-region per compliance never gets replicated at all; only the global reference/catalog-type topics cross regional boundaries. For schema governance, a single global schema registry cluster (replicated across regions, or a managed service with multi-region support) should be the system of record for every topic's schema, with compatibility mode set to FULL for globally-replicated topics specifically, since both the authoritative region's producers and every consuming region's consumers must remain mutually compatible — a region-local, weaker compatibility mode on a globally-replicated topic is exactly how one region's local schema change silently breaks consumers in another region. Schema changes to any globally-replicated topic should go through a change-management process requiring sign-off from a cross-region data governance owner, not just the originating region's team, precisely because a change that looks safe locally can break consumers thousands of miles away who have no visibility into that team's release process.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to refuse to answer 'active/active or active/passive' as one global decision, because it's really a per-topic question about who's actually authoritative. For something like the product catalog, there's exactly one source of truth, so active/passive is the obvious and simplest choice — one region produces, the other two get a replicated read-only copy via MirrorMaker 2 or a managed replication service, and there's no conflict resolution to design because there's never a conflicting write. Where I would consider active/active is for genuinely regional data that rolls up globally, like per-region order events, but only if I can guarantee each region owns a disjoint key space — active/active for me never means 'two regions might write the same key,' because that's a conflict-resolution problem I don't want to own if I can design around it. Data residency adds a hard constraint underneath all of this: anything regulated stays in-region, full stop, only the genuinely global reference data crosses borders. On schema governance, I want one registry as the system of record across all three regions, and for any topic that's globally replicated, I'm setting FULL compatibility, not backward-only, because a globally-replicated topic has producers and consumers in different regions who absolutely need mutual compatibility in both directions — and any schema change to one of those topics needs a sign-off from someone who can see the whole picture, not just the originating region's own release process.
commonMistakes: Picks one topology (active/active or active/passive) globally instead of deciding per topic class based on authoritative ownership
Proposes active/active without a disjoint key-space/partitioning strategy, reintroducing the conflict-resolution problem
Doesn't account for data-residency constraints preventing regulated data from replicating across regions at all
Proposes region-local schema registries instead of a single governed registry as system of record
Uses backward-only compatibility for globally-replicated topics instead of FULL, missing the bidirectional need
keyPoints: Decides topology per topic class based on authoritative ownership, not as one global choice
Uses active/passive for single-source-of-truth global data (e.g. product catalog)
If using active/active, requires a disjoint key-space strategy to avoid real conflict resolution
Respects data-residency constraints by excluding regulated data from cross-region replication
Uses a single governed schema registry with FULL compatibility for globally-replicated topics
Requires cross-region governance sign-off for schema changes to global topics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons topology choice per topic class, not globally
Sound active/passive vs active/active justification with conflict-avoidance reasoning
Correctly incorporates data-residency constraints
Sound schema governance model (single registry, FULL compatibility, cross-region sign-off)

questions.title: Design Exactly-Once Ingestion From Kafka Into a Delta Lakehouse at Scale
questions.prompt: Design an ingestion pipeline that reads payment-event records from a high-throughput Kafka topic (roughly 20,000 events/sec at peak) into a Delta Lake table, with a hard requirement that no payment event is ever duplicated or lost in the target table, even across consumer crashes, cluster restarts, and Kafka broker failovers.
questions.modelAnswer: Exactly-once end-to-end from Kafka into Delta requires chaining two separate exactly-once mechanisms correctly, because neither Kafka's exactly-once producer guarantee nor Delta's transactional guarantees alone span the whole pipeline. On the read side, I'd use Databricks Structured Streaming (or an equivalent Lakeflow streaming flow) reading from Kafka with checkpointing enabled against a durable checkpoint location (cloud storage, not local disk) — the checkpoint records exactly which Kafka offsets have been durably committed into Delta, and on restart after any crash, Structured Streaming resumes from the last committed checkpoint offset rather than the consumer group's own committed offset, which is what gives it crash-safe, exactly-once-from-the-source-topic semantics rather than relying on Kafka consumer group offset commits (which can drift out of sync with what was actually durably written downstream). On the write side, Delta Lake's ACID transaction log means each micro-batch write either fully commits or doesn't happen at all, so a crash mid-write never leaves a half-written batch visible to readers — combined with Structured Streaming's checkpoint-offset coordination, a batch is either fully committed to Delta with its offset range marked done, or the whole batch (data and offset progress) is retried from scratch, which is what prevents both duplicates and gaps across the Kafka-to-Delta boundary specifically. For genuine defense in depth against any remaining edge case (e.g., a schema that allows a payment event's natural key to be known), I'd add an idempotent merge pattern as a second layer: write micro-batches to a staging table, then MERGE INTO the target table using the payment event's unique transaction ID as the match key, so even in some theoretical edge case where the same offset range got reprocessed, the merge's upsert-on-key semantics make reprocessing a no-op rather than a duplicate row. At 20,000 events/sec, partition the Kafka topic and the Structured Streaming job's parallelism to match (sufficient Kafka partitions and Spark task parallelism to avoid becoming consumer-lag-bound), and size the Delta table's file layout (via OPTIMIZE/auto-compaction) to avoid the small-file problem that high-frequency micro-batch commits would otherwise create over time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about 'exactly-once from Kafka into Delta' is that it's actually two separate guarantees that need to be chained correctly, not one single setting I flip on. On the read side, I want Structured Streaming's checkpointing, pointed at durable cloud storage, because that's what gives me 'resume exactly where I left off' after a crash — critically, resuming from the checkpoint's committed offset, not from Kafka's own consumer group offset, which can get out of sync with what actually landed in Delta. On the write side, Delta's transaction log means a micro-batch either fully commits or it doesn't happen at all, so there's no such thing as a half-written batch becoming visible — and because Structured Streaming ties offset progress to that same transactional commit, a crash mid-batch means the whole batch retries, not a duplicate-or-gap situation. For something as sensitive as payment events, though, I don't stop there — I'd add a MERGE INTO using the payment's unique transaction ID as the key, so even in some edge case I haven't thought of, reprocessing the same event becomes a no-op upsert instead of a duplicate row. That's the belt-and-suspenders answer: checkpoint-coordinated streaming for the primary exactly-once guarantee, idempotent merge on a real business key as the safety net. And at this volume, I'm also paying attention to Kafka partition count and Spark parallelism matching up, plus compaction on the Delta side, because high-frequency micro-batches will absolutely create a small-file problem if nobody's watching the file layout.
commonMistakes: Relies on Kafka consumer group offset commits alone instead of Structured Streaming's checkpoint-based offset tracking
Assumes Delta's transactional guarantee alone is sufficient without addressing read-side offset/crash coordination
Doesn't propose an idempotent merge/upsert-by-business-key as defense in depth for a payment-sensitive use case
Ignores the small-file problem that high-frequency micro-batch commits create without compaction
Doesn't address partition/parallelism sizing for the stated 20,000 events/sec throughput
keyPoints: Uses Structured Streaming checkpointing against durable storage for crash-safe offset tracking
Explains why checkpoint-coordinated offsets beat relying on Kafka consumer group commits alone
Uses Delta's ACID transaction log to guarantee all-or-nothing micro-batch commits
Adds idempotent MERGE INTO on a business key as defense-in-depth for payment-sensitive data
Addresses partition/parallelism sizing and file-layout/compaction for the stated throughput

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs checkpoint-based exactly-once read coordination
Correctly explains Delta's transactional write guarantee role
Proposes idempotent merge as defense-in-depth for payment data
Addresses scale considerations (partitioning, parallelism, compaction)

questions.title: Design an Org-Wide Cost Governance Model for Databricks Clusters
questions.prompt: A company with 15 teams running Databricks workloads has no consistent cluster governance — some teams run all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs, auto-termination is inconsistently configured, and nobody has visibility into which team is driving which cost. Design a cost governance model covering cluster policy, job vs. all-purpose usage, and budget accountability.
questions.modelAnswer: The core architectural tool here is Databricks cluster policies, which let a platform team define and enforce constraints (max node count, allowed instance types, mandatory auto-termination timeout, mandatory tags) at the policy level so individual engineers can't configure a cluster outside acceptable bounds — rather than relying on 15 teams to independently remember and apply cost best practices, the policy becomes the enforced default. I'd design a small set of tiered policies: a 'job cluster' policy for scheduled/automated workloads (ephemeral, spun up per job, auto-terminating on completion, which is inherently cheaper than persistent all-purpose clusters for anything non-interactive), and an 'interactive/all-purpose' policy with a mandatory short auto-termination timeout (e.g., 30-60 minutes of idle time) and a capped max node count, since all-purpose clusters are for active development, not for running unattended scheduled jobs — the current state of 'teams run all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs' is itself the single biggest avoidable cost driver, since job clusters are billed only for the job's actual runtime while all-purpose clusters bill for however long they stay up, idle or not. Every policy should mandate cost-attribution tags (team, cost-center, environment) at cluster-creation time, enforced by the policy itself rather than relying on voluntary tagging discipline, which is what makes real chargeback possible afterward. For visibility, the Databricks system tables (system.billing.usage joined to cluster tags) feed a cost dashboard broken down by team/cost-center, reviewed on a regular cadence — and budget accountability means each team gets a visible, owned number, with alerting when a team's trailing consumption trend suggests they'll exceed a set threshold, so a cost conversation happens proactively rather than at month-end reconciliation. Migrating existing ad hoc all-purpose-for-scheduled-jobs patterns to proper job clusters, enforced going forward via policy rather than a one-time cleanup, is the single highest-leverage structural change in this list.
questions.professionalAnswer: If I only get to fix one thing here, it's that teams are running all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs — that's the single most expensive habit in this list, because all-purpose clusters bill for however long they're up, idle included, while a job cluster only bills for the actual job runtime and auto-terminates the moment it's done. So step one is cluster policies: a job-cluster policy for anything scheduled/automated, and a separate interactive policy for actual development work, with a short mandatory auto-termination timeout and a capped node count baked into the policy itself, not left to each engineer's discretion. I want cost-attribution tags — team, cost center, environment — enforced at the policy level too, because voluntary tagging never survives contact with 15 different teams' habits, and without consistent tags there's no real chargeback story. Once that's in place, the system billing tables joined to those tags give me an actual per-team cost dashboard, reviewed regularly, with alerts when a team's trend is heading toward a problem — because the goal isn't to surprise anyone with a bill at month-end, it's for each team to own a visible number and see it coming.
commonMistakes: Proposes cost dashboards/reporting without addressing cluster policy enforcement as the actual root cause
Doesn't identify all-purpose-clusters-for-scheduled-jobs as the single biggest avoidable cost driver
Relies on voluntary tagging discipline instead of enforcing tags at the cluster-policy level
Doesn't distinguish appropriate use cases for job clusters vs. all-purpose clusters
No proactive alerting on cost trend, only after-the-fact monthly reporting
keyPoints: Identifies all-purpose clusters running scheduled jobs as the primary avoidable cost driver
Proposes tiered cluster policies (job vs. interactive) with enforced auto-termination and node caps
Enforces cost-attribution tags at the policy level, not via voluntary discipline
Builds per-team cost visibility from system billing tables joined to enforced tags
Adds proactive trend-based alerting, not just after-the-fact reporting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies all-purpose-for-scheduled-jobs as the primary cost driver
Proposes sound tiered cluster policy design
Proposes enforced tagging for real cost attribution
Proposes proactive cost visibility/alerting, not just reporting

questions.title: Design the Unity Catalog Metastore Topology for a Global Enterprise
questions.prompt: A multinational retailer has workspaces in North America, the EU, and APAC, around 40 data teams total, and regulatory requirements that EU customer data never leave the EU and that APAC financial data stay within specific countries in some cases. Design the Unity Catalog metastore and catalog topology, including how shared reference data (like a global product catalog) gets made available everywhere without violating residency rules.
questions.modelAnswer: Given the regulatory constraint, I'd deploy one metastore per region that has a residency requirement — a US/NA metastore, an EU metastore, and likely more than one APAC metastore if specific countries need isolation from each other, not just from the rest of the world. Each metastore attaches to the workspaces operating in its region, and each region's regulated catalogs (customer PII, financial records) live only in that region's metastore with storage credentials/external locations pointed at storage accounts physically in that region — the residency guarantee comes from where the managed/external storage actually lives, not just from access controls. For shared reference data like a global product catalog that has no residency restriction, I'd maintain it as a single source of truth in one metastore (say, NA) and distribute it to the other regions via Delta Sharing, which is the right tool here specifically because it doesn't require merging metastores or replicating raw storage access — each region gets a read-only, versioned share of the product catalog and can join it locally against regional sales data. To keep governance consistent across what is now 3-4 separate enforcement boundaries, I'd standardize catalog/schema naming, replicate group-based grant templates via Terraform across all metastores, apply the same data classification tags, and centralize audit by exporting each metastore's system tables into one global monitoring catalog (itself subject to the same residency rule — the aggregation point either needs per-region extracts with PII stripped, or regional audit stores with a unified dashboard layer on top, not a single table holding raw cross-region audit data). The 40 data teams then operate against whichever regional metastore their workspace is attached to, using identical conventions, so onboarding a new team doesn't require learning a different governance model per region, only knowing which metastore they're in.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the constraint, not the convenience: EU data can't leave the EU, so one global metastore is off the table immediately, because metastores are region-bound and I'm not going to fight that with access controls alone — the storage itself needs to physically stay put. So the design is a metastore per residency boundary: one for NA, one for EU, and probably more than one for APAC if specific countries need to be isolated from each other too. For something like a global product catalog that genuinely has no residency issue, I wouldn't try to merge it across metastores — I'd keep one source of truth and use Delta Sharing to hand each region a live, read-only copy they can join locally, which avoids both a compliance violation and a 'whose copy is correct' problem. The part I'd spend the most time on with the governance team is making the four separate metastores feel like one system to the 40 teams using them — same naming conventions, same grant patterns pushed out via Terraform, same tags, and one audit dashboard pulling from all of them — because the regulatory requirement forces multiple enforcement boundaries, but it doesn't have to force four different ways of working.
questions.example: NA metastore holds customer_pii.* and finance_us.* catalogs on US-region storage; EU metastore holds customer_pii_eu.* and finance_eu.* on EU-region storage; the global_reference catalog (product_catalog table) lives once in the NA metastore and is shared via Delta Sharing into both the EU and APAC metastores as a read-only recipient share, refreshed live with every commit.
commonMistakes: Proposes one global metastore with access controls as the only compliance boundary, ignoring that metastores and their storage are region-bound
Tries to replicate the product catalog by exporting/copying files per region instead of using Delta Sharing
Centralizes audit logs into one raw table without considering that the audit data itself might be subject to the same residency rule
Treats '40 teams, consistent governance' as requiring one metastore instead of standardized conventions across several
keyPoints: Correctly proposes a metastore per residency/compliance boundary, not one global metastore
Ties the residency guarantee to physical storage location, not just access control
Uses Delta Sharing for the shared reference data use case with correct justification
Addresses how governance stays consistent across multiple metastores (naming, grants-as-code, tagging, audit)
Considers that centralized audit aggregation may itself need to respect residency rules

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct multi-metastore topology addressing residency constraints
Sound Delta Sharing design for the shared reference data case
Addresses consistent governance across multiple metastores
Considers residency implications for audit/monitoring aggregation

questions.title: Cross-Workspace Data Sharing: Three-Level Namespace vs. Delta Sharing vs. Mounting
questions.prompt: A platform team wants Team B's workspace to be able to query tables owned by Team A, which sits in a different workspace attached to the same Unity Catalog metastore. Compare granting cross-catalog access via the standard three-level namespace, sharing via Delta Sharing, and the legacy approach of mounting Team A's storage directly in Team B's workspace. Recommend one and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Since both teams' workspaces are attached to the same metastore, the simplest and correct option is the standard three-level namespace: Team A's tables already live in a catalog within the shared metastore, so granting Team B's group USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT on the relevant objects makes them immediately queryable as catalog.schema.table from Team B's workspace with no data movement, no extra infrastructure, and full support for Unity Catalog's lineage, audit, and row/column security features, since it's the same governed object the whole time.
