Delta Sharing is the wrong tool here specifically because it's designed for crossing a governance boundary — a different metastore, a different organization, or a workspace with no feasible path to shared metastore attachment — and using it within a single metastore adds an unnecessary layer (share, recipient, activation) for a problem that a grant already solves, plus it loses some of the native in-metastore features like fine-grained lineage tracking across the share boundary. Mounting Team A's cloud storage directly into Team B's workspace is the legacy pre-Unity-Catalog pattern and should be actively avoided: it bypasses Unity Catalog governance entirely, meaning grants, lineage, row filters, and audit logging on the underlying table do nothing for anyone querying through the mount, and it creates a second, ungoverned access path into the same data that persists even after the Unity Catalog grant is revoked, which is both a security and an audit liability. The recommendation is the three-level namespace grant, reserving Delta Sharing for genuinely cross-metastore or cross-organization needs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd rule out mounting immediately — that's a pre-Unity-Catalog pattern that completely bypasses the governance we're trying to build, so even though it technically works, it creates a second ungoverned door into the data that none of our grants, lineage, or masking touches. Between the other two, it comes down to whether these teams are actually in the same metastore, and they are, so Delta Sharing is solving a problem we don't have — it's built for crossing a governance boundary, and here there isn't one to cross. The straightforward answer is just grant Team B's group SELECT on Team A's table through the normal three-level namespace; it shows up as a queryable table in their workspace immediately, with the same lineage and security features intact, and no extra moving parts like shares and recipients to maintain. I'd save Delta Sharing for the day Team B's workspace needs to live on a different metastore or a different company entirely needs this data.
commonMistakes: Recommends Delta Sharing for an in-metastore cross-workspace case where a simple grant suffices
Doesn't flag storage mounting as bypassing governance entirely, treating it as a neutral third option
Assumes grants don't work across workspaces attached to the same metastore
Fails to note that mounting persists as an access path even after the proper grant is revoked
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the three-level namespace grant as sufficient within a shared metastore
Correctly identifies Delta Sharing's intended use case (crossing a governance boundary) and why it's unnecessary here
Identifies storage mounting as bypassing Unity Catalog governance entirely and names the resulting risk
Recommends the three-level namespace grant with clear justification

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the three-level namespace option and its sufficiency here
Correctly scopes Delta Sharing's intended use case
Correctly identifies the governance risk of storage mounting
Makes and justifies a clear recommendation

questions.title: Architecting Fine-Grained Access Control Across a 200-Table Catalog
questions.prompt: A catalog with roughly 200 tables across 12 schemas needs a mix of access rules: most tables are open to all analysts, about 20 contain PII requiring column masking, a handful require row-level restriction by region, and a small set of highly sensitive finance tables should only be visible to a named group. Design the grant, row filter, and column mask architecture so this is maintainable as the catalog grows, rather than hand-applied per table.
questions.modelAnswer: The key design decision at this scale is to make security a property of schema placement and shared, reusable functions, not something hand-configured per table. I'd organize the 12 schemas so that sensitivity level is encoded in schema structure: a general-access schema (or several, by domain) where the default grant is USE SCHEMA + SELECT to an all-analysts group; a pii schema (or a pii_enabled tag applied at the table level within domain schemas) where every table gets the same column-mask function attached by convention, not reinvented per table — one mask_pii_default function parameterized by column, reused across all ~20 tables, so a change to masking logic (e.g., a new exempt group) is one function edit, not 20 table edits. The region-restricted tables get one shared row filter function (region_row_filter) referencing a central user-to-region mapping table, attached via ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER on just those tables, again reusing one function rather than duplicating logic. The finance tables go in their own schema with no default grant at all — access requires an explicit SELECT grant to the named finance group, and critically, no broader grant (like a catalog-level SELECT to all-analysts) should exist above it, since Unity Catalog grants are additive, so a catalog-wide grant would leak into this schema unless it's deliberately excluded by not granting at that level and instead granting per-schema. I'd enforce all of this as Terraform-managed grants and function definitions rather than manual Catalog Explorer clicks, so new tables inherit the correct policy by being created in the correct schema, and a security review is a code review of the Terraform, not a manual audit of 200 tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: At 200 tables, I don't want security decisions made per table — I want them made per schema, with a small number of reusable functions behind the scenes. So I'd organize the catalog so where a table lives tells you its policy: general schemas default-grant to all analysts, a PII-bearing schema gets one shared masking function attached to every table in it rather than 20 separate custom masks, region-restricted tables share one row filter function pointed at a central mapping table, and finance tables live in their own schema with no inherited broad grant — just an explicit grant to the named finance group. The part I'd insist on regardless of how it's organized is that none of this is done by hand in Catalog Explorer; it's Terraform, so adding a 201st table means someone creates it in the right schema and the policy is already correct, and reviewing security posture means reviewing a diff, not manually checking 200 tables for a human mistake.
commonMistakes: Proposes applying a custom row filter or mask function per table instead of reusable, shared functions
Doesn't address that Unity Catalog grants are additive, risking a broad catalog-level grant leaking into the restricted finance schema
Treats this as a one-time configuration task rather than something that needs to scale as the catalog grows
Skips the manageability requirement entirely and just lists what access each table type needs
keyPoints: Organizes schema structure around sensitivity level so policy follows table placement
Uses shared, reusable row filter and column mask functions rather than per-table custom logic
Explicitly addresses the additive nature of grants and how to avoid a broad grant leaking into the restricted schema
Proposes infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) management of grants/functions for maintainability at scale
Design generalizes to new tables being added later without manual reconfiguration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound schema organization tied to sensitivity level
Uses reusable, shared row filter/column mask functions
Correctly addresses additive-grant risk for the restricted finance schema
Proposes a maintainable, as-code governance process

questions.title: Auto Loader Architecture for Thousands of Files Per Second Across Many Tenants
questions.prompt: A SaaS platform ingests usage events from thousands of customer tenants, landing in cloud storage at a combined rate of several thousand small files per second during peak hours, and each tenant's data needs to end up isolated enough that one tenant's volume spike can't delay another tenant's data availability. Design the Auto Loader-based ingestion architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: At several thousand files per second, a single Auto Loader stream reading one giant path for all tenants has two problems: directory listing mode can't keep up at that file-creation rate regardless of tuning, so this has to be file notification mode; and a single stream processing all tenants serially means a volume spike from one large tenant delays discovery and processing for every other tenant sharing that stream, which directly violates the isolation requirement. The architecture I'd build groups tenants into a fixed number of shards (not one stream per tenant, which doesn't scale operationally past a few hundred tenants) — say 20-50 shards, assigned by a consistent hash of tenant ID — each shard being its own Auto Loader stream in file notification mode with its own queue, its own checkpoint, and its own job cluster, so a volume spike in shard 7 only affects the tenants hashed into shard 7, not the other 95% of tenants. Within a shard, maxFilesPerTrigger and maxBytesPerTrigger are tuned to the shard's typical volume, and Databricks Workflows runs each shard's stream (or trigger=availableNow micro-batches on a short schedule) as an independent, horizontally scalable task, so adding capacity for growth means adding shards, not re-architecting. For storage layout, each tenant's files land under a tenant-partitioned path (e.g., /raw/events/tenant_id=X/) so bronze ingestion preserves tenant as a physical partition, which keeps per-tenant backfills, reprocessing, and even per-tenant data-residency exceptions tractable without touching other tenants' data. I'd also put a per-shard dead-letter path for files that fail schema validation, so one malformed file from one tenant can't stall that shard's whole queue.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first decision is forced by scale: at thousands of files a second, directory listing mode is off the table, this has to be file notification mode. The real design problem is isolation — if everyone shares one stream, one tenant's spike slows everyone down, but running one stream per tenant doesn't scale operationally once you're past a few hundred tenants. So I'd shard: hash tenants into a fixed number of buckets, maybe 20 to 50 depending on tenant count and volume distribution, and give each shard its own independent Auto Loader stream, queue, checkpoint, and job cluster. A spike in one shard only touches the tenants in that shard. Growth is handled by adding shards, not by redesigning anything. I'd also keep tenant_id as a physical partition in the storage layout from the start, because that's what makes a single tenant's backfill or reprocessing a contained operation instead of touching everyone's data, and I'd give each shard its own dead-letter path so a bad file from one tenant doesn't stall a whole shard's queue.
questions.example: Shard assignment: shard = hash(tenant_id) % 32. Shard 14's Auto Loader stream reads s3://raw/events/ filtered to tenants in shard 14 via the file notification queue's message filtering, writes to bronze.events partitioned by tenant_id, with its own checkpoint at /checkpoints/shard_14/ and its own dead-letter path at /deadletter/shard_14/.
commonMistakes: Proposes directory listing mode, which cannot keep pace with thousands of files per second
Proposes one giant shared stream for all tenants, violating the isolation requirement
Proposes one stream per tenant, which doesn't scale operationally at thousands of tenants
Omits tenant as a physical partition key, making per-tenant backfill/reprocessing untenable later
keyPoints: Correctly requires file notification mode given the file-creation rate
Proposes a sharded (hash-bucketed) stream design rather than one-shared or one-per-tenant
Explains how sharding achieves the isolation requirement
Uses tenant_id as a physical partition for storage layout
Addresses operational scalability (adding shards) and fault isolation (per-shard dead-letter path)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies file notification mode at this scale
Proposes a sound sharded architecture achieving tenant isolation
Correct storage/partitioning design for per-tenant operability
Addresses scalability and fault isolation operationally

questions.title: Enterprise Medallion Architecture with Multiple Lakeflow Pipelines
questions.prompt: An enterprise lakehouse serves 15 business domains, each with its own bronze-to-silver-to-gold medallion flow, but several gold tables need to join data across domains (e.g., a cross-domain customer-360 table). Design how you'd structure Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines across these domains — one pipeline or many, how cross-domain dependencies are handled, and how compute is shared or isolated.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd give each of the 15 domains its own Lakeflow pipeline covering that domain's bronze-to-silver-to-gold flow, rather than one monolithic pipeline for everything or one pipeline per medallion layer across all domains. Per-domain pipelines mean a domain team owns, deploys, and debugs its own pipeline independently — a schema change or expectation failure in the orders domain doesn't block or even touch the inventory domain's pipeline, and each domain can be on its own release cadence and its own serverless/compute sizing tuned to its data volume. For cross-domain gold tables like customer-360, I would not build that join inside any single domain's pipeline, since it would create an ownership and dependency tangle — instead I'd build a small number of separate 'aggregation' or 'consumption-layer' pipelines that read the already-published gold tables of the contributing domains (via standard three-level namespace reads, since everything's in the same metastore) and materialize the cross-domain table as its own Lakeflow pipeline with its own ownership (typically a central platform or analytics-engineering team). This keeps a clean dependency direction: domain pipelines never depend on each other, and cross-domain aggregation pipelines depend only on domains' published gold outputs, which Lakeflow's lineage view makes explicit and auditable. On compute, each domain pipeline gets its own pipeline-scoped compute (serverless or a sized cluster policy) so one domain's volume spike doesn't starve another's SLA, while the cross-domain aggregation pipelines are scheduled to run after the domain pipelines they depend on complete — orchestrated via Databricks Workflows with task dependencies across the separate pipeline-trigger tasks, since Lakeflow pipelines themselves don't have a native cross-pipeline dependency primitive; that ordering has to live one layer up, in Workflows.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this to one pipeline per domain, full stop, because that maps ownership cleanly — 15 teams, 15 pipelines, nobody's change breaks someone else's deploy. The cross-domain customer-360 problem is tempting to solve by having one domain's pipeline reach into another's tables, but I'd resist that specifically because it creates a hidden coupling between two teams' release cycles. Instead I'd build a separate, small set of aggregation pipelines owned by a central team that just read each domain's already-published gold tables and build the cross-domain views on top — clean one-directional dependency, and Lakeflow's lineage view actually shows that dependency explicitly, which is valuable when something breaks. The piece that doesn't exist natively in Lakeflow is 'run the aggregation pipeline only after all its domain dependencies have finished' — that has to be orchestrated at the Workflows level, chaining pipeline-trigger tasks with explicit dependencies, because Lakeflow pipelines don't know about each other on their own.
commonMistakes: Proposes one giant pipeline spanning all 15 domains, creating a single point of failure and a deployment bottleneck
Has one domain's pipeline directly read another domain's bronze/silver tables, creating tight coupling between teams
Assumes Lakeflow pipelines natively support cross-pipeline dependency ordering without external orchestration
Doesn't separate cross-domain aggregation into its own pipeline with distinct ownership
keyPoints: Proposes one Lakeflow pipeline per domain for clean ownership and independent deployment
Builds cross-domain tables in a separate aggregation pipeline reading published gold outputs, not inside a domain pipeline
Maintains a clean, one-directional dependency graph (domains never depend on each other)
Correctly notes cross-pipeline ordering must be handled by Workflows, not natively by Lakeflow
Addresses compute isolation so one domain's volume doesn't affect another's SLA

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes per-domain pipelines with sound ownership rationale
Correctly designs the cross-domain aggregation approach
Correctly identifies that cross-pipeline ordering requires Workflows orchestration
Addresses compute isolation across domain pipelines

questions.title: Databricks Workflows Platform Design for Multi-Team Orchestration
questions.prompt: A platform team is building a shared Databricks Workflows setup for 20 data teams, each needing to schedule their own jobs without stepping on each other's compute, secrets, or production SLAs, while the platform team still needs visibility into everything running and its cost. Design the platform-level structure.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd give each team its own service principal for running its jobs (not personal user credentials, which creates an ownership and offboarding risk) and enforce cluster policies that cap instance types/sizes and require job clusters (not shared all-purpose clusters) for anything scheduled in production, so no team's job can either accidentally or deliberately consume unbounded compute or interfere with another team's cluster. Secrets are scoped per team via separate secret scopes with ACLs restricting access to that team's service principal and admins only, so Team A's job can never read Team B's credentials even if someone misconfigures a notebook path. For job tagging, I'd make a cost-attribution tag (team, environment, cost-center) mandatory at the job level, enforced via a cluster policy that rejects job creation without it, which is what makes the platform team's cost visibility possible without manually auditing 20 teams' jobs — system.billing.usage already carries cluster tags, so a mandatory tag becomes a free, queryable chargeback dimension. For orchestration isolation, each team gets its own set of Workflows jobs; cross-team dependencies (Team A's job needing to run after Team B's completes) are handled either by Team A's job watching for Team B's output table to update (a data-dependency trigger, which is loosely coupled and doesn't require either team to know about the other's internal job structure) rather than directly chaining tasks across teams' jobs, which would couple their deploy and failure domains together. The platform team gets read access to all jobs' run history and the billing system tables for visibility, plus a shared alerting policy requiring every production job to configure failure notifications, but doesn't own or gate individual teams' job definitions day-to-day — that would turn the platform team into a bottleneck for 20 teams' routine scheduling changes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this around three guardrails rather than trying to centrally manage 20 teams' jobs by hand. First, isolation: each team runs under its own service principal, not personal credentials, with cluster policies that force job clusters for production work and cap what they can spin up — that stops one team's mistake or spike from touching anyone else's compute. Second, secrets: scoped per team, ACL'd to that team's service principal only, so there's no path for one team's job to accidentally read another's credentials. Third, cost visibility without being a bottleneck: I'd make a cost-attribution tag mandatory at job creation via policy, so finance gets a clean chargeback dimension for free out of the billing system tables, and the platform team can see everything running without having to approve every team's day-to-day scheduling change. For cross-team dependencies, I'd push teams toward watching for an upstream table to land rather than directly chaining into another team's job — that keeps two teams from being coupled to each other's deploy schedules and failure modes.
commonMistakes: Uses personal user credentials for scheduled jobs instead of per-team service principals
Doesn't enforce mandatory cost-attribution tagging, leaving chargeback as a manual, error-prone audit
Chains tasks directly across different teams' jobs, coupling their deploy/failure domains
Makes the platform team a central gatekeeper for every team's routine job changes, creating a bottleneck
keyPoints: Uses per-team service principals and cluster policies for compute isolation
Scopes secrets per team with ACLs preventing cross-team access
Enforces mandatory cost-attribution tagging for chargeback visibility
Uses loosely-coupled, data-driven cross-team dependencies instead of direct task chaining
Gives the platform team visibility without making it a bottleneck for routine scheduling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound compute/identity isolation design (service principals, cluster policies)
Sound secrets-scoping design
Cost-attribution/chargeback design
Sound cross-team dependency and platform-visibility design

questions.title: DP-750 System Design: A Governed Lakehouse Platform for 50 Teams
questions.prompt: This is a system-design question in the style of the DP-750 exam. Design a lakehouse platform on Databricks that will onboard 50 independent data teams over the next year. The platform must provide: centralized governance without being a bottleneck, per-team cost accountability, a self-service path for a new team to onboard without platform-team involvement in every step, and a consistent data-quality bar across teams with wildly different levels of data engineering maturity.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd structure this around a 'paved road' platform model: one shared Unity Catalog metastore (assuming no residency constraints forcing multiple), with a standardized catalog-per-domain convention and Terraform modules that encode the platform's required guardrails — mandatory cost-attribution tags, mandatory cluster policies limiting instance types, mandatory secret-scope ACL patterns, and a default Lakeflow pipeline template with baseline expectations (schema-break detection, null primary key checks) pre-wired in. A new team onboards self-service by running the platform's Terraform module against their team name, which provisions their catalog, service principal, secret scope, and a starter Lakeflow pipeline scaffold — no platform-team ticket required for the standard path, only for genuine exceptions. Governance stays non-bottlenecking because it's enforced structurally (policies that reject non-compliant resources at creation time) rather than through manual review gates; the platform team's role shifts from 'approve every team's change' to 'maintain and improve the paved road,' with an escape hatch for teams with unusual needs to request an exception reviewed asynchronously rather than blocking their onboarding. Cost accountability comes from the mandatory tagging flowing into system.billing.usage, aggregated into a per-team cost dashboard that's visible to each team's own leadership, not just platform/finance, so teams see and own their own spend trend rather than discovering it in a quarterly surprise. The data-quality bar for teams at different maturity levels is handled by making the baseline Lakeflow expectations (not a full custom data-quality framework) part of the starter template every team gets by default — a team with low maturity inherits a working, enforced minimum bar for free, while a highly mature team can add more expectations on top without the platform forcing a one-size-fits-all heavyweight framework on everyone. Centralized visibility into quality and health across all 50 teams comes from aggregating each pipeline's event-log metrics into a shared quality dashboard, so the platform team can spot a team trending toward trouble without owning that team's pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as building a paved road, not a gate. One shared metastore with a domain-per-catalog convention, and everything the platform requires — tagging, cluster policies, secret scoping, a baseline Lakeflow template with a few non-negotiable expectations already wired in — gets encoded as a Terraform module. A new team onboards by running that module, which gives them their catalog, service principal, and a working pipeline scaffold on day one, with no platform-team approval step for the standard path. That's what keeps governance from being a bottleneck — it's enforced by the structure of what gets provisioned, not by someone reviewing every team's PR. Cost accountability falls out of the mandatory tagging for free, and I'd make sure each team's leadership can see their own spend directly rather than that living only in a platform-team spreadsheet. For the data-quality maturity gap, I wouldn't try to mandate a sophisticated framework everyone has to learn — I'd bake a small number of baseline expectations into the starter template so even the least mature team inherits a real, enforced floor, and let the stronger teams build on top of that at their own pace. The platform team's job becomes maintaining that paved road and watching the aggregate quality dashboard for teams trending toward trouble, not owning 50 teams' pipelines directly.
commonMistakes: Designs governance as manual approval gates, directly violating the 'without being a bottleneck' requirement
Proposes a single heavyweight data-quality framework mandatory for all teams regardless of maturity, which low-maturity teams can't realistically adopt
Doesn't make cost data visible to the teams themselves, keeping it a platform/finance-only concern
Requires platform-team tickets for standard onboarding steps instead of a genuinely self-service path
keyPoints: Proposes structural (policy-as-code) governance enforcement instead of manual approval gates
Designs a genuinely self-service onboarding path via a standardized provisioning module
Ties cost accountability to mandatory tagging with visibility given back to teams, not just the platform team
Addresses the maturity-gap requirement with a baseline-template approach rather than a one-size-fits-all framework
Reframes the platform team's role around maintaining the paved road and aggregate monitoring, not per-team gatekeeping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Governance design avoids becoming a manual bottleneck
Genuine self-service onboarding design
Cost-accountability design with team-level visibility
Sound approach to the data-quality maturity gap across teams

questions.title: Delta Sharing vs. a Custom Data-Export Pipeline for External Partners
questions.prompt: Your company currently ships data to 12 external partners via individually-built nightly export pipelines (each writing CSV or Parquet to the partner's own cloud storage). Leadership wants to know whether migrating all 12 to Delta Sharing is worth the effort. Lay out the architectural comparison and give a recommendation that accounts for partners who can't yet consume Delta Sharing directly.
questions.modelAnswer: The 12 custom export pipelines each represent independent operational surface area: 12 schedules to monitor, 12 places a schema change can silently break an export, 12 sets of partner-side storage credentials to manage and rotate, and 12 copies of data that are stale the moment they land and that drift from the source as soon as any pipeline fails silently. Delta Sharing collapses this to one architectural pattern — a share per partner (or even one share with per-partner views for row-level restriction) pointing at the live tables, with no export job to schedule, monitor, or re-run, and the partner always sees current data because they're querying live pointers into our storage rather than receiving a copy. The honest caveat: Delta Sharing requires the partner's side to have a Delta Sharing-compatible client (Databricks, Spark, pandas connector, Power BI, or a few others) — a partner running a legacy system that can only ingest a CSV drop into their own on-prem ETL can't consume a share directly. For those partners, I'd recommend a hybrid migration: move the partners who can consume Delta Sharing today (likely most, since open sharing's activation-link model doesn't require them to have Unity Catalog themselves, just a compatible reader), and for the handful who genuinely can't, keep a legacy export pipeline, but have it read from the same share rather than from the raw table directly, which still collapses the 'can this export quietly drift from source' risk even for the partners not yet on Delta Sharing natively. The business case for migrating the majority is reduced operational toil (no more 12 separately-monitored export jobs), stronger security (short-lived scoped credentials vs. static bucket access keys often left in place for partners long after a relationship cools), and freshness (partners get live data instead of yesterday's batch), which is worth presenting to leadership in terms of engineer-hours saved per month plus the audit/security improvement, not just as a technology preference.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the current state honestly: 12 custom pipelines means 12 independent things that can break, 12 copies of data going stale the second they land, and 12 sets of credentials sitting in partners' buckets that we have to remember to rotate or revoke. Delta Sharing replaces most of that with one pattern — a share per partner pointing at live data, no export job, no copy, and short-lived scoped access instead of static keys. The part I wouldn't oversell to leadership is that every partner has to be able to consume it, and a couple of them probably can't if they're on legacy, on-prem tooling that only knows how to pull a CSV. So my recommendation is a staged migration: move the partners who can consume a share today, which is probably most of them since open sharing doesn't require them to run Unity Catalog themselves, and for the few who can't, keep an export pipeline but have it read from the share instead of the raw table — that way even their legacy drop is sourced from one governed, current pointer instead of yet another independent extract that can drift. I'd pitch the business case in terms of fewer pipelines to babysit and tighter security, not as 'the new shiny thing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends an all-or-nothing migration without accounting for partners who can't consume Delta Sharing directly
Treats the comparison as purely about data freshness, ignoring the operational/security burden of credential management for 12 pipelines
Doesn't propose a concrete fallback for legacy partners beyond 'keep doing it the old way'
Fails to frame the business case in terms leadership can act on (operational cost, security risk) rather than a technical preference
keyPoints: Identifies the operational and security costs of the current 12 custom export pipelines
Explains Delta Sharing's architectural advantages (no copy, live data, scoped short-lived credentials)
Correctly identifies the client-compatibility limitation for some partners
Proposes a concrete hybrid/staged migration plan rather than all-or-nothing
Frames the recommendation in business terms leadership can evaluate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the costs of the current custom-pipeline approach
Correctly explains Delta Sharing's architectural advantages
Addresses the partner-compatibility limitation with a concrete plan
Frames a business-level recommendation, not just a technical one

questions.title: Multi-Cloud External Locations and Storage Credentials Architecture
questions.prompt: Following an acquisition, your company now has data in both AWS and Azure, and the plan is to unify governance under one Unity Catalog deployment without immediately migrating all storage into one cloud. Design the external location and storage credential architecture that lets Unity Catalog govern tables living in both clouds.
questions.modelAnswer: Unity Catalog's metastore itself is deployed in one cloud/region, but it can govern external tables whose data physically lives in a different cloud, provided the compute querying those tables can reach that storage and the right storage credential is registered — so the design is: pick the home cloud for the metastore (likely wherever the acquiring company's primary workspace already runs), then register a storage credential for AWS (an IAM role Unity Catalog can assume) and a separate storage credential for Azure (a managed identity or service principal) against that same metastore. Each cloud's storage gets its own external location object pointing at the respective bucket/container, tied to its matching credential, and external tables are created against those external locations with their catalog/schema living in the single shared metastore namespace, so a user sees acquired_company_catalog.sales.orders and current_company_catalog.sales.orders side by side with consistent grants, lineage, and masking regardless of which cloud physically stores the bytes. The practical constraint to flag: compute querying the AWS-stored table needs network/credential reachability to AWS even if the workspace itself runs in Azure (or vice versa), which usually means the cluster's cloud identity needs cross-cloud permission, and cross-cloud reads carry egress cost and higher latency than same-cloud reads — so this architecture is the right transitional state, but I'd scope it explicitly as a bridge during the acquisition integration, not a permanent target, with a follow-up plan to eventually consolidate the less-business-critical cloud's data into the primary cloud once the migration can be scheduled without disrupting either team.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing people don't expect is that a Unity Catalog metastore lives in one cloud, but it can still govern tables whose actual bytes sit in a different cloud, as long as there's a storage credential wired up for that cloud and the compute can reach it. So I'd pick a home cloud for the metastore — probably wherever the surviving primary workspace already is — and register two storage credentials against it, one for AWS and one for Azure, each tied to its own external location pointing at the acquired company's storage and our existing storage respectively. Both sides' tables show up in the same catalog namespace with the same grants and lineage, so from a governance standpoint it already looks unified even before any bytes move. What I'd flag loudly to leadership is that this is a bridge, not the end state — cross-cloud reads cost more and are slower than same-cloud reads, and compute needs cross-cloud credentials to even reach the other side — so I'd pair this with an explicit plan to eventually consolidate storage into one cloud once that migration can be scheduled properly, rather than let 'temporary multi-cloud' quietly become permanent.
commonMistakes: Assumes a Unity Catalog metastore must live in the same cloud as all the data it governs
Doesn't register separate storage credentials per cloud, or conflates IAM roles and managed identities
Fails to flag cross-cloud query cost/latency and cross-cloud credential reachability as real constraints
Presents the multi-cloud setup as a permanent architecture rather than a scoped transitional bridge
keyPoints: Correctly explains that a metastore can govern external tables across clouds given the right credentials
Designs separate storage credentials and external locations per cloud
Explains the unified-namespace benefit (consistent grants/lineage/masking regardless of physical storage location)
Flags cross-cloud reachability, cost, and latency as real constraints
Frames the design as a deliberate transitional bridge with a consolidation follow-up, not a permanent end state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains cross-cloud governance capability of Unity Catalog
Sound storage credential/external location design per cloud
Identifies real cross-cloud cost/latency/reachability constraints
Frames this as a transitional architecture with a consolidation plan

questions.title: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery for a Unity Catalog Metastore
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a disaster-recovery plan for the primary region hosting your Unity Catalog metastore and its workspaces going fully offline for an extended period. Design the DR architecture, including what actually needs to be replicated versus what can be rebuilt, and what the realistic recovery time objective looks like given Unity Catalog's architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: A Unity Catalog metastore itself is a regional construct with no native cross-region failover, so DR has to be designed explicitly rather than assumed: the two things that need protecting are the underlying managed/external table storage (the actual Delta files) and the catalog metadata/grants (what tables exist, who can access them). For storage, cross-region replication of the cloud storage backing managed tables and external locations (S3 Cross-Region Replication, Azure geo-redundant storage, or an explicit Delta table replication job) gives you the data itself in a secondary region. For metadata, because Unity Catalog's catalog/schema/grant/function definitions are not automatically replicated cross-region, the pragmatic approach is to manage all of it as Terraform (catalogs, schemas, grants, row filters, masks) so the entire governance structure can be re-applied to a freshly-created metastore in the DR region in minutes rather than hours, rather than trying to achieve live metadata replication, which Unity Catalog doesn't natively support. The realistic recovery plan, then, is: stand up a secondary workspace and metastore in the DR region ahead of time (not during the incident), keep it dormant or lightly used, replicate storage continuously, and keep the Terraform-as-code governance definitions ready to apply; on a real outage, you point the DR workspace's metastore at the replicated storage, apply the Terraform to recreate the governance layer, and redirect traffic/jobs to the DR workspace. The realistic RTO is measured in low hours, not minutes, because even with everything prepared, re-applying hundreds of grants and reconnecting external locations against replicated storage takes meaningful, if scripted, time — and I'd be explicit with leadership that this is the honest number rather than promising an instant failover Unity Catalog's architecture doesn't support today.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by correcting an assumption leadership often has — Unity Catalog doesn't have a built-in cross-region failover button, so this has to be designed, not just enabled. There are really two things to protect separately: the actual data (the Delta files in storage) and the governance metadata (catalogs, grants, masks, row filters). For the data, cross-region storage replication handles it. For the governance layer, the practical answer is that everything — every catalog, schema, grant, and security function — lives as Terraform, so instead of trying to replicate Unity Catalog's internal metadata live, which it doesn't support, I can stand up a metastore in the DR region ahead of time and re-apply that Terraform to recreate the entire governance structure on demand. On a real outage, the sequence is: point the DR metastore at the replicated storage, re-apply the Terraform, redirect jobs and users to the DR workspace. I'd be upfront that the real RTO here is hours, not an instant cutover, because even a well-rehearsed version of this takes time to execute, and I'd rather leadership plan around an honest number than be surprised during a real incident.
commonMistakes: Assumes Unity Catalog has native cross-region metastore failover
Only addresses data replication and ignores that governance metadata (grants, masks, row filters) also needs a recovery strategy
Promises an unrealistically fast RTO without accounting for re-provisioning and re-applying governance configuration
Doesn't propose pre-provisioning the DR workspace/metastore ahead of an actual incident
keyPoints: Correctly states Unity Catalog has no native cross-region failover and DR must be explicitly designed
Separates the data-replication problem from the governance-metadata problem
Proposes Terraform-as-code governance as the mechanism for fast metadata recreation
Proposes pre-provisioning the DR workspace/metastore rather than building it during an incident
Gives a realistic, honest RTO rather than an idealized one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes Unity Catalog's lack of native cross-region failover
Sound data-replication design
Sound governance-metadata recovery design (Terraform-as-code)
Gives a realistic RTO and pre-provisioning recommendation

questions.title: Cost Attribution Architecture Across Databricks Workflows for Chargeback
questions.prompt: Finance wants to charge back Databricks compute cost to the 20 business units using the platform, down to the individual job level, including shared compute that multiple business units' jobs run on. Design the cost-attribution architecture, including how you'd handle the shared-compute case where a strict per-job tag isn't enough.
questions.modelAnswer: For jobs running on their own dedicated job clusters, attribution is straightforward: enforce a mandatory cluster/job tag (business_unit, cost_center) via cluster policy, which flows directly into system.billing.usage as a joinable dimension, and build the chargeback report as a query joining usage records to tags, aggregated per business unit per billing period. The harder case is genuinely shared compute — for example, a shared SQL warehouse or a shared all-purpose cluster multiple business units' ad-hoc queries run on, where there's no single job-level tag that cleanly owns the whole cluster's cost. For that, I'd attribute at the query/task level rather than the cluster level: system tables expose per-query or per-task resource consumption (DBUs or similar) that can be joined to the identity that issued the query, which can then be mapped to a business unit via a reference table (user/service-principal to business unit), giving a proportional allocation of the shared cluster's cost based on actual usage rather than an even split, which would misrepresent a business unit that barely uses the shared resource as paying the same as one that uses it heavily. I'd also flag an explicit policy decision for leadership: a small 'platform overhead' pool (shared governance tooling, monitoring, idle capacity buffers) that genuinely isn't attributable to any one business unit should be called out as its own line item rather than forced into an arbitrary allocation, because pretending every dollar is perfectly attributable to one business unit creates chargeback numbers nobody trusts once business units start comparing notes.
questions.professionalAnswer: For dedicated compute, this is simple: make a business-unit tag mandatory via cluster policy, and the billing system tables already let you join usage to that tag and roll it up by business unit and period. The real design problem is shared compute — a shared SQL warehouse or cluster where no single tag owns the whole thing. For that I'd go one level more granular and attribute by query or task, using the system tables' per-query resource consumption joined against who actually ran it, then map that identity to a business unit through a reference table. That gives a usage-proportional allocation instead of an even split, which matters because an even split would make a light user of shared compute pay the same as a heavy user, and that's the fastest way to make a chargeback report lose everyone's trust. I'd also tell finance upfront that some cost — shared tooling, monitoring, idle buffer capacity — genuinely isn't attributable to one business unit, and I'd rather call that out as its own line item than force a made-up allocation that doesn't hold up when someone asks how it was calculated.
commonMistakes: Only designs for dedicated-compute jobs and doesn't address the shared-compute attribution problem at all
Proposes an even split of shared compute cost across business units regardless of actual usage
Doesn't propose query/task-level attribution as the mechanism for shared resources
Forces 100% of cost into business-unit buckets without acknowledging genuinely unattributable platform overhead
keyPoints: Designs mandatory tagging and billing-system-table joins for dedicated compute
Identifies shared compute as requiring a different, finer-grained attribution approach
Proposes query/task-level attribution joined to identity-to-business-unit mapping for shared resources
Explains why usage-proportional allocation is preferable to an even split
Acknowledges genuinely unattributable platform overhead as its own line item

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound dedicated-compute attribution design via tagging
Correctly identifies and solves the shared-compute attribution problem
Justifies usage-proportional allocation over an even split
Acknowledges unattributable overhead rather than forcing full allocation

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem — number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower — specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors — number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it — and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right — I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction
keyPoints: Quantifies the backlog and the competing-urgency problem
Introduces a concrete, weighted prioritization framework
Makes the framework and resulting rankings visible to stakeholders
Shows willingness to revise the framework when a legitimate gap is found
Establishes a repeatable intake/grooming process, not a one-time fix
Gives a measurable improvement in delivery time or escalation volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness of the prioritization framework
Transparency with stakeholders about rankings and reasoning
Willingness to revise the framework when challenged
Repeatability of the process going forward
Measurable outcome

questions.title: Making the Business Case for Infrastructure-as-Code to Skeptical Leadership
questions.prompt: Your engineering director believes Terraform and Bicep are 'process overhead for a team that already knows how to click through the Azure portal carefully.' Tell me about a time you had to convince leadership who saw infrastructure-as-code as unnecessary bureaucracy to invest in adopting it, including how you dealt with the fact that the benefits are mostly about avoided future pain rather than immediate speed.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes the core difficulty of this pitch: IaC's value is largely preventive and shows up as incidents that didn't happen, which is a hard sell against the visible, immediate cost of slowing down a team that feels productive doing manual changes. It should describe grounding the pitch in the organization's own history rather than abstract best-practice arguments — a specific outage or painful incident caused by configuration drift, an inconsistent environment, or a change nobody could reproduce, that leadership already remembers and regrets. It should show translating technical benefits into business language leadership cares about: mean time to recovery, audit and compliance readiness, onboarding time for new engineers, or the cost of an environment that can't be safely rebuilt. It should describe proposing a low-risk, bounded pilot — codifying one well-understood, non-critical environment first — rather than demanding a wholesale rewrite of all infrastructure, so leadership can see a real before/after without betting the farm. It should address the honest tradeoff: IaC adds some initial friction and learning curve, and a credible answer doesn't pretend otherwise but frames it as a near-term investment against a recurring future cost. The close should include a concrete leadership reaction or decision, not just a vague 'and eventually they agreed.'
questions.professionalAnswer: My director's actual words were close to 'we already know how to configure Azure, why add a layer,' and arguing abstract best practices at him was getting nowhere, so I stopped trying that and instead pulled our last two incident postmortems where the stated root cause was literally 'production environment configuration didn't match what we thought it was' — one of those had cost us four hours of a Saturday. I reframed the pitch around those two incidents specifically: not 'IaC is a best practice' but 'here's two incidents, both preventable by the same missing thing, and here's what each one cost us in engineer-hours and customer impact.' Rather than asking for a full migration, I proposed codifying just our Fabric capacity and workspace provisioning in Bicep first, since it was well-understood, lower risk than our core Databricks environment, and still painful enough from manual portal drift that a win there would be visible. That pilot took about three weeks, and the real persuasion moment wasn't the code, it was a live demo where I intentionally 'broke' the dev environment and rebuilt it from the Bicep templates in under ten minutes in front of him, compared to the two-plus hours it had historically taken us to manually reconstruct a misconfigured environment. He didn't become an IaC evangelist overnight, but he approved extending it to our Databricks workspace provisioning next quarter, and he's since referenced that ten-minute rebuild demo himself when talking to his own leadership about why we invest in it.
commonMistakes: Argues from abstract best practice instead of the organization's own incident history
Pretends IaC has no near-term cost or learning curve to make the pitch easier
Asks for a wholesale infrastructure rewrite instead of a bounded, low-risk pilot
Frames the benefit only in engineering terms, never translated to business impact
No concrete leadership reaction, decision, or follow-on investment described
keyPoints: Grounds the pitch in a real, remembered incident rather than abstract best practice
Translates technical benefits into business terms leadership cares about
Proposes a bounded, low-risk pilot rather than a full rewrite
Is honest about the near-term cost and learning curve of adoption
Uses a concrete demonstration to make the benefit visceral, not theoretical
Shows a specific leadership decision or follow-on investment as the outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use of real incident history to ground the pitch
Translation of technical value into business language
Quality of the bounded pilot strategy
Honesty about tradeoffs and adoption cost
Concreteness of the leadership outcome

questions.title: Moving a Team from an Ungoverned Lakehouse to Unity Catalog
questions.prompt: Your Databricks workspace has grown organically for three years with no catalog structure, inconsistent permissions, and analysts who are used to querying anything from any notebook. Tell me about a time you convinced a team accustomed to that kind of free-for-all access to adopt Unity Catalog governance, including how you handled the engineers who felt it was slowing them down.
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should acknowledge honestly that governance, from the perspective of someone used to unrestricted access, really does add friction, and a credible answer doesn't pretend Unity Catalog adoption was universally welcomed. It should describe identifying the actual risk the ungoverned state created — perhaps a near-miss where sensitive data was exposed to the wrong group, inconsistent lineage making audits painful, or duplicate tables with no clear source of truth — as the concrete motivating case rather than governance for its own sake. It should describe a migration approach that didn't just flip access off overnight: a catalog and schema structure mapped to existing team boundaries so the new structure felt familiar rather than arbitrary, and a transition period where old patterns were deprecated with warning rather than an abrupt lockout. It should address the specific friction complaints directly — slower onboarding for a new table, more steps to grant access — and show how those were mitigated with something concrete, like a self-service access-request workflow or clear catalog documentation, rather than just telling people to get used to it. It should close with evidence the team's own behavior changed for the better, not just that governance was technically turned on.
questions.professionalAnswer: The precipitating event was an audit where we genuinely couldn't answer 'who has access to this PII table and why' with any confidence, which was the opening I used rather than a general pitch about best practices. I mapped our existing ungoverned Hive metastore tables into a Unity Catalog structure that mirrored how our teams actually already organized themselves, so the new catalog and schema boundaries matched the mental model people already had instead of introducing a new one on top of the migration itself. I ran a six-week parallel period where the old metastore access still worked but threw a visible deprecation warning in notebook output, so nobody was locked out mid-project, and that warning included a link straight to a self-service access-request form rather than a ticket queue, because the complaint I anticipated and got anyway was 'now I have to file a ticket and wait two days for something I used to just have.' One senior analyst was vocal that this was slowing her down for no benefit she personally cared about, and rather than arguing governance philosophy with her, I showed her the specific audit finding and asked her directly whether she'd be comfortable being the name attached to that table if it came up again, which reframed it from abstract bureaucracy to a real question she actually cared about. Grant turnaround on the self-service form averaged under four hours, which undercut most of the friction complaints within the first month, and six months in we passed a follow-up security review with a clean answer to the exact question that had failed the first time.
commonMistakes: Pretends governance added no real friction instead of acknowledging and mitigating it honestly
Flips access off abruptly instead of a transition period with warning
Pitches governance as an abstract best practice instead of a concrete risk the team experienced
No mitigation for the specific friction complaints (slower onboarding, more access steps)
Measures success only by 'governance is turned on' rather than an improved audit or review outcome
keyPoints: Grounds the push for governance in a real, specific risk or audit failure
Designs the new catalog structure to match teams' existing mental model
Uses a transition period with warnings rather than an abrupt lockout
Mitigates specific friction complaints with concrete self-service tooling
Reframes resistance around a concern the resistant person actually cares about
Shows a measurable downstream outcome, like a passed audit or review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use of a concrete risk or incident to motivate the change
Quality of the migration/transition approach
Honest handling of real friction and resistance
Concreteness of mitigations (self-service tooling, documentation)
Measurable downstream outcome

questions.title: Running a Blameless Postmortem After a Costly Kafka Pipeline Outage
questions.prompt: A malformed message from an upstream producer crashed a Kafka consumer group feeding your real-time fraud-detection pipeline for nearly five hours, during which fraudulent transactions went undetected, and finance wants someone held accountable. Tell me about a time you ran a cross-functional incident retrospective after a costly outage and had to actively protect a blameless postmortem culture under real pressure to name a culprit.
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should take seriously that 'blameless' is easy to claim and hard to actually do when there's real financial or reputational cost and real pressure from outside the engineering org to identify who's at fault. It should describe how the candidate structured the retrospective itself to stay focused on systems and decisions rather than people — a clear timeline of what happened and when, grounded in logs and data rather than reconstructed from memory, and facilitation that redirected 'who' questions toward 'what in our system allowed this' questions. It should address the external pressure directly: how the candidate communicated with finance or other outside stakeholders in a way that gave them the accountability and seriousness they needed without sacrificing the internal blameless process, since those two things can coexist if handled well. It should name the actual systemic gaps uncovered — missing schema validation at the consumer boundary, no dead-letter queue or circuit breaker to isolate a bad message, insufficient alerting on consumer lag — and describe concrete follow-up actions with owners and deadlines, not just a discussion. A strong answer shows the postmortem culture surviving the pressure test, for example by citing that engineers kept reporting near-misses honestly afterward rather than becoming more guarded.
questions.professionalAnswer: Finance asked, almost immediately, whose code caused this, and I made a deliberate choice in my first message to them to separate two things explicitly: a commitment to a full accounting of financial impact and timeline, which they were owed, and a refusal to turn the internal retrospective into a blame exercise, which I framed as the actual best way to prevent a repeat. I built the incident timeline from Kafka consumer lag metrics, broker logs, and our alerting history before the retrospective meeting even started, specifically so the conversation wouldn't dissolve into competing memories of who said what. In the room, every time the conversation drifted toward a specific engineer's decision, I redirected it — not by shutting people down, but by literally asking 'what would have had to be true in our system for that decision to be safe,' which kept surfacing structural gaps instead of personal ones. What came out of it was that we had zero schema validation at the consumer boundary and no dead-letter queue, so one malformed message could take down the whole consumer group instead of being isolated and skipped. We assigned three concrete fixes with named owners and two-week deadlines — schema validation at ingestion, a dead-letter queue for the fraud-detection topic, and a consumer-lag alert tuned to catch this in minutes instead of hours — and I personally wrote the finance-facing summary emphasizing those fixes rather than any individual's role in the incident. The real test of whether it worked came about two months later when a different engineer proactively flagged a near-miss with a similar shape before it became an outage, specifically telling me he felt safe raising it because of how the fraud-pipeline postmortem had gone.
commonMistakes: Lets external pressure from finance or other stakeholders turn the internal postmortem into blame
Builds the incident timeline from memory or opinion instead of logs and metrics
Facilitates the retrospective passively, letting it drift toward naming individuals
Produces a discussion with no concrete, owned, deadlined follow-up actions
No evidence the blameless culture actually held up under real pressure afterward
keyPoints: Separates stakeholder accountability for impact from internal blame for the retrospective
Builds the incident timeline from logs and metrics, not reconstructed memory
Actively facilitates away from blame toward systemic root cause
Surfaces concrete structural gaps (validation, isolation, alerting) rather than individual error
Assigns specific owners and deadlines to follow-up fixes
Shows evidence the blameless culture held up under real pressure afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Protection of blameless culture under real external pressure
Rigor of the incident timeline and root-cause process
Quality of stakeholder communication with finance
Concreteness of the resulting systemic fixes
Evidence of lasting cultural impact

questions.title: Designing an Org-Wide Unity Catalog Governance Model Across Many Workspaces
questions.prompt: You've been asked to design and roll out a single Unity Catalog governance model across 15 workspaces that currently each have their own ad-hoc access control conventions. Describe how you'd approach building consensus across that many teams, and what you'd do about the teams whose existing conventions directly conflict with the new standard.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by auditing what actually exists today across the 15 workspaces rather than designing in a vacuum — pulling current grants, group structures, and naming conventions to find the patterns that are already common versus the genuine outliers, because a governance model that ignores how most teams already work will face needless resistance even where it's objectively better. I'd then draft the standard (catalog naming, group-based grant patterns, tagging taxonomy) as a proposal, not a mandate, and run it past a representative subset of teams, specifically including the teams whose conventions conflict most, before it's finalized, because their early pushback usually reveals either a real constraint I didn't know about or a misunderstanding I can clear up before rollout rather than during it. For teams with directly conflicting conventions, I'd distinguish between conventions that are merely different (cosmetic, easy to migrate) and ones that encode a real requirement the new standard doesn't yet account for (e.g., a team that built fine-grained row filters the standard template doesn't support yet) — the former get a migration deadline and support, the latter get folded back into the standard as a legitimate addition before it's declared final, because forcing a real requirement to disappear just to hit a rollout date creates exactly the kind of workaround that erodes governance long-term. I'd roll out with a grace period, self-service migration tooling (a Terraform module that converts a team's existing grants into the standard pattern), and a clear escalation path for exceptions reviewed by a small governance group rather than unilaterally by me, so the standard has institutional buy-in rather than being 'the thing one architect decided.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't walk in with a finished standard — I'd walk in with an audit of what's already there, because across 15 workspaces there's usually more existing consistency than people assume, and I want governance that extends the good patterns rather than replacing everything the hard way. I'd draft the standard as a proposal and specifically go find the teams I expect to push back on before I lock anything in, because their objections usually tell me either a real gap in my design or something I can address with better communication. When a team's existing setup genuinely conflicts, I ask whether that's because they're doing something wrong or because they solved a real problem the standard doesn't yet handle — if it's the latter, that becomes an amendment to the standard, not an exception I grant quietly, because quiet exceptions are how governance erodes. Then I'd roll out with real support — migration tooling, a grace period, and an actual escalation path reviewed by a small group, not just me — so it lands as 'the platform's standard' rather than 'one person's opinion that everyone has to comply with.'
commonMistakes: Designs the governance standard in isolation before consulting any teams, then tries to sell it after the fact
Treats every conflicting existing convention as something to simply override, without checking whether it encodes a real, unaddressed requirement
Rolls out with a hard cutover and no migration tooling or grace period
Positions the standard as one architect's personal mandate rather than something with broader institutional ownership
keyPoints: Audits existing conventions before designing, to find common patterns to build on
Engages conflicting teams early in the draft process, not after the standard is finalized
Distinguishes cosmetic differences from conflicts that encode a real, unaddressed requirement
Provides migration tooling, a grace period, and a legitimate escalation/exception path
Builds institutional ownership of the standard rather than presenting it as a personal mandate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sound approach to building consensus across many teams
Correctly distinguishes cosmetic conflicts from real unmet requirements
Proposes concrete migration support (tooling, grace period)
Addresses institutional ownership/governance process, not a personal mandate

questions.title: Leading the Migration from Siloed Workspaces to a Unified Unity Catalog Metastore
questions.prompt: You're leading a migration of a dozen teams from their own isolated, pre-Unity-Catalog workspaces (using the legacy Hive metastore and ad-hoc storage mounts) into one unified Unity Catalog metastore. Several teams are skeptical this is worth the disruption to their current, working pipelines. Describe how you'd lead this migration.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd lead with honesty about the disruption rather than downplaying it — a legacy-to-Unity-Catalog migration does touch working pipelines, and pretending otherwise to get buy-in just burns trust the first time something breaks. Instead I'd make the case concretely: pick one team's real, current pain point (a security gap from storage mounts bypassing any central audit, or a cross-team data-sharing request that's currently impossible without copying files) and show how the migration solves that specific problem for them, rather than selling 'unified governance' as an abstract good. I'd run the migration as a phased rollout starting with one willing, lower-risk team as a pilot, documenting exactly what broke, how long it took, and what the migration tooling automated versus what needed manual fixing — then use that real data, not a projection, to make the case to the skeptical teams, because 'here's what actually happened to a team like yours' is far more convincing than a slide deck. For teams that remain skeptical even with evidence, I'd dig into whether their skepticism is really about the migration or about something else — a past bad experience with a platform-team mandate, a fear of losing autonomy over their own access control — because the real objection sometimes isn't the technical one being voiced. I'd also protect their current pipelines explicitly during the transition: dual-running on the legacy and new setup for a defined window before cutover, so nobody has to take it on faith that the new setup works before their old one is decommissioned.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't oversell this — moving off a legacy Hive metastore and storage mounts genuinely touches pipelines that currently work, and I'd rather say that plainly up front than have someone feel misled the first time something breaks. My pitch to skeptical teams is concrete, not abstract: I'd find their actual current pain — usually something like 'you can't share this table with another team without a manual export' or 'there's no real audit trail because of the storage mount' — and show exactly how Unity Catalog fixes that for them specifically. I'd run one willing team through first as a real pilot, keep honest notes on what broke and how long it took, and bring that evidence to everyone else instead of a promise. For the teams still skeptical after that, I'd ask what's actually behind it, because sometimes 'this migration seems risky' is really 'I don't trust the platform team after the last mandate that didn't go well' — and that's a different conversation. And I'd never ask a team to cut over on faith — dual-running both setups for a real window before decommissioning the old one is how I'd earn that trust rather than just ask for it.
commonMistakes: Downplays or hides the real disruption to current pipelines to make the migration easier to sell
Pitches the benefit abstractly ('unified governance is better') instead of tying it to a team's specific current pain
Forces a hard cutover without a dual-running transition window
Dismisses continued skepticism as unreasonable instead of investigating whether it stems from a prior trust issue
keyPoints: Is honest about real disruption rather than downplaying it
Ties the migration's benefit to a specific, concrete pain point per team rather than an abstract pitch
Uses a real pilot team's evidence to build the case for skeptical teams
Investigates whether persistent skepticism has a root cause beyond the stated technical objection
Proposes a dual-running transition window rather than a forced hard cutover

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows honesty about disruption rather than downplaying it
Ties the pitch to concrete, team-specific pain points
Uses pilot evidence to build the case for broader rollout
Proposes a safe, dual-running transition approach

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer Through a Major Lakeflow Production Incident
questions.prompt: A junior engineer on your team pushed a change to a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that, due to a misconfigured expectation, silently dropped a significant percentage of production rows for three days before anyone noticed. They're visibly shaken and worried about their job. Describe how you'd handle this, both the incident response and the conversation with them.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd separate the incident response from the people conversation and handle the first one first, because the engineer needs to see the team treat this as a system failure to fix, not a person to blame, before anything else lands. On the incident itself: assess the actual damage (how many rows, which downstream consumers, whether any decisions were made on the bad data), get the fix deployed (correct the expectation, likely reprocess the affected date range), and then run a blameless post-incident review focused on the real question — why did a misconfigured expect_or_drop run in production for three days before anyone caught it, which is a monitoring and review-process gap, not solely a human-error problem, since good engineers make this exact kind of mistake regularly and the system should catch it faster than three days. For the conversation with the engineer specifically, I'd acknowledge the mistake plainly — minimizing it wouldn't help them learn or trust my feedback — but immediately separate the mistake from their standing on the team: I'd point out that a silently-passing expectation misconfiguration is an easy, common error, that the three-day detection gap is on the team's monitoring, not on them, and that how they respond to this (owning it, helping fix it, contributing to the post-incident review) is what actually matters now. I'd also use this as a concrete teaching moment on expectation severity — a drop-type expectation silently removing rows is exactly the kind of mistake a fail-type or at least an alerting threshold on drop-count catches fast, so I'd pair them on implementing that guardrail themselves rather than having someone else fix it for them, which turns the incident into their learning rather than just their failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: First I'd make sure the engineer knows, quickly and clearly, that we're going to fix this together and figure out why it happened — not that I'm here to assign blame. Then we go handle the actual incident: figure out real impact, get a fix out, and reprocess the affected data. The post-incident review I'd run blameless and pointed at the real question, which isn't 'how did they make this mistake' — it's 'why did it take three days for anyone to notice a drop-type expectation silently removing rows,' because that's a monitoring gap the team owns, not something this one engineer should carry alone. In the actual conversation with them, I wouldn't pretend it wasn't a real mistake, because that doesn't help them learn and it doesn't feel honest to them either — but I'd be very clear that this specific kind of mistake is common, it's not a reflection of whether they belong on the team, and the three-day gap is on us collectively. Then I'd have them actually build the alerting threshold on expectation drop-counts themselves as the fix, because I want this to become the moment they learned something durable, not just the moment they got scared.
commonMistakes: Frames the post-incident conversation around blame rather than the systemic monitoring gap
Minimizes the mistake to make the engineer feel better, which undermines genuine learning and trust
Fixes the guardrail/monitoring gap without involving the engineer, missing the mentorship opportunity
Conflates handling the technical incident with handling the people conversation instead of treating them separately
keyPoints: Separates and sequences incident response from the mentorship conversation
Runs a blameless post-incident review focused on the systemic detection gap
Is honest about the mistake without minimizing it, while clearly separating it from the engineer's standing
Reframes the three-day detection delay as a team/monitoring gap, not solely an individual failure
Involves the engineer directly in building the fix/guardrail as a concrete learning opportunity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound incident-response sequencing and blameless review approach
Correctly reframes the detection gap as systemic, not purely individual
Handles the people conversation with honesty and genuine support
Turns the incident into a concrete mentorship/learning opportunity
