questions.title: Making the Case for Delta Sharing Over Custom Export Pipelines to Skeptical Stakeholders
questions.prompt: The team currently maintaining 12 custom export pipelines to external partners is skeptical of your proposal to migrate to Delta Sharing — they built those pipelines, know them well, and see the proposal as implying their work was wrong. Describe how you'd make the technical case while handling that underlying tension.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd address the underlying tension directly before getting into the technical comparison, because if the team hears 'migrate to Delta Sharing' as 'your work was wrong,' no amount of architecture diagrams will land — I'd acknowledge explicitly that those 12 pipelines were a reasonable, correct solution with the tools available when they were built, and that this isn't a retrospective judgment on the team, it's a response to tooling that didn't exist yet. Then I'd frame the proposal around what it does for them specifically, not just what it does for partners: fewer pipelines to get paged for at 2am, less credential-rotation toil, and freeing up their time for work with more visible impact than babysitting nightly exports — making the pitch about reducing their operational burden reframes the conversation from 'your solution is being replaced' to 'your job is about to get less tedious.' I'd also involve them directly in evaluating the migration rather than presenting it as a decision already made — having them pilot one of the simpler export pipelines' migration to Delta Sharing themselves means they're the ones generating the evidence (dropped pipeline-maintenance time, faster partner onboarding) rather than receiving someone else's conclusion, which tends to dissolve defensiveness because they're now co-authors of the case rather than subjects of it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I show a single diagram, I'd name the thing I think is actually making this hard: this can land like 'the thing you built and have maintained well is wrong,' and that's not what I mean, so I'd say so plainly — those pipelines were the right call with the tools that existed at the time. Then I'd pitch this in terms of what changes for them, not for the partners: fewer 2am pages, less time spent rotating credentials in twelve partners' buckets, more time for work that isn't just keeping twelve nightly jobs alive. And instead of presenting a finished recommendation, I'd ask them to pilot the migration on the simplest of the twelve pipelines themselves, because if they're the ones who see the pipeline-maintenance time actually drop, that's their evidence, not my argument — and that tends to turn a defensive conversation into a genuinely collaborative one.
commonMistakes: Leads with the technical architecture comparison without addressing the implied criticism of past work
Frames the pitch entirely around benefits to external partners, missing what's in it for the team being asked to change
Presents the migration as a decision already made rather than inviting the team to pilot and evaluate it themselves
Dismisses the team's skepticism as resistance to change rather than a legitimate reaction to feeling criticized
keyPoints: Directly and genuinely addresses the implied-criticism tension before the technical pitch
Validates that the original solution was reasonable given the tools available at the time
Reframes the pitch around reducing the team's own operational burden, not just partner benefit
Involves the skeptical team in piloting and generating their own evidence rather than presenting a finished decision
Treats the team as collaborators in evaluating the change, not subjects of it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Directly and genuinely addresses the underlying tension
Reframes the pitch around benefit to the team itself
Proposes involving the team in a real pilot rather than a top-down decision
Shows genuine respect for the prior work rather than dismissing it

questions.title: Resolving a Dispute Between Teams Over Databricks Workflows Cost Attribution
questions.prompt: Two data teams are in an escalating dispute: Team A insists their jobs are being over-charged because of cost attributed from a shared SQL warehouse that Team B's jobs also use heavily, and Team B insists the attribution is fair. Both have brought the dispute to you as the platform lead. Describe how you'd resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by getting both teams to agree on the facts before anyone argues about fairness, because a dispute like this often turns out to be about disagreement over what's actually happening, not disagreement over the policy once the data is clear. I'd pull the actual system-table data — per-query or per-task resource consumption on the shared warehouse, attributed to the identity that ran each query — and show both teams the same breakdown, rather than let the conversation stay anecdotal ('we think we're being over-charged'). If the current attribution model is a flat/even split of the shared warehouse's cost rather than usage-proportional, I'd point out that's very likely the real issue regardless of which team raised it, since an even split systematically overcharges the lighter user and undercharges the heavier one, and I'd propose switching to usage-proportional attribution as a policy fix that benefits accuracy generally, not as a ruling in favor of either team specifically — which matters for how it's received, since 'the platform is fixing a methodology flaw' lands very differently than 'the platform sided with Team A.' I'd also use the moment to ask both teams whether the shared warehouse itself is still the right setup, since a dispute like this sometimes signals that one team has grown enough to warrant its own dedicated compute, which would remove the shared-attribution problem at its root rather than just getting better at measuring it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to get both teams looking at the same real numbers instead of arguing from impressions. I'd pull the actual per-query resource consumption on the shared warehouse from the system tables, attributed by who ran what, and put that in front of both teams together. In my experience, when the attribution model is an even split of a shared resource rather than usage-proportional, that's very often the actual problem, and it's worth checking before assuming either team is wrong or acting in bad faith. If that's what I find, I'd propose fixing the attribution methodology itself rather than ruling for one side — I want this to land as 'we found a flaw in how we measure this for everyone,' not as me picking a winner, because the second version just sets up the next dispute. And I'd use this as a prompt to ask a bigger question: if these two teams are big enough to be fighting over a shared warehouse's bill, maybe the real fix is giving the heavier one its own dedicated compute so there's nothing left to share and argue about.
commonMistakes: Tries to adjudicate the dispute based on each team's narrative without pulling the actual usage data
Picks a side between the two teams rather than focusing on the fairness of the underlying attribution methodology
Fixes the immediate dispute without considering whether the shared-resource setup itself should change
Frames the resolution as 'who was right' instead of 'what does the data show and how do we measure this better going forward'
keyPoints: Grounds the resolution in actual system-table usage data rather than each team's narrative
Identifies even-split vs. usage-proportional attribution as the likely real issue
Frames the fix as a methodology correction benefiting everyone, not a ruling favoring one team
Considers whether the shared-resource setup itself should change given the dispute
Handles the political dimension (how the resolution is perceived) as carefully as the technical one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the resolution in real usage data
Correctly diagnoses likely even-split attribution flaw
Frames the fix as a methodology correction, not a ruling for one side
Considers the deeper structural fix (dedicated compute) beyond the immediate dispute

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Team Requesting Broad Unity Catalog Admin Access
questions.prompt: A data science team's lead is requesting account-level or metastore-level admin access for their whole team, arguing it would let them move faster without waiting on the platform team for routine grants. You believe this violates least-privilege and would create real risk. Describe how you'd push back.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by taking their actual complaint seriously rather than just citing the policy — 'we're slow for routine grants' is a legitimate problem even if the proposed fix is wrong, and dismissing the request without addressing the underlying friction just pushes them toward requesting the same broad access again later, or worse, finding a workaround outside of governance entirely. So I'd ask specifically what 'routine grants' they're waiting on most often, and in most cases it turns out to be a narrow, repeated pattern — granting SELECT on new tables within their own team's schema, or adding members to their own team's group — which can be solved with a much narrower delegation: making them owners of their own schema (so they can grant within it without needing account-level admin) or delegating a specific, scoped admin role limited to their catalog. I'd be direct about why metastore/account-level admin specifically is the wrong fix regardless of the real friction behind the request: that scope of access can read, alter, or drop any team's data and grants across the whole organization, which is a blast radius wildly disproportionate to 'we want to add our own team members faster,' and a single compromised credential or mistake at that scope affects everyone, not just their team. I'd present the scoped-ownership alternative as actually solving their stated problem, not as a consolation prize, and I'd commit to a concrete SLA improvement on any residual grant requests that do need to go through the platform team, so the tradeoff is visibly fair rather than 'you don't get what you asked for and you still wait.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say no and cite least-privilege — that doesn't fix their actual problem, it just tells them to be slower in a different way. I'd dig into what specifically they're waiting on us for, and almost always it's something narrow and repeated, like granting access on their own new tables or adding their own team members to a group. That's solvable without giving them the keys to everyone else's data — making them schema owners within their own catalog, or giving them a scoped admin role limited to just their catalog, gets them the speed they actually want. Then I'd be very direct about why I'm saying no to the broader ask specifically: account-level admin can touch every team's data and every team's grants, and that's a wildly bigger blast radius than the problem they described, so one mistake or one compromised account at that level is everyone's incident, not just theirs. I'd make sure the scoped alternative isn't presented as a downgrade — it's the thing that actually solves what they asked for — and I'd commit to tightening our SLA on whatever grant requests still do need to come through us, so they're not just hearing 'no.'
commonMistakes: Refuses the request by citing policy without addressing the real operational friction behind it
Grants the broad access to avoid the uncomfortable conversation
Doesn't propose a concrete, narrower alternative that actually solves the team's stated problem
Frames the pushback purely in terms of 'no' rather than explaining the specific, disproportionate blast radius
keyPoints: Takes the underlying operational friction seriously rather than dismissing the request outright
Investigates the specific, usually narrow pattern driving the request
Proposes a concrete, scoped alternative (schema ownership, limited admin role) that solves the real problem
Clearly explains why the broad access is disproportionate to the stated need
Offers a fair tradeoff (SLA commitment) rather than leaving the team with only a refusal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes the underlying friction seriously rather than dismissing it
Proposes a concrete, scoped alternative solving the real problem
Clearly explains the security rationale for refusing broad access
Offers a fair, concrete tradeoff rather than a bare refusal

questions.title: Convincing Leadership to Fund an Auto Loader Migration from Legacy Batch Ingestion
questions.prompt: Your team's current ingestion is a brittle, scheduled batch job that's increasingly missing its SLA as data volume grows, and you want to migrate it to Auto Loader. Leadership sees this as 'if it's not fully broken, why spend a quarter rebuilding it.' Describe how you'd make the case.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd avoid making the case in purely technical terms ('Auto Loader is architecturally better') and instead quantify the actual cost of the status quo in terms leadership already tracks: how many SLA misses happened last quarter, what each one cost in downstream impact (a delayed report, a blocked decision, an on-call engineer's weekend), and the trend line showing it's getting worse as volume grows, not stable — 'not fully broken' is a much weaker argument once it's clear it's on a trajectory toward being fully broken, just not there yet. I'd then scope the migration as narrowly as possible to make it a low-risk ask rather than 'a quarter rebuilding it' — proposing to migrate the single highest-volume or most SLA-sensitive source first, in parallel with the existing batch job still running as a safety net, so leadership isn't being asked to bet the quarter on an all-or-nothing rewrite, and the first migrated source becomes concrete proof (measured latency improvement, measured cost difference) for the rest. I'd also translate the benefit into what leadership cares about directly: faster data availability for whatever downstream decision depends on it, reduced on-call burden (fewer 3am pages for a stuck batch job), and in many cases a real cost reduction from not running full-volume batch jobs on a fixed schedule regardless of actual new-data volume. I'd present it as a phased, de-risked proposal with a clear checkpoint to continue or stop after the first migrated source, not as a single big commitment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't open with 'Auto Loader is the better architecture' — that's not the argument that moves leadership. I'd open with what the current batch job is actually costing us: how many SLA misses, what happened downstream each time, and the fact that the trend is getting worse as volume grows, not flat — so 'it's not fully broken yet' is really 'it's on a path to being fully broken, and here's the data showing the slope.' Then I'd scope the ask small on purpose: migrate just the worst-offending source first, keep the old batch job running in parallel as a safety net, and treat that as a cheap, low-risk proof point rather than asking for a quarter up front. Once that first migration shows a measurable latency or cost improvement, I have real evidence instead of a projection to make the case for the rest, and leadership is approving the next phase based on something that actually happened, not a promise.
commonMistakes: Pitches the migration on architectural merits alone instead of quantifying the real cost of the current system
Asks for the full migration as one large, high-risk commitment instead of a phased, de-risked rollout
Doesn't propose keeping the legacy job running in parallel as a safety net during the transition
Fails to translate the benefit into terms leadership already tracks (SLA impact, on-call burden, cost trend)
keyPoints: Quantifies the real cost and worsening trend of the status quo rather than arguing on architecture alone
Proposes a narrowly-scoped, low-risk first phase rather than a full upfront rewrite
Keeps the legacy system running in parallel as a safety net during migration
Uses the first phase's measured results as evidence for the broader migration
Translates technical benefit into terms leadership already tracks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quantifies the real cost/trend of the status quo
Proposes a phased, de-risked migration approach
Proposes a safety-net parallel-run strategy
Translates the benefit into leadership-relevant terms

questions.title: Handling a Junior Engineer's Costly Uncontrolled Cluster in Databricks Workflows
questions.prompt: A junior engineer configured a Databricks Workflow job without a cluster policy cap, and it auto-scaled to a very large, expensive cluster size over a weekend before anyone noticed, generating a cost spike finance is now asking about. Describe how you'd handle the engineer, the immediate cost conversation with finance, and the systemic fix.
questions.modelAnswer: With finance, I'd be direct and own it at the team level rather than individualizing blame to the engineer in that conversation: explain exactly what happened mechanically (a job without a cluster policy cap scaled up under unexpectedly high load over an unmonitored weekend), what it cost, and specifically what's changing so this particular failure mode can't recur — finance generally wants a credible fix more than a name to blame, and naming the individual engineer in that conversation does nothing for them while potentially damaging the engineer unfairly for a gap that was really the platform's. With the engineer, separately, I'd make sure they understand this wasn't really their fault in the way they probably fear — the absence of a cluster policy cap on new jobs by default is a platform gap, and expecting every engineer, especially a junior one, to manually remember to configure a cost ceiling on every job they create is not a reliable control; I'd be clear that I don't want them to walk away from this afraid to create or modify jobs, which is a worse long-term outcome than the cost spike itself. The systemic fix is making the safe behavior the default rather than relying on anyone remembering: enforce a mandatory cluster policy cap on max cluster size for all job creation going forward via policy, not documentation or a reminder in onboarding, so this specific failure mode becomes structurally impossible rather than dependent on individual vigilance, and I'd audit existing jobs for the same gap rather than assuming this was an isolated case.
questions.professionalAnswer: With finance, I'd keep this at the team level — here's mechanically what happened, here's what it cost, here's the specific policy change going into effect so this exact thing can't happen again. I wouldn't bring the individual engineer's name into that conversation; it doesn't help finance and it's not really fair, because the real gap is that we didn't have a mandatory cluster size cap on job creation, and expecting every engineer to remember to set one manually isn't a real control. With the engineer, I'd make sure they know this one's on the platform, not on them — I don't want someone junior walking away from this afraid to touch job configuration, because that's a worse outcome for the team than one cost spike. The actual fix is making the safe default structural: a mandatory cluster policy cap enforced at job creation, not a wiki page asking people to remember, and I'd go audit other existing jobs for the same gap rather than assume this was a one-off.
commonMistakes: Names or blames the individual engineer in the conversation with finance
Treats the incident as the engineer's personal failure rather than identifying the missing structural control
Fixes only this specific job instead of auditing for and closing the same gap across other existing jobs
Leaves the engineer feeling blamed in a way that damages their confidence going forward
keyPoints: Handles the finance conversation at the team/systemic level, not by naming the individual engineer
Correctly identifies the missing cluster policy cap as a platform gap, not an individual failure
Protects the junior engineer's confidence and standing in the direct conversation with them
Proposes a structural fix (mandatory policy) rather than relying on individual vigilance
Proactively audits other existing jobs for the same gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Handles the finance conversation appropriately without individualizing blame
Correctly reframes the root cause as a systemic/platform gap
Handles the engineer conversation with genuine support
Proposes a durable structural fix plus a proactive audit

questions.title: Negotiating a Shared SLA for a Lakeflow Pipeline Between Platform and Data Science
questions.prompt: The platform team built and now maintains a shared Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that a data science team depends on heavily, but ownership of its SLA has never been formally agreed — when it breaks, both teams assume the other is responsible for the fix, and incidents drag on while that gets sorted out. Describe how you'd negotiate a clear, working agreement between the two teams.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by getting both teams to separate 'who built it' from 'who's on call for it,' because the ambiguity usually comes from assuming those are the same question when they don't have to be — the platform team may have built the pipeline and understands its internals best, but that doesn't automatically make them responsible for every incident if the actual failure mode is a data-science-side expectation or transformation they added on top. I'd propose a concrete RACI split by failure type rather than a single blanket owner: platform team owns infrastructure-level failures (cluster/compute issues, Unity Catalog access problems, Lakeflow runtime errors), data science team owns logic-level failures (a transformation they wrote producing wrong results, an expectation they added firing incorrectly), and both teams agree on a triage protocol for the ambiguous cases — whoever gets paged first does a 10-minute initial triage to classify which bucket it's in, then routes to the owning team, rather than debating ownership while the pipeline stays broken. I'd document this as an actual written agreement both team leads sign off on, with a defined SLA (time to triage, time to resolution per severity) attached to each bucket, and I'd build in a quarterly review of real incidents against the agreement, because the first version of a RACI split like this is never perfect and needs to be corrected based on what actually happened rather than argued about in the abstract.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core fix is separating 'who built this' from 'who's on call for this' — those got conflated, which is why every incident turns into a debate instead of a fix. I'd propose splitting ownership by failure type instead of by team: platform owns infrastructure and runtime failures, data science owns the logic and expectations they wrote on top, and for the genuinely ambiguous cases, whoever gets paged does a quick triage first and routes it, instead of arguing about whose incident it is while it's still broken. I'd get this written down and signed off by both team leads with actual SLA numbers attached, not just a verbal understanding, because verbal understandings are exactly what got us here. And I'd build in a regular review of how it's actually playing out against real incidents, because the first split is a reasonable guess, not a perfect answer, and it should get corrected based on what actually happens.
commonMistakes: Assumes the team that built the pipeline is automatically responsible for every incident regardless of failure type
Proposes a verbal or informal understanding instead of a documented, signed-off agreement with concrete SLA terms
Doesn't define a triage protocol for ambiguous cases, leaving room for the same ownership debate to recur
Treats the first version of the agreement as final rather than building in a review/correction cycle
keyPoints: Separates 'who built it' from 'who's on call for it' as the core reframing
Proposes ownership split by failure type rather than by a single blanket owner
Defines a concrete triage protocol for ambiguous incidents
Documents the agreement formally with concrete SLA terms, not a verbal understanding
Builds in a periodic review to correct the agreement based on real incident history

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reframes ownership as separate from who built the system
Proposes a sound failure-type-based ownership split
Defines a concrete triage protocol for ambiguous cases
Proposes formal documentation and a review cycle

questions.title: Communicating a Scope Cut on a Unity Catalog Migration Under Deadline Pressure
questions.prompt: You're leading a large Unity Catalog migration with a hard deadline tied to a legacy system's planned decommission. Three weeks before the deadline, it's clear the fine-grained row-level security portion of the migration won't be ready in time, though the core table migration will be. Describe how you'd communicate this scope cut to stakeholders.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd surface this the moment it became clear, not at the deadline, because stakeholders losing three weeks of reaction time to a problem I sat on is a far worse outcome than the scope cut itself, and it damages trust in every future estimate I give. I'd frame the communication around what's actually at risk if we force the full scope: either slipping the hard deadline, which has its own real cost since the legacy system's decommission is presumably tied to something else (a contract, a cost saving, another team's dependency), or shipping the row-level security logic rushed and under-tested, which given that it's a security control is a worse risk than being late. I'd present a concrete proposal, not just the bad news: ship the core table migration on schedule, since that's the piece actually gating the legacy decommission, and treat row-level security as a fast-follow with a committed date and an interim compensating control for the gap — for example, keeping the subset of currently-restricted data out of the migrated catalog until its masking/filtering logic is ready, rather than migrating it unprotected. I'd be explicit about why I'm recommending this split rather than just reporting that we're behind: the alternative of either slipping everything or shipping a rushed security control are both worse than this option, and I'd want stakeholders to have that reasoning, not just the conclusion, so they can push back if they see a constraint I'm missing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go to stakeholders as soon as I knew, not at the deadline — three weeks of lead time to react is worth a lot more than me hoping it resolves itself. I wouldn't just say 'we're behind' — I'd bring a specific recommendation: ship the core table migration on time, since that's what's actually gating the legacy decommission, and treat the row-level security piece as a committed fast-follow, with the sensitive subset of data held back from the migrated catalog until that's ready rather than exposing it unprotected just to hit the date. I'd walk through why I think that's better than the alternatives — slipping the whole deadline, or rushing a security control that really shouldn't be rushed — so stakeholders are seeing my reasoning, not just a status update, and have a real chance to tell me if I'm missing something on their end.
commonMistakes: Waits until close to the deadline to surface the risk instead of raising it as soon as it became clear
Reports the problem without a concrete recommendation for how to handle it
Proposes migrating the sensitive data without its row-level security protections just to hit the date
Presents the scope cut as a unilateral decision rather than explaining the reasoning so stakeholders can weigh in
keyPoints: Surfaces the risk as early as possible, not near the deadline
Brings a concrete recommendation, not just a status update
Proposes a compensating control (holding back unprotected sensitive data) rather than shipping security gaps to hit the date
Explains the reasoning behind the recommended tradeoff, inviting stakeholder input
Separates what's actually gating the hard deadline (core migration) from what can safely fast-follow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Surfaces the issue early with appropriate urgency
Brings a concrete, well-reasoned recommendation
Proposes a safe compensating control rather than shipping a security gap
Communicates reasoning transparently, inviting stakeholder input

questions.title: Giving Difficult Feedback to a Peer Architect Over a Unity Catalog Security Gap
questions.prompt: A fellow senior architect, a peer rather than someone you manage, designed a Unity Catalog access model for a new business domain that you've discovered has a real security gap — a broad grant at the catalog level that unintentionally exposes a PII schema to a much wider group than intended. They're well-respected and somewhat defensive about their designs. Describe how you'd raise this.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise it privately and promptly rather than in a group setting or a design review where being corrected publicly would put them in a defensive position before we've even discussed the substance — a real security gap needs to get fixed quickly, and the fastest path to that is a conversation where they're not also managing how it looks to others while processing the finding. I'd lead with the specific, concrete evidence rather than a general critique: show the actual grant hierarchy and exactly which broader group inherits access to the PII schema because of the catalog-level grant, phrased as 'I think I'm seeing something and want to check my understanding' rather than 'your design has a flaw,' which keeps the conversation collaborative rather than adversarial even when the finding itself is unambiguous. I'd also assume competence rather than carelessness — catalog-level grants interacting unexpectedly with a later-added restricted schema is an easy, common mistake, not a sign they didn't think it through, and I'd say that plainly, because a well-respected peer who feels accused of incompetence is far more likely to get defensive about the fix than one who feels like a colleague caught a subtle interaction together with them. Once we agree on the finding, I'd let them own the fix and the communication about it rather than taking over, since it's their design and their credibility that benefits from fixing it themselves rather than visibly being corrected by someone else — my job here is to make sure the gap closes quickly and that they don't feel undermined in the process, both of which matter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go to them directly and privately, not in a design review where they'd have an audience while absorbing this, because the quickest path to actually closing a security gap is a conversation that stays about the problem, not about how it looks. I'd bring the specific evidence — here's the grant, here's exactly which group inherits access to the PII schema because of it — and frame it as 'I want to check my understanding of this' rather than 'you missed something,' because that's genuinely true, I am checking my understanding, and it also keeps the door open if I'm somehow wrong. I'd also say plainly that this is an easy mistake, not a careless one, because a catalog-level grant quietly covering a schema added later is exactly the kind of interaction that's hard to see in advance. And once we're aligned on the finding, I'd let them drive the fix and however they want to communicate it to their team, because this should land as them catching and closing a gap, not as me correcting them.
commonMistakes: Raises the issue in a group setting or design review instead of privately first
Frames the feedback as a critique of competence rather than evidence-based and collaborative
Takes over the fix and the communication about it instead of letting the peer own their own correction
Delays raising it to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, leaving a real security gap open longer than necessary
keyPoints: Raises the issue privately and promptly, not in a public or group setting
Leads with specific, concrete evidence framed collaboratively rather than as an accusation
Assumes competence and frames the mistake as common/easy rather than careless
Lets the peer own the fix and its communication rather than taking over
Balances urgency (closing the real security gap quickly) with respect for the peer's standing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Chooses an appropriately private, prompt setting for the conversation
Frames the feedback with specific evidence and a collaborative tone
Assumes competence rather than framing it as a careless error
Lets the peer own the fix while ensuring the gap closes promptly

questions.title: Designing a Petabyte-Scale Telemetry Ingestion Path with Zerobus
questions.prompt: Your organization needs to ingest IoT telemetry at genuinely massive scale -- potentially petabytes per day, from thousands of concurrent devices -- directly into the lakehouse, with the lakehouse as the sole destination. Design the ingestion approach using Zerobus Ingest, explain the specific engineering properties that let it scale this way, and identify the one real limitation you'd need to architect around.
questions.modelAnswer:
At this scale, I'd use Zerobus Ingest specifically because the lakehouse is the sole destination -- that's exactly the case it eliminates a message bus for, removing the Kafka-plus-Structured-Streaming hop entirely and letting devices write straight to a target Delta table via the Zerobus SDK, authenticated with OAuth and validated against the table schema on each write.

Three specific engineering properties are why this scales to genuinely massive volumes rather than just moderate ones. First, dynamic partitioning: ordering is guaranteed at the stream connection level rather than a fixed partition level, so compute can be added and removed elastically as load changes, rather than being bound to a partition count decided up front. Second, Zeroparser, an open-sourced, single-pass, zero-allocation Rust protobuf decoder sustaining roughly 1 GB/sec per CPU core with fully dynamic descriptors -- no compile-time schema is required, which matters when thousands of devices might have slightly different field sets. Third, a latency-optimized write-ahead log that keeps clients lean: push, get an acknowledgment, free the buffer -- the same low-latency, durable handoff that historically made teams choose Kafka, without requiring Kafka. Databricks' own published benchmark against NASA's real NEOWISE dataset -- 1 petabyte in 24 hours, 12 GB/s sustained, 12 million rows per second, into a single table, with zero pre-configuration -- is a real, not synthetic, proof point for designing at this scale.

The one real limitation I'd architect around today: Zerobus does not natively support Change Data Feed on its target table. If any downstream consumer at this scale needs CDF -- for example, syncing curated telemetry into an operational database -- I'd plan for the documented workaround from day one: a second streaming hop that reads the Zerobus target table and writes it into a CDF-enabled copy, rather than discovering this gap after the ingestion path is already in production.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd design this around Zerobus from the start, precisely because the lakehouse is the only destination -- that's its exact use case, removing the message-bus hop entirely so devices write straight into a Delta table through the SDK.

What actually lets it hold up at petabyte scale is three specific engineering choices: dynamic partitioning that scales elastically at the connection level instead of a fixed partition count; Zeroparser, their open-sourced Rust protobuf decoder that's fast and doesn't need a compile-time schema, which matters with thousands of slightly different device payloads; and a lean write-ahead log that gives you the same durable, low-latency guarantee Kafka is known for, without needing Kafka. Their own NEOWISE benchmark against real NASA telescope data -- a petabyte in 24 hours at 12 GB/s -- is the real proof point I'd cite, since it's genuine production-shaped data, not a synthetic test.

The one thing I'd flag to the team up front, not after we've built everything: Zerobus doesn't give you native Change Data Feed on the table it writes to. If anything downstream needs CDF -- say, syncing curated data into Lakebase -- I'd build the second-hop workaround (reading the Zerobus table and writing a CDF-enabled copy) into the architecture from day one, instead of treating it as a surprise gap we discover in production.
questions.example:
# Architecture at scale:
# Thousands of devices --[Zerobus SDK, OAuth]--> Delta target table (Bronze)
#   --[streaming hop, since Zerobus has no native CDF]--> CDF-enabled copy
#   --[continuous sync]--> Lakebase, for any operational consumer
# Benchmark reference: 1PB/24hr, 12GB/s sustained, 12M rows/sec, NEOWISE dataset
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a Kafka-plus-Structured-Streaming design out of habit, ignoring that the lakehouse-only destination is exactly Zerobus's use case
Citing generic 'it's fast' claims instead of the three specific engineering properties (dynamic partitioning, Zeroparser, the WAL)
Not identifying the CDF limitation as something to architect around proactively
Treating the NEOWISE benchmark as synthetic or irrelevant, rather than real production-shaped proof
keyPoints: Zerobus eliminates the message-bus hop when the lakehouse is the sole destination
Scales via dynamic partitioning, the Zeroparser Rust decoder, and a latency-optimized WAL
Real benchmark: 1PB/24hr, 12GB/s sustained, 12M rows/sec on real NASA NEOWISE data
The real limitation to architect around: no native CDF, requiring a second streaming hop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the Zerobus-based ingestion architecture
Correctly explains all three scaling engineering properties
Cites the real benchmark accurately
Proactively identifies and architects around the CDF limitation
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Stateful Real-Time Mode Pipeline Without a Separate Streaming Engine
questions.prompt: You need to build a sub-second operational pipeline that counts how many connected devices are currently active within each of several monitored zones, writing live counts to an operational database, without introducing a separate engine like Apache Flink. Design this using Real-Time Mode (RTM) for Spark Declarative Pipelines, including how you'd handle the fact that a device leaving a zone produces no explicit 'left' event.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is exactly the use case Real-Time Mode exists for: sub-second, in-the-loop decisions, without standing up Flink as a second engine alongside the batch pipeline. I'd build it with pyspark.pipelines (dp), using two primitives. First, declare an external sink -- RTM is built for operational delivery, so results write straight to an operational system (Lakebase, in this case) via dp.create_sink, rather than landing in an analytical table. Second, define an @dp.update_flow targeting that sink, with the RTM switch set in its spark_conf: pipelines.trigger set to 'RealTime', combined with the pipeline-level real-time-mode flag, which moves the flow onto the continuous engine. The trigger.interval here is not a micro-batch size -- it only governs how often state and offsets get checkpointed, since in RTM the underlying execution is a long-running continuous process, not discrete micro-batches.

Counting active devices per zone requires state, so I'd implement this as a single keyed stateful operator using the Arbitrary Stateful Processing API, transformWithState, through a StatefulProcessor keyed by zone. It would hold a MapState mapping each device id to its last-seen timestamp, refreshed on every incoming position. To handle a device leaving a zone with no explicit event -- there's genuinely nothing to react to -- I'd use staleness-based eviction: a recurring processing-time timer sweeps the MapState, evicting any device not seen within a short TTL, and re-emits the refreshed count so a zone that empties naturally clears itself. Critically, I'd register that sweep timer idempotently -- only arming a new timer if one isn't already pending in a ValueState -- because handleInputRows fires once per incoming row in RTM, and naively arming a timer on every row would pile up thousands of redundant timers very quickly.

The entire design stays inside one shuffle and one stateful operator on the real-time path (groupBy(zone).transformWithState(...)), which is deliberately the kind of design RTM is strong at -- a single hop, not a chain of separate stateful stages.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd reach for RTM here precisely because this is the use case it was built to remove Flink for. The shape is two pieces: declare an external sink, in this case straight to Lakebase since RTM is meant for operational delivery, and write an @dp.update_flow targeting it with pipelines.trigger set to RealTime in its spark_conf -- that's the actual switch onto the continuous engine. I'd make sure the team understands trigger.interval here isn't a batch size, it just controls checkpoint cadence, since RTM runs as a long-running continuous process underneath.

For the actual counting logic, since this needs real state, I'd use transformWithState with a StatefulProcessor keyed by zone, holding a MapState of device-to-last-seen-time. The genuinely tricky part is handling a device silently leaving a zone -- there's no 'left' event at all, so I'd handle that with a TTL-based sweep timer that evicts anything not seen recently and re-emits the count. And I'd be careful to only register one pending sweep timer at a time, since RTM calls the handler once per row, and naively arming a new timer every row would be a real bug that piles up thousands of stale timers. The whole thing stays as one shuffle, one stateful operator -- that's intentional, since that's exactly the shape RTM is designed to handle well.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Flink or another separate engine out of habit instead of RTM
Treating pipelines.trigger.interval as a micro-batch size rather than a checkpoint cadence
Reacting to an explicit 'left zone' event that doesn't actually exist, instead of staleness-based eviction
Registering a new timer on every incoming row, causing timer buildup instead of idempotent registration
Splitting the counting logic across multiple stateful operators instead of one keyed operator in a single shuffle
keyPoints: RTM is built for exactly this: sub-second, in-the-loop decisions, without a separate engine like Flink
dp.create_sink plus @dp.update_flow with pipelines.trigger: RealTime is the complete authoring shape
trigger.interval governs checkpoint cadence, not batch size, under RTM
transformWithState with staleness-based eviction and idempotent timers handles state with no explicit 'left' event

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the sink + update_flow RTM authoring shape
Correctly explains trigger.interval's actual role under RTM
Correctly designs the stateful transformWithState solution
Correctly identifies staleness-based eviction and idempotent timer registration
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Building a Production Document Intelligence Pipeline with Agent Bricks
questions.prompt: Your organization receives thousands of vendor invoices as PDFs weekly, currently unqueryable and manually reviewed. Design a production pipeline using Agent Bricks' Document Intelligence pattern to turn these into governed, structured Delta tables, including the medallion layers, the orchestration, and what becomes possible once this data is structured.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd build this as the same medallion pattern used everywhere else in this course, applied to unstructured PDFs instead of structured events. Bronze: Auto Loader ingests raw invoice PDF bytes from a Unity Catalog Volume as they land, exactly the ingestion pattern from earlier in this course. Silver: an incremental streaming table calls ai_parse_document against the Bronze layer, extracting raw text, table structure, and layout from each PDF -- turning an opaque file into usable content, but not yet structured fields. Gold: a second incremental streaming table calls ai_extract against the Silver layer with a declared schema (invoice number, vendor name, line-item totals, due date), pulling out the specific typed columns the business actually needs to query.

Rather than hand-writing all three layers from scratch, I'd consider using the 'Use Agent' authoring shortcut to generate a first-draft Declarative Pipeline from a natural-language description of the desired schema, then review and refine the generated pyspark.pipelines code directly, the same review discipline as reviewing a Lakeflow Designer output.

For orchestration, I'd wire this into a Lakeflow Job with the standard three-task reference pattern: an Ingest task (Auto Loader into Bronze), a Parse and Extract task (the Declarative Pipeline building Silver and Gold, depending on Ingest succeeding), and a Refresh Dashboard task depending on Parse and Extract succeeding, so a downstream BI report only refreshes once Gold is actually current -- the same fan-out dependency pattern taught in Chapter 4.

Once invoice data is structured and governed in Gold, five real categories of use case open up: an AI agent or chatbot can query invoice data directly via SQL instead of re-parsing a PDF on every question; the data becomes searchable and filterable in ways raw PDF text never was; it joins cleanly with the rest of the lakehouse's structured data (vendor master data, GL postings) under the same Unity Catalog governance; and a BI dashboard can report directly against Gold instead of requiring manual review of individual PDFs.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this as a completely standard medallion build, just with an unusual Bronze source. Auto Loader brings the raw PDFs into Bronze from a volume like always. Silver is where ai_parse_document turns each PDF into usable parsed content -- text, tables, layout -- as an incremental streaming table. Gold is where ai_extract pulls the actual fields we care about -- invoice number, vendor, line items, due date -- against a schema we declare, also incremental.

For the actual authoring, I might start with the 'Use Agent' shortcut to generate a first pass of the pipeline from a plain description of what we want extracted, then review that generated code the same way I'd review any new pipeline before it goes to production -- it's real pyspark.pipelines code, not a black box.

For orchestration I'd use the standard three-task Lakeflow Job pattern: Ingest, then Parse and Extract once Ingest succeeds, then Refresh Dashboard once Parse and Extract succeeds -- the same fan-out dependency structure we'd use for any other pipeline. And the real payoff once this is live: instead of someone manually opening a PDF to answer 'what's our total spend with this vendor this quarter,' that's just a SQL query against the Gold table now, and it can feed a dashboard, a chatbot, or a search tool directly.
questions.example:
-- Gold layer, once built:
SELECT vendor_name, SUM(line_item_total) AS total_spend
FROM gold.invoices
WHERE invoice_date >= '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY vendor_name
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
-- Previously required manually opening PDFs one at a time.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a new architecture rather than the same medallion pattern applied to a new source type
Running ai_extract before ai_parse_document, or skipping the Silver layer entirely
Building the pipeline as a one-off batch job instead of an incremental streaming pattern that handles new invoices automatically
Missing the orchestration layer entirely and not chaining dashboard refresh to pipeline completion
Not naming the concrete downstream use cases this structured data actually unlocks
keyPoints: Bronze (raw PDF bytes via Auto Loader), Silver (ai_parse_document), Gold (ai_extract against a declared schema)
'Use Agent' can generate a first-draft pipeline as real, reviewable pyspark.pipelines code
Standard three-task Lakeflow Job orchestration: Ingest -> Parse and Extract -> Refresh Dashboard
Unlocks chatbots/agents, search, unified analytics, and dashboards against previously unqueryable documents

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the Bronze/Silver/Gold medallion layers for documents
Correctly describes the three-task orchestration pattern
Mentions the 'Use Agent' authoring shortcut and review discipline
Names concrete, realistic downstream use cases this unlocks
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Why Genie ZeroOps Must Run Inside the Platform to Verify a Fix Safely
questions.prompt: A VP asks why your team can't just build an internal tool using a generic external coding agent, with API credentials to your Databricks workspace, to replicate what Genie ZeroOps does -- detecting and fixing broken pipelines automatically. Walk through ZeroOps's full four-step process, and explain specifically why the Verify step is the one that an externally-hosted agent cannot safely replicate, even with full API access.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd walk through all four steps, because the VP's question is really about one specific step, and showing the other three first makes clear that API access alone would actually get you reasonably far on three of them -- just not the fourth. Detect requires continuous access to platform observability, including catching silent failures that show up in data quality metrics before anything throws an actual error; an external agent with API access could plausibly poll logs and metrics, though it would likely choke on very large Spark logs the way generic coding agents are known to. Assess requires the full Unity Catalog lineage dependency graph to trace a failure back to a code bug, an upstream schema change, or bad data introduced elsewhere; again, with sufficient API access, an external tool could query that lineage data. Remediate is agentic code generation using the team's real development workflow (GitHub PRs, Jira tickets) as context -- also plausible for an external tool with the right integrations.

Verify is where this breaks down architecturally, not just practically. Verification means testing the proposed fix against real production data in an isolated environment, and that's precisely the step where production data can't be freely handed to an external tool -- either you deny the agent real data access, in which case it can't actually verify anything meaningful, or you grant real access, in which case you've created a genuine risk of real side effects against production during the 'test.' ZeroOps solves this specifically because it's part of the Databricks Data + AI Platform itself: its sandbox uses zero-copy clones -- a table clone built from metadata, not duplicated data -- combined with scoped permissions and network isolation, so the proposed fix runs against a true copy of production data without ever touching production, and nothing is applied until a human approves it. An externally-hosted agent, no matter how good its credentials are, cannot replicate zero-copy cloning and network-isolated sandboxing without effectively becoming part of the platform's own storage and compute layer -- which is exactly what 'build an external tool' is trying to avoid building in the first place.

The honest answer to the VP: you could plausibly approximate three of the four ZeroOps steps with enough engineering effort and API access, but the fourth step, Verify, is specifically the one requiring platform-native sandboxing that an external tool structurally cannot provide without rebuilding a meaningful chunk of what Databricks already built.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd actually concede ground on three of the four steps before making the real point, because it's more convincing that way. Detect, Assess, and Remediate -- with enough API access and engineering effort, an external tool could get reasonably close: poll observability data, query Unity Catalog lineage, generate a fix using GitHub/Jira context. I wouldn't pretend those are impossible for an external tool to approximate.

Verify is where I'd draw the real line. Verifying a fix means testing it against actual production data in an isolated environment, and that's exactly the step where handing an external tool real production data access is genuinely dangerous -- either it doesn't get real access and can't actually verify anything, or it does get real access and now has the ability to cause real side effects during what's supposed to be a safe test. ZeroOps gets around this because it's built into the platform itself -- it uses zero-copy clones, which are metadata-based table clones, not real data duplication, plus scoped permissions and network isolation, so the fix runs against a real copy of production data that can never reach production itself, and nothing ships without a human approving it.

So my answer to the VP would be: building the first three steps externally is a real, if expensive, possibility. Building the fourth safely means either accepting real risk to production data, or essentially rebuilding Databricks' own sandboxing and zero-copy clone infrastructure from scratch -- at which point you haven't actually avoided building a platform-native tool, you've just built a worse version of one.
questions.example:
# What an external tool CAN plausibly approximate:
# Detect (poll logs/metrics), Assess (query lineage via API), Remediate (generate a PR)
# What it structurally cannot replicate without becoming platform-native:
# Verify -- zero-copy clone + scoped permissions + network isolation, tested against
# real data with zero risk to production, approved by a human before anything applies
commonMistakes: Claiming none of ZeroOps's four steps could ever be approximated externally, which overstates the case
Missing that the real architectural barrier is specifically the Verify step, not the whole process generically
Not naming zero-copy cloning, scoped permissions, and network isolation as the specific sandbox mechanisms
Treating 'API access to Databricks' as equivalent to 'running inside the platform's governed sandbox'
keyPoints: Detect, Assess, and Remediate could plausibly be approximated by a well-integrated external tool
Verify is the step that genuinely requires platform-native sandboxing
Zero-copy clones, scoped permissions, and network isolation are the concrete mechanisms that make safe verification possible
Replicating Verify externally means either real production risk or rebuilding platform-native infrastructure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly walks through all four ZeroOps steps
Honestly assesses which steps an external tool could plausibly approximate
Correctly and specifically explains why Verify cannot be safely replicated externally
Clear, accurate overall explanation
